Update and presentation from representatives for the Department of Transportation on the final design and construction plans for enhancements to the Grand Army Plaza area.
There will be no changes to the design. The parking protected bike lane on Plaza St will not move forward at this time.
The 4 primary goals in the current project 1)Shorten Pedestrial Crossings 2)Add Pedestrial Crossings 3)Reduce vehicle conflict 4)Add connections to the park for Bikes
Schedule for construction: June 6 -concrete work will begin at night. July- new island construction and new signal installation, day and night. August- all concrete work complete, begin milling and paving at night.
Discussion: CB6 is very disappointed that the bike lane will not move forward. Transportation Committee proposes pervious pavement in the pedestrian accessible area. Transportation Committee asks that the noisiest work be done earlier in the evening than later. DOT responds that night work takes place for worker safety. The statue of Lincoln will come to GAP from the concert grove. Transportation Committee asks if traffic cameras can be installed @ GAP.
DOT responds that traffic cameras are in limited number. Transportation Committee asks if the street markings can be repainted on Union St. DOT responds that repainting must wait for repaving.
Presentation and discussion with representatives for the Department of Transportation on the findings from their Brooklyn Streetcar Feasibility Study, which studied the possibility of providing streetcar service within Red Hook with a connection to Downtown Brooklyn.
Funds from Congresswoman, Nydia Velazquez supported the study. The full report is on the DOT Website Key points: -Red Hook is a very transit dependant area 81% of households do not own vehicles. -The streets are very narrow and cannot support 2 way streetcar transportation, as well as, bicycle lanes and 2 way vehicular traffic. -Improved bus transportation is offered as an alternative.
CB6 expressed disappointment Blum: Are buses really cheaper than a streetcar? Armer: Is DOT committed to improved surface transit offered as an alternative?
Transportation Committee asks about differences in bus capacity and streetcar capacity
DOT answers: Buses have a capacity of 80 people vs. 200 person capacity in streetcar. B61 bus will be considered for real time reporting (where is the bus). It is next in line after Staten Island buses.
Transportation Committee asks that: 1. MTA board move forward on addressing transit inequity in Red Hook.
2. Transportation Committee asks for a comprehensive Red Hook transit plan.
3. Transportation Committee asks for alternative bus schedules @ peak times, making every other bus a truncated run.
4. Transportation Committee asks if a speed bump can be installed on Hamilton Avenue to slow traffic for pedestrians.
Red Hook Waterfront will stay a working waterfront for a while.

Chairperson Daniel M. Kummer began his report by stating that the Borough President has sent out his official letters of appointment to Community Board members. He reminded all Board Members to sign in whenever they attend a meeting, and that they can make an appointment to meet with the District Manager to help them get up-to-speed on their responsibilities and issues.
Chairperson Kummer reported that last month Board Member Barbara Ginsberg chose not to reapply for membership; however, she will remain on our Parks/Recreation/Cultural Affairs Committee. We have also since learned that Lisa Cirando, Anthony Pugliese, and Maria Reca-Heyer have chosen not to reapply for membership. The Chairman took the opportunity to thank them all for their service to the board and our communities.
Chairperson Kummer congratulated our Treasurer Gary Reilly and his wife Mia who celebrated the birth of their first child, Vaughan Marie Reilly early this morning. According to Gary, “Mom and baby are excellent.” Vaughan came in at 7 lbs, 11.6 oz. and 21 inches long. If anyone would like to send a card or note to the Reilly family, District Manager Craig Hammerman has Gary’s address and will make it available on request.
Chairperson Kummer informed the Board that at a formal merging ceremony last week our Continuum Health Partners Long Island College Hospital formally became part of the SUNY Downstate network. According to all of the new signage immediately posted to signify the change, the hospital is now officially the SUNY Downstate Medical Center’s University Hospital of Brooklyn at Long Island College Hospital. He thanked District Manager Hammerman for attending the ceremony on our behalf and would like to extend a welcome to Dr. John LaRosa, President of SUNY Downstate, and express to him our thanks that our hospital is open for business and continues to serve our community’s medical and health care needs. I’d also like to thank our elected officials – Borough President Markowitz, Council Members Levin and Lander, Assemblywoman Millman, Senator Squadron and Congresswoman Velázquez – whose intervention and leadership were critical and made it possible for us to celebrate this moment.

Chairperson Kummer advised the Board that we received a response from Con Edison on the issue related to employee parking at their Third Avenue Yard. In their letter, they reiterated that their primary goal is to no longer provide free parking for employees to help save money for their customers. They are actively promoting the possibility of carpooling, the use of pre-tax transportation spending accounts, and other messages to encourage mass transit options, but they will not commit to continuing to provide parking for their employees, regardless of who pays for it, at this time.
Chairperson Kummer informed the Board that on June 14th Empire State Development Corporation and Brooklyn Community Boards 2, 6 & 8 will be co-sponsoring a Community Forum on the latest traffic changes that will be taking place near the Atlantic Yards project. These changes were originally due to begin on or around July 15th, but the start date has since been pushed back to on or around July 24th. Sam Schwartz, their traffic consultant, will be on hand to make the presentation and there will be an opportunity to ask questions and learn more about the plan.
Chairperson Kummer reported to the Board that District Hammerman and I recently met with Senator Eric Adams to talk about overlapping issues of interest that affect our board and the Senator’s district. The Senator was extremely clear that he is strongly in favor of seeing marriage equity legislation in New York State and that he is doing as much as he can on the issue. We have invited him to visit our Public Safety Committee to talk about some of the public safety initiatives he has been working on.
Chairperson Kummer also reported to the Board that they recently met with Emily Lloyd, Tupper Thomas' replacement as the new Administrator for Prospect Park, to discuss our interests in Prospect Park, which is not technically in our district, but is certainly an important asset and one which affects daily life in the district. We talked about a wide-range of issues – everything from parking around the park to the impact of barbequing and large-scale events on our district. With her varied background in government, having been in charge of transportation, sanitation and environmental agencies, we believe she has the potential to make some great contributions that will enhance our quality of life, firm up Prospect Park as the major regional park attraction that it is, and build upon Tupper’s wonderful legacy.
Chairperson Kummer further reported to the Board that they also met with Michael Cairl, the President of the Park Slope Civic Council to get a better understanding of some of the local issues that the council is dealing with and see how we can best support each other’s goals. The Civic Council has really embraced a proactive livable streets agenda, is continuing to push for a further expansion of the Park Slope Historic District, and has really forged some strong ties with the local merchant community and continues to promote support for local businesses.
Chairperson Kummer ended his report by reminding the Board Members that the board will not meet in July or August but will resume its meetings in September. If there is an issue of a time-sensitive nature that arises over the summer then the Executive Committee is empowered to act on behalf of the board according to our by-laws. Should the Executive Committee need to meet, we will make sure that all Board Members are aware of the meeting so they have the option of attending.

***MINUTES***
Presentation and discussion with representatives for the Department of Transportation on the preliminary design investigation for the Prospect Park West bicycle lane raised medians.
Preston Johnson made the presentation on behalf of Department of Transportation in response to the resolution passed by CB6. He began by reviewing the list of the requested changes/recommendations and then reported on their status:  Rumble strips completed June 2011.  Drop-off zone adjustments made.  Seasonal regulations will be implemented for loading zones.  Narrowed buffer near Union Street will be implemented along with upcoming GAP changes.  DOT believes it can restore 14 parking spaces.  DOT declines signalization of the entrance to Litchfield driveway.  Monitoring of safety will continue through 2013.  DOT declines signalization of pedestrian crossing at bike path because they feel that it de- prioritizes the pedestrian.  Island improvements will consist of exposed aggregate concrete, cobblestone lined tree pits, grey tinted concrete curbs unless funding is obtained for granite curbs.
   DOT believes that their length and widths for the islands are correct: they need access along the curb and the length of the island maintains good visibility for pedestrians.
The presentation included plan drawings of each intersection and renderings of the proposed island design. Construction of the islands is expected in Spring 2012.
Q: How long will construction take? A: Approx. 2 – 3 months.
Q: There are no pedestrian ramps at some intersections – can they be included? A: DOT would like to include them; need to see where they are required.
Q: Is there enough room for a truck exiting Litchfield to wait for traffic without blocking bike lane? A: Acknowledge that a large truck would block the bike lane while waiting to pull out, but DOT believes riders will adjust to the circumstances.
Q: Can signage be provided to direct vehicles not to block the bike lane? A: Yes.
Q: Can the whole island have a permeable surface in the interest of ensuring that trees get enough water? A: DOT will work with Parks Department to maximize the permeable surface.
Q: How much do you need for granite curbs? A: About $200K. Councilmember Landers office is working on securing funds.
Q: Are relocated pedestrian signals included in the island work? A: Yes.
Q: Concern that the space between the islands may be used by cars for parking – can it be marked to prevent this? A: Generally there is not enough space between the islands for a car.
Q: Are any more parking spaces available? A: DOT continues to work on this.
Q: What is the lead-time needed for the granite curbs. A: Need commitment ASAP so that orders can be placed. The sooner, the better.
A general discussion ensued about further CB6 input on the design and materials and the final date for funding of the granite curbs. DOT noted that if construction was to begin on schedule next Spring, all further comments needed to be submitted ASAP.
Q: Why is there no signal at President Street? It is difficult for bikers to cross PPW to access President. A: Only streets with traffic approaching PPW are signalized.
Lisa Napolitano introduced a recommendation that approval of the DOT island design conditional upon the inclusion of granite curbs.
VOTE: 3…..YEAS            3…..NAYS        3…..ABSTENTIONS
MOTION FAILS
Jerry Armer introduced a recommendation that DOT investigate and provide pedestrian ramps at the east sidewalk as necessary and make this part of the island construction work.
MOTION APPROVED UNANIMOUSLY
Daniel Kummer introduced a recommendation that the pedestrian signals be left on the east sidewalk rather than move them to the islands because it introduced visual clutter, and possibly reduced pedestrian safety.
General discussion of the issue, Ryan Russo of DOT explained that it was their practice to place pedestrian signals on either side of street containing vehicles; that leaving them beyond the bike path might create confusion between pedestrians and bicyclists.
MOTION FAILS
Q: Who maintains the tree pits? A: Parks Department.
Q: Has DOT considered that park features might be obscured by the plantings in the islands? A: Will continue to discuss with the Parks Department.
Q: Is a copy of this presentation available? A: It will be on the website tomorrow.
Review and discussion of Whole Foods Market’s traffic study and transportation remediation plans for the project site at 214 3rd Street (area bounded by 3rd Avenue, 3rd Street, 4th Street basin and Gowanus Canal) and environs.
Question and Answer Session about the Whole Foods Traffic Study Marty Taub of Eng-Wong, Taub and Associates was present, also Jerry Johnson of Wachtel and Masyr, LLP (representing Whole Foods). Tom Miskel reviewed the background of this topic: discussion of the traffic study was referred to the Transportation Committee from the Land Use Committee.
Q: The report mischaracterizes some of the streets: why is 3rd Avenue called a ‘commuter’ route when it is really a truck route? There is a school across the street but no mention of drop off and pickup activity – why not? How can Whole Foods ensure control over delivery times?
A: Marty Taub: Commuter traffic does exist on 3rd Avenue and this seemed most relevant. All school traffic is included in the counts and it is not necessary to single it out, but it can be mentioned in the final revision. A: Jerry Johnson: will check with Whole Foods, but they are confident they can control delivery times.
Q: The B103 bus is listed as ‘local’ but it actually is a ‘limited’. A: The traffic study only distinguishes between local and express. The limited bus is considered local.
Q: Will signalizing the entrance to the parking lot meet minimum distance requirements between signals? A: Yes, it is 200 – 250 feet from the corner.
Q: The study radius seems too small. How can we expand it to make it more meaningful? A: Will review with DOT.
Q: Why was Union and 3rd Avenue intersection not included? A: We’ll look into that.
Marie Brown of the 3rd Street Block Association described the traffic problems residents of 3rd Street experience and submitted a list of recommendations for consideration. Included was a request for a right turn lane into the parking lot.
Marty Taub: We will review these recommendations and discuss with DOT. Initial studies do not indicate that a dedicated right turn lane is necessary but it will be reviewed.
Chris Hrones of DOT: DOT will review the list.             Some of the items may be addressed by new Downtown Brooklyn traffic calming measures.
Comment: Please look at the 3rd Street/2nd Pl congestion problem. Comment: There is a lot of truck traffic and congestion at 3rd Street and 3rd Ave.
Q: Is there a number for average daily trips? A: Not a meaningful statistic – the amount of trips at specific hours is most important.
Jerry Armer introduced a recommendation comprising the following: 1. BSA mandate that Whole Foods continue to work with the Community Board and affected community when planning, reviewing and refining the specific traffic mitigation plan that NYC DOT will be implementing.
2. BSA and DOT mandate that the scope of the study be expanded beyond the CEQR minimum ¼- mile radius, given the size of the store and the fact that it is widely viewed as a regional rather than a local business.
3. BSA mandate that one year after the store opens that Whole Foods perform a follow-up traffic study to compare actual conditions with the study’s projections to see if additional traffic mitigation directly related to the store’s impact on the area are warranted.
4. NYC DOT review the list of recommendations prepared by the 3rd Street Block Association and respond to each item to the Community Board and the community.
General discussion preceded a vote
MOTION PASSED UNANIMOUSLY
A discussion ensued concerning efforts to reduce automobile usage. Ikea was cited as an example of how the company tried to encourage alternative means of transportation to the store. Members of the committee encouraged Whole Foods to look into methods of promoting alternatives to driving to the store.
Motion to adjourn.

***MINUTES***
Presentation by representatives for NYC DOT on an interim proposal to improve safety and access in the vicinity of Brooklyn Bridge, Park Pier 6 at Atlantic Avenue, Columbia Street and Furman Street.
This would include more and better striping of crosswalks. Better and clearer signage at the northbound entrance to the BQE on Atlantic Avenue limiting the times of day and days of week that a right turn into the entrance can be made on a red light in order to allow pedestrian traffic to cross safely.
Re-routing the B-63 into the park on the park road; in order to turn the bus around and avoid possible conflict with pedestrians and bicyclists at the base of Atlantic Avenue and the park entrance where the bus presently makes a U-turn.
Other improvements around the entrance to the Park to better guide pedestrians more safely in get in to the park; placing the bicycle path on the street and separated from traffic by use of Jersey barriers. (Reps from the Brooklyn Greenway Initiative were present and approved the idea.) By moving, the bikes to the street pedestrians would use the west-side of Columbia Street to enter the park. Make improvements to the area in front of the container port
Much discussion about where DOT intended to place traffic signal on Columbia Street, between Congress and Atlantic Avenue. DOT favored entrance-exit of BQE on Columbia Street. Community and committee favored Congress Street.
Motion by Jerry Armer, seconded by Madelaine Murphy:
Though we thank DOT for these interim improvements, they are far from the permanent solutions needed at the Atlantic Avenue entrance to Brooklyn Bridge Park.
We approve the DOT’s interim safety and access plan for the vicinity of Brooklyn Bridge Park with the following conditions:
1. In order to make the pedestrian crossing of Columbia Street safer install a traffic light on the corner of Congress and Columbia Streets, instead of having a pedestrian crossing marked at the traffic light between the southbound entrances and exits to the BQE on Columbia Street. Then re-open the truck entrance-exit to the container port at Congress Street and close the one at Atlantic Avenue making the entrance to the Park safer for all.
2. DOT and Brooklyn Bridge Park work with the community to come up with permanent pedestrian and cyclist improvements that would include not only safer, but also more a elegant solution to the problems in these areas.
3. Further, that our elected officials should provide the Capital funds necessary to fund these needed permanent safer solutions.
4. In addition, reposition the traffic signal for left-hand turns from eastbound Atlantic Avenue on to the northbound BQE entrance to prevent illegal turns on red.
Minutes submitted by Madelaine Murphy.

Update and presentation by representatives for National Grid and the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation on the development of remediation plans for the Public Place aka Citizen’s manufactured gas plant site at the southeast corner of Smith and 5th Streets.
The Department of Environmental Conservation was unable to attend due to the fact that Metro North was not in service because of the storm. National Grid made the presentation.  Nearly 7,000 gallons (thousands of gallons) of coal tar have already been removed from the ground.  DEC approved the initial design concept – specific plans being worked on now.  Coal tar has been found at depths of over 100 feet. Selected remedy is to excavate to 8 feet throughout the site; backfill to street grade; holders will be excavated to their base.  HDPE liner at 2 feet below grade throughout site for storm water management.  NAPL recovery wells – NAPL barrier wall to 50 feet.
HDPE – High Density Polyester is the projected barrier material. National Grid is not finding tar on the Smith Street side – just mainly along the bulkhead and areas that held tanks.
The barrier wall will require sewer relocation. The design of the barrier wall is different in each of 3 sections.
1. Smith/5th Streets corner - Large 2. Ferrara area 3. Abadi area
There will be pilot testing (field demonstrations driving the street piles) starting in October.  Heavy equipment noise  Vibration  MTA elevated structure issues will abound  Barrier wall seal is tricky – using/trying 3 different joint seals, then a primary seal and a secondary seal.
The test pits will examine how various existing bulkheads, cribbing, dock cribbing and sheeting are installed and supported and how to address them in creating the barrier wall. One test pit site is not yet found at ground level. Manhole 13 is around Bond/4th Streets looking up from the sewer (via video camera) but not yet found above – need complete sewer study. Sheet pile steel corrosion study is needed. Need to test grouts and joint seals.
DEC has approved the plan. Environmental Protection (EPA) has questions about cap material to be used, about barrier wall and about being able to build above.
Site 4 – Hoyt/5th Streets had a newer holding tank which leaked far less and will be easier to clean up according to National Grid.
If someone comes into the site to develop, they must do that respecting the safeguards put into place by National Grid in the remediation.
How can foundations be sunk through the HDPE? There must be a plan for restoring the integrity of the barrier. In addition to the remediation there is need for a long term monitoring and management plan including who does it and to what standards for what length.
The minutes were submitted by Bette Stoltz.

Jane Marshall was introduced as the representative for Forest City Ratner and a representative from the Department of Transportation was there as well. The temporary certificate of occupancy and soft opening for the Barclay Center Arena is slated for August of 2012. CCO is September 2012 and the pre- season is in October 2012.
They discussed the security bollards and benches intended for installation at the Barclay Center. Brooklyn Events Center will maintain them according to DOT specifications.

Note: Currently, where the Long Island Railroad yards exist, the sidewalk narrows to approximately 9+ feet. Forest Ratner will review with IECS to confirm the area can handle the flow of pedestrian foot traffic. CHAIRPERSON’S REPORT……..………………………...……..………….....…...DANIEL M. KUMMER
Chairperson Daniel M. Kummer began his report by congratulating Assistant District Manager Leroy Branch, who recently purchased a co-op in Red Hook and will be relocating there by the end of this month. All these years Assistant District Manager Branch and his family has been living in Boerum Hill in CB2, across the street from CB6 so I’d like to welcome him home and wish him and his family many years of happiness in their new home.
Chairperson Kummer thanked Board Members Rick Luftglass, Glenn Kelly and Bob Levine for joining him, District Manager Craig Hammerman and Assistant District Manager Branch at this year’s borough-level budget consultations. We will be hearing more about the highlights of that evening when Budget Chairperson Luftglass gives his Budget Committee report, but I especially wanted to thank those members for volunteering their time to come out to participate at this year’s meeting.
Chairperson Kummer also thanked District Manager Hammerman for representing the Board before the City Planning Commission at their hearing on September 21st on the Special Fourth Avenue Enhanced Commercial District application. District Manager Hammerman informed him that he was the third of three speakers who attended to testify in support of the action – following Council Member Lander and a representative for Borough President Markowitz. It did not appear as if there was any controversy over this item so we are expecting the Commission to adopt it. Hopefully, we will start to see this zoning action’s impact result in livelier and more engaging pedestrian designs for new buildings along 4th Avenue moving forward.
Chairperson Kummer announced to the Board that the Landmarks/Land Use Committee would have a special guest visiting them at their next regularly scheduled monthly meeting. Robert Tierney, the Chairperson of the Landmarks Preservation Commission, has agreed to attend our committee meeting for an evening of dialogue on the City’s landmark regulations and historic districts – the process and practices of the agency and how our work intersects with theirs. Since our district has an active historic district expansion project underway in Park Slope, and another possible project for Carroll Gardens, in addition to several important locations that we have requested the commission’s consideration for landmarking, such as the Pacific Branch Library on 4th Avenue, this should prove to be a most interesting discussion. The meeting is at 6:00pm on Thursday, October 27, 2011 at the 78th Precinct, 65 6th Avenue (between Dean/Bergen Streets).
Chairperson Kummer ended his report by commenting on the recent pattern of sexual assault crime that have been perpetrated in the South Park Slope and Park Slope areas over the last few months. In fact, there have been at least 12 cases since last March. One of those 12 cases has been in the 78th Precinct, the remainder having taken place in the 72nd Precinct, south of our district. Brooklyn Community Board 7 has been working 2
closely with the 72nd Precinct to hold meetings, and share information about what people can do to be safer and feel safer in their communities. To do our share in helping inform our residents, Deputy Inspector Argenziano, the Commanding Officer of the 78th Precinct, has agreed to come in and brief our Public Safety Committee at their next meeting, which will be at 6:30pm on Monday, October 24, 2011 at the 78th Precinct, 65 6th Avenue (between Dean/Bergen Streets). All of our committee meetings are open to the public so if you know anyone that you think might be interested in attending please encourage them to come.
DISTRICT MANAGER’S REPORT……………..................................................…CRAIG HAMMERMAN
District Manager Craig Hammerman began his report by informing the Board that the District Office is recovering from the water pipe burst and resulting flood we had in the office. The ceiling is being repaired and we are still not certain if our carpeting will be redone since they found asbestos-containing floor tiles beneath it. We are in a situation where our property owner is the State of New York and the building owner is the City of New York. He thanked everyone for their support and asked for their patience in terms of the staff getting back to people in a timely matter.
District Manager Hammerman reported that the Department of Transportation has determined that a speed hump on St. Johns Place between 5th and 6th Avenues is a good candidate for the installation of a speed hump.
District Manager Hammerman ended his report by inviting everyone to the 18th Annual Domestic Violence Vigil on October 14th sponsored by Good Shepherd Services’ Safe Homes Project. Volunteers, participants, supporters, and community members will light 20 candles in memory of those who died because of domestic violence this past year in Brooklyn. This annual event marks Domestic Violence Awareness Month, remembers the victims and honors the survivors of domestic violence.
Chairperson Kummer recognized the representatives of the elected officials.
Tamar Smith, representing Assembly Member Joan Millman, stated that the Assemblywoman would again collaborate with Long Island College Hospital to administer free flu shots on October 18th and 19th. For more information, please call 718-246-4889. The Assemblywoman has been working closely with the NYPD to assist in any way she can to inform residence how they can be safe while walking alone in lieu of the recent sexual assaults in Park Slope. She is also working with the Department of Transportation to see if they can install additional lights beneath the Prospect Expressway overpass in the interest of public safety. It is extremely important that we all take safety precautions when walking alone day or night. The Police Department recommends being extra cautious and aware of your surroundings, taking off headphones as they may inhibit the ability to hear someone approaching and using a route that is well lit and well populated. Below are resources that provide late night walks or rides home:  Brooklyn Bike Patrol - provides walks home 7 days a week from subway stops in Park Slope, Prospect Heights and Carroll Gardens. Call 718-744-7592 to arrange an escort.  Right Rides - provides free, safe rides home for women and LGBTQ individuals after midnight on the weekends. Call 888-215-SAFE  Safe Slope - provides free walks home in Park Slope, Greenwood Heights and Windsor Terrace on Thursday, Friday and Saturday nights from 8pm-3am by calling 347-709-8852
She also reported to the Board that the Brooklyn District Attorney's office has begun a public safety program called "Safe Stop" (formerly Safe Haven), which allows merchants to display a decal to alert the public that their business is a safe place to go in the event of an emergency. Applications for businesses, which would like to become Safe Stops, are available in her district office at 341 Smith Street. Presentation and discussion with representatives for the South Brooklyn Industrial Development Corporation on the programs and services that are offered by the organization to support the industrial and manufacturing businesses in the Gowanus, Red Hook and Sunset Park communities.
David Meade, Executive Director of the South Brooklyn Industrial Development Corporation made the presentation along with Elizabeth Demetriou.

CHAIRPERSON’S REPORT……..………………………...……..………….....…...DANIEL M. KUMMER
Chairperson Daniel M. Kummer began his report by reporting to the Board that we have received resignations from Board Members Terry Alexander and Yvonne Roman. Board Member Alexander has gone through a job transition and while he does not anticipate having the time to commit as a Board Member and Co-Chair of our Public Safety Committee, he has asked to remain on the committee as an active member. Board Member Roman has become more active in her church and Wednesday nights are a conflict for her so before her attendance became an issue for us she has voluntarily resigned. Chairman Kummer thanked them both for their selfless service to the Community Board for these past few years.
Chairperson Kummer informed the Board that the Borough President has appointed several new Members to our Board. He welcomed Sister Rosanna Cervone of the Koinonia John the Baptist Catholic order, appointed by the Borough President, who has been attending our meetings regularly since coming to Visitation Parish in Red Hook, and also Dominique Bravo of Park Slope and Sayar Lonial of Carroll Gardens who were both appointed at the recommendation of Council Member Brad Lander. We hope they find their new role as a Board Member fulfilling and would suggest that each of them reach out to our District Manager Craig Hammerman to help get them situated.
Chairperson Kummer thanked our Parks Committee Co-Chair Glenn Kelly, District Manager Craig Hammerman, and Board Member Yvonne Girela for attending an on-site meeting with our Parks Borough Commissioner Kevin Jeffrey and other members of the surrounding community of Ennis Park, which is located between 2nd-3rd Avenues and 11th-12th Streets, to talk about the landscaping in the park and several other park usage issues. Some of the issues involved the need for more Capital investment in the park, and some of them are more operational issues, so Ennis Park should appear on a future Parks Committee agenda for further discussion.
Chairperson Kummer also thanked our Environmental Protection Committee Chair Gary Reilly and District Manager Hammerman for meeting with DEP Commissioner Carter Strickland to discuss several issues of concern to our district. Tamar Smith, representing Assembly Member Joan Millman, reported to the Board that The Senior Citizen Rental Increase Exemption, called SCRIE, is an invaluable program for seniors (62 and older) living in New York City. SCRIE helps many stay in their apartments by freezing their rents at current levels while property owners receive tax abatements by the city to compensate for a loss of rental income. Increasing problems in the program's administration, currently run by the New York City Department of Finance, led to a planning meeting held recently by City and State elected officials to discuss strategies for improving the SCRIE program and increasing outreach and education efforts so that the many thousands of seniors who are eligible for the program actually are enrolled. One change is that the administration of SCRIE should be moved back to the Department for the Aging, where there were better outreach efforts and more sensitivity to the needs of seniors. The City Council will be proposing legislation to set up a program where a SCRIE specialist would be dedicated to one senior center in each Community Board in the City. This person would be responsible for education, outreach, assisting seniors with the application process, recertification, and working through any problems that arise. To be eligible for SCRIE you must be:  62 years or older  Live in a rent regulated apartment  Your income for the year must be $29,000 or below  You must spend at least 1/3 of your monthly income on rent
If you think you, a family member or a friend might be eligible, call 311 for a SCRIE application.

Chairperson Daniel M. Kummer began his report by wishing the assemblage a Happy New Year!
Chairperson Kummer welcomed to the dais the 2 new Brooklyn CB6 Officers for 2012, namely, Elizabeth Shipley who is taking over for Nica Lalli as Secretary for the Board, and Lou Sones who is the new Second Vice Chairperson after Elly Spicer. We have received a resignation from longtime Board Member Connie Molinari. We will also plan a couple of open, “town hall” meetings to give the residents an opportunity to bring any other items of concern to our attention. Once we’ve compiled our agenda it is our intention to sit down with the Chairperson of the New York City Housing Authority to review and discuss our concerns and ideas. Presentation and discussion with representatives for Council Member Brad Lander on “Next Bus Please: Improving the B61 Bus,” a report that assesses the level and quality of bus service along the B61 line.
The Co-chair, Steve Burzio introduced Councilman Lander who explained the study process and introduced the team from his office who conducted the study – Michael Freedman-Schnapp and Matt Green. Data was collected by volunteers on over 700 bus runs.
Four bus lines serving Community Board 6 have been eliminated since 2005. Only two bus lines remain with only one serving Red Hook.
Findings:  7% of all B61 buses arrive outside of acceptable headway times.  B61 buses arrive late and experience “bunching” in the A.M. and P.M. hours.  B61 buses carry many more passengers than the loading guidelines prescribed by the

Recommendations:  Increase service during peak ridership hours  B61 should be included in MTA “Bus Time” programs as soon as possible.  Stop improvements at Smith/9th Street stop to include a new bus shelter, countdown clock, lighting, street trees, planters and bike share.  Route improvements - Extend B57 line into Red Hook - B61/B103 transfer - Improve B61 route across the BQE

Committee comments:  More enforcement by Police to keep traffic moving on Van Brunt and Columbia Streets.  Has off-board fare collection been considered?  Lack of loading zones contributes to delays.  Lack of investment in bus transit is primary issue.  School bus garages in Red Hook significantly contribute to congestion, resulting in delays.  State funding level is a primary issue.
Actions by Council Member Lander’s office:  Lander’s office will meet with the MTA  Presented report at MTA Board meeting.  Met with bus drivers union.  Publicizing issue.

The committee’s proposed policy on waiver letters is therefore as follows:
(i) that the liquor license application be for renewals only (no new applicants would be considered); (ii) that any requests for a waiver letter be considered on a one-time basis; (iii) that the liquor license establishment not have a history of complaints, which would have triggered a committee-level review of the renewal application; (iv) that the district office shall check with the respective local precinct and, if possible, the City's 311 system to determine if there were substantial complaints about the establishment; and, (v) that when the above conditions are met, in the absence of any substantial complaints, the district office can issue a waiver letter.

District Manager Craig Hammerman reported to the board that on March 30th the United States Postal Service will be terminating services at their contract station located at 257 Columbia Street in our district. The District Manager informed the board that he and Assistant District Manager Leroy Branch recently attended a meeting with the Street Activity Permit Office to discuss the new changes they have implemented since instituting and online electronic application system 2 years ago. Highlights of the changes are as follows:  Applicant will receive a notification from SAPO directing them to our website to see our requirements for block parties. Starting next year all “Single Block Festival” applications must be submitted by December 31, 2012.

CHAIRPERSON’S REPORT………………………………………………………....….DANIEL KUMMER
Chairperson Daniel Kummer began his report by informing the board that 3 of our members have opted not to reapply for Board Membership – specifically, Linda Blyer, David Reiss and Derrick Vito. The Chairperson thanked all of them for their exemplary, selfless service to our communities. Their presence at our general meetings will be missed, and their contributions to the board will not be forgotten.
Chairperson Kummer reported to the Board that in response to the concerns raised by various board and committee members, he’s taken a long, hard look at the challenge of how best to rebalance the workload of our Public Safety/Environmental Protection and Permits & License Committee to free up more space for our Public Safety and Environmental Protection items. The Chair, with the consent of the Executive Committee, has reorganized the committee as follows: Public Safety will merge with Transportation and Environmental Protection/Permits & License will remain together. The new committee configuration will be reflected in the Committee Membership Applications that we distribute in June and will formally take effect September 1st for the 2012-2013 meeting session.
Chairperson Kummer advised the board that in response to the motion we adopted last month regarding the proposed community garden at Columbia and Sackett Streets, District Manager Craig Hammerman has spoken to a representative from HPD’s Brooklyn Planning Office who did confirm that this lot was slated to be developed under their New Foundations RFP that was issued several years ago but the City has put those plans on hold indefinitely because they do not have the money for development in their budget at this time. The department also confirmed that they did not foresee that budget becoming available in the immediate future either. The representative made it clear that his agency is in the business of building housing but given that they will not be able to advance this project they suggested that it would be more beneficial to have a positive, active community-engaging use like a community garden than a vacant lot which the City would be challenged to maintain until development plans could move ahead. He was also clear that the terms of any community garden lease are month-to-month and that they have exercised their development rights in the past when they have had money to build on community garden sites.
Chairperson Kummer invited everyone to tomorrow night’s Transportation Committee meeting that will be run by the Department of Transportation on the Bike Share plan for our district. Bike Share is the program being rolled out by the City this summer that will involve setting up 600 bicycle docking stations throughout Manhattan and portions of Brooklyn, to make 10,000 bicycles available for rent. The City is not paying for the program. The company that will be operating Bike Share under contract with the City will be funding it themselves, primarily through advertising revenue. This company has already operated successful Bike Share programs in Washington DC, Boston, London, and other major cities around the world. There will be a modest annual membership fee, then for rides that last longer than either 30- or 45-minutes, a small hourly charge will be billed to the rider. DOT had come to our committee several months ago to introduce the program concept, and said they could come back to engage the community in a discussion about where the docking stations would be located. Tomorrow night’s meeting will offer us, and the community-at-large, an opportunity to weigh in directly with the agency over where we think the docking stations should and should not be located.
Chairperson Kummer ended his report by informing the Board that next month, at 6pm on April 12th at our office at 250 Baltic Street, we will be holding our annual Bar & Restaurant meeting which is an open forum designed to educate the community and business owners about the rules that govern the operation of bars and restaurants. We have been hosting this annual meeting for many years now and have found it to be an excellent way to promote better relationships between bar/restaurant owners and their neighbors by making sure that everyone knows what the rules are. We will have representatives from the State Liquor Authority, local 2
precincts and every other city agency that plays a role in regulating these types of businesses. The meeting is not designed to focus on specific problems at specific locations but rather to broadly educate the community on the roles that the various agencies play in helping to balance a thriving and competitive business environment without unduly sacrificing the community’s quality of life in the process.
DISTRICT MANAGER’S REPORT………………………………………….…….CRAIG HAMMERMAN
District Manager Craig Hammerman began his report by informing the board that the recent story reported in the New York Post stating that the NYPD has chosen the 78th Precinct to police the Barclays Center when it opens in September, bypassing the 88th Precinct is not true. No decisions have been made and the police are unable to identify who leaked the information to the press. CB’s 2, 6 & 8, the Police Department, the Borough President's office, the Mayor's office and City Council will all be involved in the discussion, but ultimately it is up to Police Commissioner Ray Kelly to put forward a recommendation to the Mayor. The Mayor will make the final decision, consulting with the City Council. We should be receiving a decision sometime in July.
District Manager Craig Hammerman reported to the board that he sent a letter to the United States Postal Service expressing the Boards objections to the closing of the small postal station at 257 Columbia Street. He is hopeful that we will get a written response soon.

State Assembly Member James Brennan thanked all the Board Members for their commitment and service to the residents of the district. He then gave an overview of this year’s state budget. He stated that there has been four years of cutting the budget but this year there were no cuts. To the contrary we have increased certain funding particularly in the area of Education. NYC Department of Education received a 4% increase; Community Colleges got about a 6% increase; and Libraries received about a 5% increase. What the budget reflects is a healing of the State economy, some much needed revenue at the last minute related to the national mortgage settlement, the retention of a surcharge on multi millionaires that was enacting in December. Last year the Elderly Pharmaceutical Insurance Coverage (EPIC) Program a prescription drug program for seniors was almost abolished but this year they restored it. Governor Cuomo wanted to eliminate the Neighborhood Preservation Program which provides financial support for not-for-profit community-based housing corporations to perform housing and community renewal activities statewide. This program was saved. The MTA received its full funding for its operating and capital programs.
State Assembly Member Joan Millman advised the board that she and State Assembly Member Brennan spent the day at an Education hearing in which they heard from New York State Education Commissioner, Dr. John B. King, Jr., Dennis M. Walcott, Chancellor of the New York City Department of Education, Ernest Logan, President of the Council of School Supervisors & Administrators, Teachers Union and students. After listening to everyone we kept asking how State money will be spent in the NYC Education System and Commissioner King and Chancellor Walcott kept “punting the question”. One of the things troubling her is that the Mayor runs the school system as a business model and schools are not a business. So this administration has adopted a policy of either closing schools or using a “turn-around” model in which they remove the administration of the school and 50% of the teachers in the hopes that this infusion of new administration and teachers will turn the school around. What is also upsetting is that the Department of Education received about $60 million in federal School Improvement Grant funds to support implementation of the Transformation, Turnaround, or Restart Model in 44 Persistently Lowest Achieving (PLA) schools. This money will be used to enter into contracts with Educational Partnership Organizations, i.e. Southern Governors Association in which these schools must buy into and make a decision about which one in a 48 hour period, which is ridiculous. No one seemed to know, except the DOE people how these EPO’s were selected, i.e. RFP process. Instead of investing in our own people the City is now “contracting out” to run our schools. We walked away from the hearing with as 3
many questions as we had when we walked in. Last week we had a meeting with Council Member Levin in regards to the new management at the senior residence at 1 Prospect Park West. The rents for seniors are between $3 - 5 thousand per month. They are all freighting that once their leases are up the management company will try and get rid of them. It has not happened yet, but because of the location of the building she can understand the senior’s fears. She will keep monitoring this situation very carefully. She ended by thanking all of the Board Members for participating on the Board.
Council Member Brad Lander started by thanking all of the Board Members for their time and service to the Board. He then stated that although the City will receive a little extra money from the State the City’s budget is still challenging. The budget is still in a $3 billion structural deficit, which is going to be closed by a $1 billion rollover of this year’s budget, $1 billion Mayor’s rainy-day fund, $1 billion from the sale of the new taxi medallions. Even with all of this, there are still substantial cuts to services in the Fire Department, Libraries, Child Care and Afterschool programs; hopefully we can restore the cuts like we did in the past. This year there will not be any proposed teacher layoffs but the budget would reduce the teacher force by 1100 through attrition. As a result class sizes have been growing dramatically. A bit of good news is that the wait list in CB6 kindergarten class is pretty modest as compared to last year. He is trying to help the DOE get a long time lease with the Diocese of Brooklyn at St. Thomas Aquinas school on 4th Avenue and 9th Street in our district to create an early childhood center to help alleviate any overcrowded classrooms in the district. This weekend, over two thousand residents from the district came out to vote in NYC’s first “participatory budgeting” election, a groundbreaking initiative that lets community members decide how to spend their own tax dollars on projects in their neighborhood. Voters selected from among twenty projects proposed by neighborhood residents. The seven projects receiving the most votes will be prioritized for funding as part of the City’s FY2013 budget, which will be adopted in June, with just over $1 million in committed by the Councilmember. Presentation and discussion with representatives for the Barclays Center on the job hiring process and other employment and economic development opportunities at the arena.
Presentation and discussion with representatives of Barclay’s Center regarding job opportunities and hiring plan.
Rick Luftglass chaired the meeting. Guests representing Barclays Center, their consultants and operators included Ashley Cotton, Brigitte Labonte, Roberta Fearon, Jason Sandovar, Jenny Irving, Lorraine Vega, Julie Margolin, Andrew Hirsh and David Anderson.
Ashley Cotton made introductory remarks, the following summarizes her presentation and the questions asked during it:
The center will open in about 5 months. They expect significant participation of MWBE contractors. All hires will be union.
Q:     Any idea of FTE (Full Time Equivalent) rate? A:     Not at present.
There the main operating entities will include Levy’s Restaurants for food service and AEG for security.
Q:     Are all jobs union? A:     Yes.
Job fairs will be held at which potential employees can meet with employers to arrange for interviews. There are planned partnerships with SBS Workforce 1 and NYCHA and BUILD. Local hiring will be prioritized. The hiring process will be the same for all entities operating at the arena.
Q:     How is NYCHA publishing opportunities and reaching their residents? A:     The process is just starting - no job postings as of yet.
Job fairs will be held on a variety of days at different times to maximize ability for people to attend. There are approximately 2,000 jobs available among the operating entities: 1,900 part time and 100 full time. Part time jobs are event based.
Q:     What are benefits of F/T versus P/T, and what kind of benefits? A:     F/T will include health care, P/T will not. Benefits will be the usual: health, dental, etc.
Q:     Are jobs available for the disabled? A:     Yes, it depends on the job description; they would be P/T jobs.
All employees will be trained by Disney Institute. Hourly wages will be set by union collective bargaining agreement. The number of people working at an event varies by the type of the event. There will be a quarterly report on employment: no. of people, where they are from, etc.
Q:     How will reports be made accessible? A:     Website.
Q:    Will you be hiring from ‘within’ (meaning current employees moving into new positions)? A:     We are primarily looking for local hires but there could be some hires within; these are primarily management positions.
Q:      How many hours/year for P/T? A:      Hard to answer that - depends on events. P/T employees will have a lot of control over their schedules.
Q:     Regarding reporting, what about including information about retention rate, promotions. A:     We haven’t thought about that, will get back to you.
Q:     Seems like a low number of F/T positions. A:     That is the number of positions we need.
Q:     Any training programs? A:     Depends on circumstances - all employees will be trained for their specific jobs.
Q:     Any training for disabled? A:     Depends on the job - all employees will be trained.
Q:      What about P/T employees who work more hours than typical for part time - will they get benefits? A:      Yes, as required by labor law.
Q:      We have a concern about the organization limiting employees’ time to keep them at P/T status. A:      The number of hours worked is a function of scheduling and the requirements of the events.
Q:     What will be approximate wages relative to minimum wage/living wage? A:     Can’t say at this time, will be determined by the collective bargaining agreement which can’t be started until there is a pool of employees. Wages will certainly be greater than minimum wage.
Q:     Are there any union deals yet? A:     We should have agreements in place by July or August.
Q:     What is initial wage offering? A:     Not set; the union has to be established and agreements concluded.
Q:     Will wages vary by time of day as in other venues? A:     Don’t know yet.
Q:     If you have worked with unions before, what is the approximate pay scale? A:     Union wages will always be above minimum wage.
Q:     Where will jobs be posted? A:     Website and other locations.
Q:      Are all management jobs local, not remote? A:      Yes. Other contracts will be let for things such as uniforms, housekeeping, drycleaning to local businesses.
Q:     How many jobs for these contracts? A:     These jobs are included in the estimate given earlier.
Q:     Will people with felony records for non-violent infractions when they were young be excluded? A:     We will do background checks, will consider employees on a case-by-case basis. No automatic exclusion due to a record.
Q:     What is the time frame for hiring? A:     Job fairs June and July; hiring and training July and August.
Q:     Can report break down jobs by entity and subcontract? Can it include hours worked? A:     Yes.
Comment from Board member emphasizing that we expect local hires to be retained and replacements to also come from the local community.
Q:     Will food supplies be sourced locally? A:     Yes, looking to feature local products and culinary talent.
Q:     Any limits on food trucks around the center? A:     Will look into it; DOT regulates.
Q:     Will you use neighborhood papers to notify of job openings? How will you publicize information about what is expected from applicants in terms of preparing for the job fairs? A:     Will publicize where possible in order to get to the largest possible pool of candidates.
Q:     Why are Red Hook Houses not on the list of housing projects that you are contacting? A:     The list was established in the Community Benefits Agreement; we’ll try to reach out to all.
Meeting adjourned.

Presentation and discussion with representatives for the Citizens’ Committee for Children on their Campaign for Children, an advocacy effort to oppose the proposed cuts to child care and after-school services in the City’s budget.
Moira Flavin of the Campaign for Children made the presentation. The CCC is a multi-issue child advocacy organization engaged in a joint campaign between the NYC Youth Alliance and the Emergency Coalition to Save Child Care joined forces to fight against cuts to childcare and after school care.
Mayor Bloomberg proposed cuts for 2012: • 47,000 children lose child care and after care – cuts for past 5 years. • 90,000 children will have lost child care and afterschool in past 5 years.
The CCC is asking for Community Board support for resolution. They have had strong support from Community Boards so far. Moira briefly reviewed the handouts: • Impact brief • Tool kit • Brooklyn impact brief • Resolution
In Brooklyn, DYCD and ACS have used a priority versus non-priority zip code determination. CCC believes this is a false choice and the information is skewed – not a clear depiction of need. The city is slated to lose 25,000 afterschool slots and elimination of 7 Beacon programs and NYCHA cornerstone programs.
Pushing to restore cuts and baseline the funding.
Proposed cuts this year: 16,000 childcare slots and 32,000 after school slots.
The question was asked if these resolutions really have an effect? Moira explained that last year similar cuts were proposed and the majority was restored due to advocacy.
Calling on all Community Boards citywide to endorse the resolution.
The committee was unable to vote because there was not a quorum present but will request a resolution before the full Board at the upcoming general meeting. The Mayor’s budget comes out tomorrow and CCC will let the committee know if any of the numbers change.
Presentation and discussion with a representative for the Department of Education’s Office of Space Planning on the department’s planning process for determining how school spaces are allocated, outfitted and utilized and how that effects our district.
Thomas Taratko of the Department of Education Office of Space Planning made the presentation. His office authorizes changes in space usage. Responsible for determining co- location in schools. The Office of Space Planning originally created to support principals who were forced to navigate space changes in schools. • Identifies underutilized spaces for new schools to be located. • No politics behind it – facilities against space facts. • Planning to engagement for new placements i.e., charter schools. • Work closely with School Construction Authority. • What should go into the building – assist architects in SCA. They have models for middle schools, high schools, etc.
Facilities team contact list was reviewed. - Can help with utilization issues, room conversion, how to maximize City Council discretionary resolution grants. - Space analysis during phase cuts and closures. - Dispute resolution at co-located schools.
Reviewing the Blue Book – capital planning document that describes the capacity and utilization for all Department of Education buildings. - Historic utilization – if SCA is building a school, they would have x amount of offices, x amount of classrooms – all based on square footage per student. - Target capacity – all teachers fill out a facility survey to say how all the space is utilized. Look at full size, half size and quarter size spaces. - When it comes to space decisions, the Office of Space Planning has never lost a case in court. - DOE instructional footprint – tool used by all stakeholders in the analysis and assessment of space usage in NYC DOE buildings. The instructional footprint tells you how you have to use and share space.
The Office of Space Planning has no input on what organization goes into the building only what the space has the capacity for. They survey 150-200 buildings a year – frequently say “no” you can’t turn that into a shared space.
-   The Education Construction Fund gives schools extra square footage for air rights. -   To meet the needs of communities with more and more kids and not enough space – DOE will build new schools but it will take 5 years to complete. -   Middle schools are also overtaxed. -   Temporary classrooms are also opened if schools outgrow themselves.
-   There are 80,000 underutilized seats in NYC schools. • 300 vacant seats and up – co-locate • 150-300 = District 75 programs • K-655 – 400 seats in air district

Any dollar spent on a co-location is matched for all organizations located in the same space.
Expanding community school model for the future – medical/mental health/dental facility/24- hour computer lab – all accessible to parents and community members.

Brooklyn CB6 voted to endorse these plans at our March general meeting.

Chairperson Daniel Kummer began his report by congratulating all of the Perfect Attendance Award recipients.
Chairperson Kummer thanked Parks Committee Co-Chair Nica Lalli and our District Manager for attending a recent meeting at the Prospect Park Alliance in response to the impact that events at the Bartel Pritchard Square entrance to the park have had on the adjacent residential community. At this meeting, Prospect Park Administrator Emily Lloyd committed to several meaningful steps that will reduce the impact of events beginning with next year’s season of events as permits have already been granted to this year’s event organizers. Probably the most significant concession is that they will no longer allow bands and DJ’s to entertain from this location. Our new members include: Eric Andersen (BP), a resident of the northern section of 4th Avenue; Paul Basile (BP), one of our Gowanus industrial business owners and current member of our Transportation Committee; Eladia Causil-Rodriguez (BP), a resident of north Park Slope; Marco Chirico (BP), a resident of Carroll Gardens; Joni Kletter (39), a resident of south Park Slope and member of our Parks Committee; Lance Pinn (BP), the owner of Brooklyn Boulders across from the Thomas Greene Playground in Gowanus, and; Matthew Silverman (BP), resident of north Park Slope and long- standing member of our EWCDH and PSEPPL committees. Committee assignment notifications will be sent out in August.
Chairperson Kummer welcomed back Assistant District Manager Leroy Branch who was unable to attend last month’s meeting because of some elective surgery.

Park Slope will experience a fairly substantial change in local elected leadership as most of the area that is currently being represented by State Senator Eric Adams will be transferred over to the district currently represented by State Senator Kevin Parker. Randy Wade of the Department of Transportation presented information on a new proposal to improve Bartel-Pritchard Square. Kelly Gimson of DOT’s pedestrian group was project manager and presented.
Community Boards 6 and 7 requested improvements to the circle. Crosswalks are violated, double right turns create danger onto Prospect Park Southwest.  Fast Action Toolkit – new signage, signal timings, new crosswalks, new traffic signal  DOT also wants to relocate existing B61 shelter.  Lanes would be widened to help stay within lane during turns.  Painted curb extensions.  Net loss of only one parking spot at new crosswalk.  Turn lanes will be turn lanes only, not also thruways.  Crosswalk distance will be shortened from 50 feet to 30 feet.

Q. Any parking loss? A. The bus stop will not be any parking losses. It is purely a swap.
Q. Who is responsible for flowers in circle? A. Parks Department.
Q. Other than paint, what prevents wrong turns? A. Flexible delineators will do it.
Q. Anticipate any spill back on 15th Street? A. Looked at signal timings, giving extra time to Prospect Park West. They will also monitor it after installation.
Park Slope Neighbors hears many concerns about it and appreciates this change.
Q. Thought about overhead signs? A. Yes, there will be terracotta overhead signs.
Q. Crosswalks are all very angled – increases distances. A. Angles are to match existing pedestrian ramps.
Any plan to fix these lanes is commended.
Q. It is continuous movement with signal timings changed? A. Yes. It made for smoother continuous flow.
Q. Countdown clocks? A. Eventually, yes. They are being rolled out slowly.

CHAIRPERSON’S REPORT………………………………………………………....….DANIEL KUMMER
Chairperson Daniel Kummer began his report by welcoming everyone back from the summer hiatus.
Chairperson Kummer announced that everyone should have received their committee appointment letters. If you did not, or if there was a problem with your appointment, please let District Manager Craig Hammerman or myself know immediately. I’m very pleased to announce that we have some additions to our Executive Committee. Paige Bellenbaum will now be co-chairing our Human Services Committee with Benjamin Solotaire; Norman Cox will be chairing our Housing Committee; Sayar Lonial will be chairing our Public Safety Committee, and; Mark Shames returns to our Executive Committee as the Chair of our Environmental Protection Committee. I want to thank these board members for agreeing to take on these new roles and I look forward to working with them, and all of you, as this busy year ahead of us progresses.
Chairperson Kummer reported that Board Member Peter Fleming will continue in his role as Chair of our Election Committee. Letters will be sent to every board member outlining our election procedures. We do have term limits, as officers are only permitted to run for a maximum of four consecutive one-year terms in the same office. All of our current officers are eligible to run again for their seats in 2013.
Chairperson Kummer informed the Board that in a series of meetings over the last few months we have been working with IKEA, the South Brooklyn Industrial Development Corporation, and the Red Hook Initiative, to facilitate stronger ties between IKEA and Red Hook so that more people can take advantage of potential employment opportunities locally. We’re pleased to hear that these groups have continued to meet on their own and are finding ways to work together and support one another. I’d especially like to thank our Economic Development Chair Rick Luftglass and Human Services Co-Chair Benjamin Solotaire for making time to attend these meetings and encouraging us to play a more pro-active role in this area.
Chairperson Kummer advised that he attended the State Liquor Authority’s (SLA) hearing on June 20th on the Barclays Arena and presented testimony on behalf of our board. As a follow-up, District Manager Hammerman attended the SLA hearing on August 29th where they closed the record and decided the matter. The applicant represented that they had met the conditions that we had listed in our conditional approval of their application, with the exception of the post-event service in the VIP areas of the arena which we had not considered as part of our review process. SLA Chairman Dennis Rosen questioned the applicant to see whether an absolute service cut-off time of 10pm, as suggested by some members of the community, would be harmful to the business model for the arena. The applicant stated that it would. The Chairman then asked how many events they expected would last past midnight and would, therefore require the need for them to be able to serve alcohol up to 2am. The Chairman ultimately suggested that instead of being allowed to serve up to 2am, a condition that we had proposed and the operators had accepted, that instead they only be permitted to serve up to 1am since it would not infringe on any of the planned events at this time. The Chairman also promised that the SLA would 2
be open to reexamining this restriction in as little as 6 months should it proves to be too constrictive to their operation.
DISTRICT MANAGER’S REPORT………………………………………….…….CRAIG HAMMERMAN
District Manager Craig Hammerman began his report by informing the board that the NYPD arrested six alleged drug dealers and arrested six others in a joint sweep at the Red Hook Houses on Wednesday, September 5th, wrapping up a six-month investigation titled "Operation Red Dawn" by the NYPD and the Brooklyn District Attorney's Office. As a follow-up Kings County District Attorney Charles J. Hynes and NYPD Housing Bureau Chief Joanne Jaffe will be meeting residents and taking questions at a town hall-style meeting at the Red Hook Community Justice Center on September 19th.
District Manager Hammerman reported to the Board that Mayor Michael Bloomberg on behalf of Police Commissioner Ray Kelly has sent a letter to City Council Speaker Christine Quinn asking the City Council to formally change the boundaries of the 78th Police Precinct to include the entire Atlantic Yards development area and also gives it jurisdiction over the area between Vanderbilt Avenue and Flatbush Avenue, from Hanson Place in Fort Greene, all the way to (and including) Plaza Street East. There will be a broader and more robust opportunity to review all of this next year because that is the decennial review of the New York City Community District boundaries.
District Manager Hammerman advised the board that the Department of Transportation has determined that a speed hump on President Street between Smith and Court Streets is a good candidate for installation, and denied a speed hump on Hoyt Street between President and Carroll Streets.
District Manager Hammerman informed the board of an emergency condition at 440 5th Avenue in the Park Slope section of our district. Department of Buildings has ordered the owner to remedy this situation by demolition the building.
District Manager Hammerman reported to the Board that on July 26th a lightning bolt struck the 16-foot northwest pinnacle of Christ Church causing the stone structure to collapse and bringing down part of its scaffolding. The debris struck Richard Schwartz, a prosecutor in the State Attorney General’s office. He was pronounced dead at SUNY Downstate University Hospital at the Long Island College Hospital. Due to an unstable building, the following streets will be closed indefinitely to both vehicular and pedestrian traffic: Clinton Street from Degraw Street to Kane Street; Kane Street from Strong Place to Court Street.
District Manager Hammerman advised the board that the district office is now wired for wireless. We are also working on other forms of technology upgrades in the office before the end of the year.
District Manager Hammerman ended his report by inviting everyone to the next The Economic/Waterfront/Community Development & Housing Committee Meeting on October 15th where we will hear a presentation by the consultants that the Friends of Brooklyn CB6, Inc. have hired to perform our Gowanus Brownfield Opportunity Area (BOA) Study. The BOA program provides municipalities and community-based organizations with assistance, up to 90 percent of the eligible project costs, to complete revitalization plans and implementation strategies for areas or communities affected by the presence of Brownfield sites, and site assessments for strategic Brownfield sites.

The meeting was called to order at 6:40pm.
Presentation and update on construction of the Brooklyn Bridge Park
Committee co-chair Nica Lalli introduced guest speaker Regina Myer, President of the Brooklyn Bridge Park Conservancy. Ms. Myer listed on-going and planned developments at the park, and noted several upcoming park events.
Ms. Myer presented the following previous, on-going and planned developments at the park: • Phase 1 was completed in March 2010 with the opening of Pier 1. Additional phases of work have thus far been completed through the summer 2012, with the opening of the Pop-up Pool at Pier 2. • In June of 2012, their Board of Directors approved additional work at Pier 1, including the development of a hotel and an apartment complex. This work will create 210 permanent jobs and 300 temporary construction jobs. • The Field House project has a commitment for a track cycling facility, and will include additional multi-use recreational facilities. • There will be a request for proposal (RFP) targeting commercial and retail development among vacant buildings in the north end of the park. • Fall 2012 construction (to be completed in early November) includes: Completion of Pier 5 and portion of Pier 5 uplands, which include 5 acres of multi-use active recreation and the picnic peninsula with a concession, barbeque and play area. Completion of the Squibb Park Bridge spanning Furman Street to provide a more direct connection into the park at Pier 1. • Additional details on the phases of park development can be found here: http://www.brooklynbridgepark.org/progress/park-phasing
A number of events at the park were noted, including: • Brooklyn Book Festival Bookend Event, 9/23/12 • Harvest Festival, 10/20/12 • Additional details on park events can be found here: http://www.brooklynbridgepark.org/events
Additional points that were raised during a question and answer period included: • Permitting will be handled by the Brooklyn Bridge Park Conservancy, and will be aligned with NYC Parks and Recreation policies and procedures. • Pier 2 facilities will include 5 basketball courts, shuffle board courts, bocce ball courts, and facilities for in-line hockey, handball and chess. There will also be 5 acres of open space for general use. • The Department of Transportation (DOT) is looking into a stop sign at the juncture of Congress Street and Columbia Street. Several community members in attendance voiced concern over the safety of children crossing over to the park, particularly at this location. • Construction on the apartment building project is expected to begin next summer.
The following suggestions were made to Ms. Myer by community members in attendance: • Consider adding signage to highlight the distance between the north side park entrance and the first exit, as that distance is considerable.
•   Consider adding signage that can provide information on businesses in adjoining neighborhoods, as a local economic development action. •   Consider adding concrete table tennis courts.
Review and consideration of a request for an extension to the Cobble Hill Park closure hours Committee co-chair Nica Lalli introduced guest speaker Nelson Fung, New York City Parks Department’s District Manager for CB’s 6 & 7. Mr. Fung noted the following: • The issue being considered by the Parks Department is whether to extend the open hours of the park from 9pm to 10pm. • Mr. Fung’s understanding is that the New York Police Department (NYPD) supports this adjustment. • Mr. Fung is aware that patrons have been ticketed for being in the park after hours, which is one reason this change has been requested. • Current standards in New York City is for all playgrounds to be closed at 9pm; however, there are no set standards for how late non-playground park areas may remain open.
Committee co-chair Nica Lalli introduced guest speaker Jeff Strabone, of the Cobble Hill Association. Mr. Strabone noted the following: • Other parks in the vicinity are open till 10pm or later, with at least one open till 1am. • There has been recent, strict enforcement by the NYPD, and the cost of a ticket is $250. This has caused a strain in the relationship of the community with the 76th Precinct. • The Cobble Hill Association (CHA) has an email from the 76th Precinct Community Affairs Officer supporting the adjustment of the closing time from 9pm to 10pm. • The CHA compromised on requesting a 10pm close time, with some members preferring a range of different times. • The seven member CHA board unanimously supported the decision to request adjusting park hours to close at 10pm. However, that position was not supported by all CHA members.
Additional points raised during a general discussion period included: • The closing time of the park was originally dusk. • Among community members who spoke, there was general consensus that the NYPD’s 76th Precinct has been unusually aggressive this past summer in issuing tickets. Some community members complained of what they considered inappropriate tactics, including aggressive use of patrol vehicles. One speaker commented that she was advised to take down the badge number of any officer who behaves in a ways considered inappropriate. • A number of different community members who live near the park noted a range of illegal and/or disruptive activities which typically occur, including marijuana use, sexual activity, music and instrument playing, and loud conversations. These activities occur both during normal park hours and after hours. • The NYPD was invited to participate in the committee meeting, but did not attend.
Arguments in favor of extending the closing time to 10pm included: • A number of community members noted that the park is used as a convenient short-cut, and that recent NYPD 76th Precinct ticketing practices curtailed this use.
•   A number of community members believed that a 10pm closing time would help improve relations with the 76th Precinct. •   One Committee Member noted that increasing the use of the park during evening hours by law- abiding community members would decrease the level of illegal/disruptive behavior, during that time. •   Jeff Strabone of the CHA noted that there are not facilities at the park associated with inherently noise-making activities, like basketball courts.
Arguments against extending the closing time to 10pm included: • A number of community members considered the potential for additional noise, and generally disruptive activities, between 9pm-10pm to be highly significant. • One community member believed that the police would be less/non-responsive to noise complaints that occurred during open park hours, as opposed to complaints that occurred after the park is closed. • One community member stated that when the construction of the park was originally debated, a closing time of dusk was the compromise position agreed to at the time. • Regarding relations with the 76th Precinct, one community member felt that the issue had been addressed and that enforcement of the 9pm closing time had been moderated already.
MOTION:
Judy Francis made a motion to accept the Cobble Hill Association’s recommendation to adjust the closing time of Cobble Hill Park from 9pm to 10pm. Rosemary Graham seconded the motion.

The committee reviewed and discussed a petition to co-name a single block of Sackett Street (between Third Avenue and Nevins Street) for the late Thomas A. D’Alessio, a long-time resident of the block. The motion to recommend the petition to the CB6 Board was carried.
Presentation and update from representative for New York City Transit on the ongoing Culver Viaduct Rehabilitation project, including an update on the reopening of the Smith-9th Street subway station.
A presentation from NYCT-MTA featured Andy Inglesby, spokesperson, and Raymond Wong, head of construction, who shared current information on the opening of the rehabilitated station at Smith/9th Street (late fall of 2012), completing the re-construction of the Culver viaduct (2013), and opening street level shops at Fourth Avenue/9th Street (Oct/Nov 2013).
Discussion included questions about the use of express shuttle buses during certain work periods, and about the inclusion of modest signage at the Fourth Avenue/9th Street station to direct travelers to nearby B61 and B63 bus routes on 9th Street and Fifth Avenue, the latter of which had been recommended through Council Member Brad Lander’s Participatory Budget Project in 2011-12.
The meeting adjourned at 7:35 pm.
Minutes submitted by Marilyn H. Pettit.
