CHAIRPERSON’S REPORT………………………………………………………....….DANIEL KUMMER
Chairperson Daniel Kummer began his report by explaining to the Board that tonight we will be voting on our Fiscal Year 2014 Capital and Expense budget requests. As part of our annual budget process we meet with the City agencies to talk about the status of our past requests. Many of our requests are not funded either because the City just hasn’t allocated funding yet, or we simply haven’t made a strong enough case for why the request deserves funding. Some of our requests have been funded and are either in the pre-design, design or pre- construction phase. The process of tracking our budget requests is complex as each request has a unique history. To help make the job manageable, I’d like to thank Board Member Rick Luftglass and our Assistant District Manager Leroy Branch who sat through this year’s marathon budget meeting and our District Manager, Craig Hammerman, who assembles our agendas and tracks these requests for us. I’d also like to thank the members of our Executive/Budget Committee for their thoughtful contributions when we reviewed the draft requests at our committee meeting.
Chairperson Kummer announced that this year’s annual holiday party is going to be held on Monday, December 17th from 6-9pm, at the Sheep Station on the corner of 4th Avenue and Douglass Street. The cost is $30 per person and we will get hors d’oeuvers and non-alcoholic beverages included. Of course, this event is also an end-of-the-year fundraiser for our non-profit organization so tax-deductible donations above the $30 are encouraged. To that end we usually have a raffle of prizes that board members collect and donate for that purpose. I’m looking for volunteers who would help collect prizes this year and would like to thank, in particular, Board Members Glenn Kelly and Lou Sones who have really helped us out in prior years. Maybe they, and a few others, would be willing to help us out this year? District Manager Hammerman will send out an email with more details.
Chairperson Kummer highlighted the upcoming meeting of our Economic/Waterfront/Community Development & Housing Committee, which is scheduled for 6:30pm on Monday, October 15th at PS 32, corner of Hoyt and Union Streets. Our Friends of Brooklyn Community Board 6, Inc. group had received a grant from the State of New York for $275,000 to complete a Brownfield Opportunity Area project for portions of the Gowanus Canal corridor. At this meeting we will hear from our consultants who have a good deal of information to share – they will report on the data they have gathered from their door-to-door surveying of existing businesses, from their land use analysis and supplemental field work, and from a recent stakeholder’s group meeting held with representatives from indigenous Gowanus-based organizations. This will be their first public presentation and we are encouraging a good turnout for this meeting.
Chairperson Kummer reported that last Thursday after the close of business our district office was faxed a letter notifying us that Aguila Inc. and Housing Solutions USA, a Bronx-based non-profit organization that was established in 2001 and provides social services to over 1400 homeless families in the Bronx and Manhattan, intends to submit a proposal to the Department of Homeless Services to provide social services to 170 single 2
male adults that will be living at 165 West 9th Street between Court Street and Hamilton Avenue in Carroll Gardens. Needless to say, the news took us all by surprise and we really don’t have much more information at this time. The letter we received is posted on our website under our Human Services committee’s webpage. We have invited representatives from Housing Solutions USA to attend and present the details of their proposal at our next Human Services Committee meeting, which will be at 6:30pm on October 24th at a location to be announced. This meeting will be an Informational Presentation, since it does not appear as if the Community Board or any other elected official is required to conduct a public review of this proposal. It is our hope that by providing a venue for interaction between the proposer and the community that we can hopefully replace some fear with fact and give our community directs access to firsthand information. Of course, as we learn more about this proposal and have more information to share we will continue to broadcast that information to the community through our website, the area’s elected officials’ offices, the Carroll Gardens neighborhood list server and direct email. If anyone is here tonight to speak on this matter, please understand that this item is not on our agenda tonight, which means the Community Board will not be taking action on this item, and that you should be prepared to attend the meeting on October 24th.
Chairperson Kummer ended his report by reminding the public/guests that all of the items that are on our agenda for a vote tonight came from a recommendation by one of our committees which hosted a public review and discussion previously. If you are interested in following along the work of the Community Board we have an online Calendar on our website which is updated frequently, you can sign up to receive announcements of all of meetings, or you can always call over to our district office to find out if we are discussing any particular item of interest to you. Some of you, for example, may be here tonight because we are going to be discussing and voting on a recommendation regarding The Lightstone Group’s proposal to construct 700 units of housing at 363-365 Bond Street by the Gowanus Canal. If you are here to speak about this issue or any issue on tonight’s agenda you will not have the opportunity to do so until after our vote. The Lightstone Group proposal was heard by our Landmarks/Land Use Committee at their regularly scheduled meetings in August and again in September. That would have been the public’s opportunity to share their comments, concerns, questions and opinions with us. I wanted to make this announcement now in the hope of alleviating any further frustration that our guests may experience, because they are not familiar with our procedures.

Land Use Committee Chair Peter Fleming reported that the committee reviewed a “Minor Modification” application at 363-365 Bond Street.
Motion:       by Committee;
Recommendation to request that the City Planning Commission table an application (N 130044 CMK and M 090048(A) ZSK) submitted to the Department of City Planning on behalf of The Lightstone Group requesting (a) a three-year renewal of the previously approved special permit, and (b) a “minor modification” to the previously approved special permit (C 090048 ZSK) involving the updating of the previously approved plans and zoning calculations to reflect changes to the Large-Scale General Development at 363-365 Bond Street (Block 452, Lots 1 & 15 and Block 458, Lot 1), between Carroll and 2nd Streets, until such time as various specific conditions are met:       A supplemental EIS has been conducted and finalized       Affordable units are increased to 30%       Height is reduced to 8 stories from 12 stories       Responsible development policy passed by CB6 is followed
Board Member Richard Bashner asked if the developer could accommodate the number of units they are requesting if they reduce the height from 12 stories to 8 stories. If so, would it have to go through another ULURP process or would it be classified as a minor modification. Land Use Committee Chair Fleming stated 4
that we don’t know if reducing the height would send this back to a ULURP process or if they can accomplish their goal of 700 units. A representative from City Planning stated that a reduction in building height would still fall under a minor modification because it is still within the building envelope.
Board Member Lou Sones stated that the issue the community has about this development is not the minor modification but the entire project, they feel the infrastructure will be a challenge in regards to schools, sewers, fire and police, etc. Although we are suppose to be speaking to the minor modification, the motion speaks to a supplemental EIS, affordable housing going to 30%, and height reduction. The fact of the matter is because of the rezoning of this plot of land this makes it as-of-right and if we don’t approve this proposal another developer could come in and build the project as originally proposed and approved by the City. Unless I was guaranteed that there would be a supplemental EIS I would have to vote against this motion.
Board Member Mark Shames spoke out against the motion by reading a statement which request that the project be tabled. He further stated that the increase in affordable housing is good but not agreeing to the use of union labor is something he cannot support. Lastly, City Planning has failed us because they have not begun the discussion in regards to the rezoning of the entire Gowanus corridor.
Board Member Eric Anderson asked what a supplemental EIS would achieve. Chairperson Kummer stated that it would be an update of the original EIS and the Department of City Planning has concluded that another EIS is not required.
Board Member Robert Levine stated that he is reluctant about this motion because the board is being asked to vote on something that really exists already. We had a proposal by Toll Brothers that they can follow and it would not have to come before us. They are coming to us because they are making it a little higher in one place and a little lower in another and if we say no they can go back and withdraw the modifications and build the original design. They could even add the additional apartments without our recommendation because it will be within the building envelope. It’s not a matter of stopping the project; it’s a matter of whether or not we can deal with the project with the minor modification. He would prefer to see a conditional approval so that we have a say in what our preferences are. We don’t have the right to say no to whether we agree with what’s there or not.
Board Member Dolly Williams spoke in favor of the project but stated that she also has some concerns about the challenges the infrastructure will bring to the neighborhood.
Board Member Gary Reilly asked how the committee came up with 30% required affordable housing when they are building more units with the same square footage. Especially since it is more that Toll Brothers was willing to do. Land Use Committee Chair Fleming stated that this is guaranteed, they are not counting on any additional funding. They have already partnered with the Fifth Avenue Committee to administer the affordable housing, and yes this money is better than the one before. Chairperson Kummer also stated that these units will be integrated with the market rate units as well as the same size and the Toll Brothers project was not.
Board Member Elizabeth Shipley stated that she voted against this motion because rather than be top of the market condominiums these will be rentals. Our community is in desperate need of new, modern, accessible affordable rental housing. As landlords they could be the best neighbors that this community could have in the sense that they could bring their political muscle and their resources to win things for the community that they wanted for years including addressing the many issues regarding the infrastructure.
Board Member Glenn Kelly spoke in favor of the motion stating that the Carroll Gardens Neighborhood Association was opposed to the “spot rezoning” when it occurred and is still against this because this project is happening in a vacuum absent the rezoning of the entire corridor. If we look at just this development as a model, we are going to have an enormous amount of housing units along the Gowanus corridor in the future. 5
When the EIS was done they did not take into account the development on 4th Avenue or the Barclays Center. With that much development of housing in the future no one is talking about the infrastructure concerns regarding schools, sewers, transit and sanitation. The time to develop along the canal will come but we are not there yet and we have not done our due diligence to make sure it is done properly.
Board Member Elly Spicer stated that The Lightstone Group has not kept its promise to honor and respectfully follow the process the Toll Brothers followed. They have not in a very key way that is important to this community and she is shocked and dismayed that the Fifth Avenue Committee would participate in their process of undercutting the wages of workers. Toll Brothers made a commitment to pay union wages and The Lightstone Group has not. For this reason she cannot support the project and/or the motion.
Board Member Norman Cox spoke out against the motion stating that he did not approve the process by which this property was rezoned and he believes this development is overly dense for this location. He thinks there are two problems with the motion. (1) Requirement of 30% affordable housing is a plus since they have increase the number of units. (2) The reduction of 12 stories to 8 stories is irrelevant because the height of the building remains relatively the same.
Board Member Debra Scotto spoke out against the motion because she also believes The Lightstone Group needs to make a commitment to pay union wages. She believes the EIS is fine and that the development is fine, the problem is that the rezoning of the rest of the corridor has not begun and we as a board made it one of the conditions when we rezoned this property for the Toll Brothers. It is inappropriate for City Planning to be sending us this when they know that our approval the last time had conditions that a comprehensive review of the rezoning of the Gowanus canal corridor begin with an EIS. We all should abstain and refuse to look at any more projects until City Planning restarts the process of area-wide rezoning.
Board Member Judith Thompson stated that she also agrees with her colleagues in regards to the lack of union workers because it is an important economic opportunity that we would be losing in our community. She also believes that rezoning along the Gowanus piecemeal is not what should happen, but it should be a part of a comprehensive area-wide rezoning. Lastly, the City should spend the necessary dollars to clean up the Combined Sewer Overflows in the canal like they have done in other areas in our city.
Board Member Debra Scotto stated that contrary to some comments made tonight we should not table or wait on this issue because we have the EPA overseeing the superfund site and they can be our allies in this process.
Board Member Eric Anderson spoke out against the motion stating that the only thing before this board is the minor modification and not the rezoning which has already been approved by this board.
VOTE:    10 YEAS, 26 NAYS, 1 ABSTENTION WITH CAUSE, 1 ABSTENTION WITHOUT
CAUSE
MOTION FAILED

Presentation was made by NYC DOT regarding new Neighborhood Slow Zone in Boerum Hill.
The Boerum Hill Association asked for the Neighborhood Slow Zone and DOT is planning on implementing it between November 2012 (speed humps) and Spring 2013 (signage).
Neighborhood Slow Zones: establish speed limit to 20 MPH, introduce signage at gateways of the zone and introduction of speed “humps” into zone area. At entrances narrow the roadway to further indicate the change from non-zone to zone.

CHAIRPERSON’S REPORT………………………………………………………....….DANIEL KUMMER
Chairperson Daniel Kummer began his report by reminding everyone that this year's annual holiday party is going to be held on Monday, December 17th from 6-9pm, at the Sheep Station on the corner of 4th Avenue and Douglass Street. The cost is $30 per person and we will get hors d'oeuvres and non-alcoholic beverages included. This event is also an end-of-the-year fundraiser for our non-profit organization so tax-deductible donations above the $30 are encouraged. To that end we usually have a raffle of prizes that board members collect and donate for that purpose. Please let District Manager Craig Hammerman know if you'd be willing to solicit raffle prizes and help work at the event itself. This is a great opportunity for us to socialize, and I'd highly recommend that everyone make a special point of attending especially our newer board members.
Chairperson Kummer reported that Hurricane Sandy recovery efforts are still underway in our district. As of today there are still a few buildings without electricity in Red Hook Houses and all of Gowanus Houses has been restored. The tidal surges experienced in our community had a devastating effect on some of our businesses, many of whom are not fully insured and are wondering how they will be able to continue. Thankfully, the flow of information from our district office, from our local elected officials - particularly Council Member Lander's office - has enabled us to plan, act and react accordingly. The tremendous outpouring of volunteer efforts and donations - contributions of time, talent and resources - has been nothing short of extraordinary. While the experience is still fresh in our minds, I've asked our Economic/Waterfront/Community Development & Housing Committee to host a discussion on the hurricane impacts and particularly the responses we saw from our public agencies and organizations so that we could put together some recommendations in areas that can be improved. For example, it took NYCHA over one week to have information posted on their website about which of their buildings was without electricity, heat and elevators. Clearly, they could have done a much better job managing the public's expectations if they were faster getting information out. I would encourage anyone who is interested in participating in this discussion to come to their next meeting which will be at 6:30pm on Monday, November 19th at SUNY-Downstate LICH, Atlantic Avenue & Hicks Street.
Chairperson Kummer ended his report by advising the board that at last month's meeting we discussed the developing issue regarding a proposal to establish a 170-bed single adult male shelter at 165 West 9th Street in Carroll Gardens. We held an extremely well-attended meeting on October 24th in the largest venue we could find in Carroll Gardens and it was a standing room only event. He thanked our Human Services Co-Chairs, Benjamin Solotaire and Paige Bellenbaum who made sure our meeting was both informative and orderly since this issue has evoked a strong emotional reaction by many neighbors. We will be hearing from them when they give their committee report, but I thought you should know that as a result of Hurricane Sandy, another contracted shelter facility at Borden Avenue in Long Island City was affected so on Tuesday, November 6th the Department of Homeless Services temporarily relocated 120 homeless male veterans into the W 9th Street building. We have been told that they expect to be there "less than a month" while the Borden Avenue facility 2
is under repair, and the department is in the process of setting up a Community Advisory Committee meeting for some time next week.
2nd Vice Chair Lou Sones stated that the outpouring of volunteers to help with the restoration of Red Hook after Hurricane Sandy from Red Hook Initiative, National Guard, Community Board 6 district, and neighbors has been extraordinary. There are still families in Red Hook Houses without heat and hot water and very spotty electricity. There are many seniors and sick people who cannot get up and down in the buildings. Red Hook GAGS is looking for donations to hire a person to visit 30 families for the next two weeks who have medical conditions to check on them and bring water, food and medication.
DISTRICT MANAGER’S REPORT………………………………………….…….CRAIG HAMMERMAN
District Manager Craig Hammerman began his report by informing the board that the Lower East Side Ecology Center's electronic waste recycling program is a unique and innovative program allowing residents to dispose of working and non-working electronics in an environmentally responsible way. Their e-waste warehouse is located at 469 President Street (at Nevins Street) in our district. Anyone can drop-off unwanted electronics for free. If your equipment works, let them know and they will try to reuse it, if not they will recycle it. They will guarantee data security. Drop-off hours are as follows: Tuesdays, Thursdays and Fridays – 10am-5pm; Wednesdays 12pm-5pm; Saturdays 10am-4pm. They will be hosting an electronic waste (e-waste) recycling event at P.S. 321,180 7th Avenue between 1st and 2nd Streets in Park Slope on December 8th from 10am-4pm.
District Manager Hammerman reported that the SLA public hearing for Kemistry Entertainment Group LLC located at 260 Flatbush Avenue in the Park Slope section of our district has been rescheduled for November 21 at 11am. The hearing will take place at 317 Lenox Avenue in Manhattan.
District Manager Hammerman advised the board that the Department of Transportation has sent us a list of approved CityBench sites in our district. The CityBench program is a three-year federally-funded initiative to increase the amount of public seating on New York City’s streets, particularly for elderly and mobility-impaired individuals. The locations in our district are as follows: 7 Wolcott Street, 315 4th Avenue, 248-250 4th Avenue, 35 4th Avenue, and 250 9th Street.
District Manager Hammerman ended his report by informing the Board that some of the messages that we were sending regarding the storm on the various social media tools were helpful in responding to the hurricane. It allowed everyone to disseminate accurate and timely information to residents and business owners regarding hazardous conditions, street closures, service changes, the need for volunteers, etc. In a normal week Community Board 6 has about 900-1,200 constituents who receive our Facebook postings or tweets. During the entire week of the hurricane that number jumped to 25,000, an increase of over 2000%. This shows that social media is a powerful tool to get information out there in the district. We at the district office would like to have a focus group discussion to develop a comprehensive plan for using the various social media tools. It would be useful to have a number of people to talk to inside, and outside, of the board to discuss this topic. If you are interested in participating in this discussion please let our District Manager know.

Human Services Co-Chairpersons Paige Bellenbaum and Benjamin Solotaire both reported to the Board that the committee reviewed an application for the use of 165 West 9th Street as a 170 bed shelter for single adult males.
Motion:        by Board Member Richard Bashner, seconded by Board Member Peter Fleming; Recommendation to oppose the use of 165 West 9th Street as a 170-bed shelter for single adult males, and call upon the Department of Homeless Services to reject the application based on the lack of both process and merits.
Board Member Hildegaard Link stated that she has had direct experience with Aguila Inc., she has done a lot of lighting and mechanical inspections and find their facilities to be fairly restrictive. Quite frankly she is horrified at the restraint of personal freedom that the residents experience. It seems as though there is some degree of security and structure, but having said that she would not want this facility near her.
Board Member Dolly Williams asked if the men would come from the surrounding area. Human Service Co- Chairperson Bellenbaum stated no, they would be referred via the intake center in Manhattan.
Board Member Noel Berk-Rauch spoke in favor of the motion stating that this vote is only advisory because we do not have a formal role to play in this process. It was also brought up at the committee meeting that there was alleged conflict of interest between the landlord and the housing group. For that reason the Board should take a more pro-active and aggressive role in this process.
Board Member Roger Rigolli asked if the homeless men would be working. Chairperson Kummer responded that they would be employable, and some would be working.
Board Member Neena Dutta stated that we should be also sending a letter to the NYS Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance (OTDA). District Manager Hammerman stated that if the motion passes we will be sending a letter to all City and State agencies that are involved in this decision.
Board Member Judith Thompson stated that the current lot is 45ft wide by 100ft deep with a floor area ratio (FAR) of 3. The maximum size of building that should be there is 13,500 square feet. At the meeting they mentioned that the current size of the building is 25,000 square feet. She does not see how it can be legal to have a building that large. She also asked where the beds will be placed in the facility and it was stated that they would be placed all over the building not just in the apartments but also in the commercial space. How can this be a wise use of the City’s money to pay $110 a night to house men in a dormitory-style facility. Also, how can this be a safe environment for men because some of the men could have a criminal background since they do not do background checks. 5
Board Member Suzanne Turet stated that when the members created the motion it was implicit that we had major concerns with the process. We also wanted to bring out that there were going to be too many men in that space and that they should not be subjected to inhumane conditions.
Board Member Monique Verret stated that short of over-crowdedness these homeless men will be employable and hopefully will receive some training so they would be working. She understands that there are a number of facilities in our district but we must not lose sight of the concerns of those less fortunate than us that need these services.
Board Member Rigolli stated that we as a board should really be asking pertinent questions about the homeless men quality of living in this shelter.
Board Member Sr. Rosanna Cervone asked about the ratio between men to showers. She does not believe that 15 men per shower is a good ratio.

The meeting was called to order at 6:40pm.
Discussion on the effectiveness of Hurricane Sandy responses from public agencies and organizations, and the development of future disaster planning recommendations based on recent experiences.
There was a debriefing on Hurricane Sandy to develop the committee’s recommendations on improving response.
Rick Luftglass opened with a statement of purpose of the meeting – constructive criticism is the goal. He handed off to District Manager Craig Hammerman for background. Craig discussed communication and coordination effort. CB6’s Facebook page hits jumped from 900-1500 daily to 24,000, an increase of 2000%. The grayed-out subway map showing the NYC Transit limited service was the most popular posting. The district office will work to develop more useful, aggressive and targeted social media outreach strategy.
Plaudits for city response overall – “proactive”. • Plaudits for Sanitation Department (rarely praised) for debris removal. • Collaboration across community groups and cooperation among individuals.
• Government focus on long term (e.g. sea wall, building code changes, etc.).
SPECIFIC ISSUES
-   Pharmacies and prescription drugs not available to people who evacuated. -   Turning up the volume of the evacuation and preparedness message, especially for people with medical conditions. -   9th Street bridge as an evacuation route, but it floods right away. -   Update Zone A contours in light of experience? -   Reading letter from Red Hook small business owner. -   Availability of flood insurance – need to make more clear where and how to get it (including from IRS – past filings) – possible issue especially if more than 2 year tax filings.
November 30 is FEMA/SBA deadline for starting process? (Rick-Craig). FEMA and SBA are in IKEA at the Disaster Recovery Center. Outreach outside church masses and at Red Hook Initiative.
•   Does it make sense to rebuild in-kind and repeat prior mistakes? •   Should building code be revised to require flood-safe reconstruction? •   What about a “Shop Red Hook” initiative? Elizabeth Demetriou said SBIDC is working on a specific marketing initiative designed to support local businesses post-Sandy. •   Ask NYC Partnership for funding for “recoverable grants” to Red Hook businesses. •   Solar power streetlights/traffic lights in Red Hook. •   Should Police and Fire Stations all have back-up generators/fuel tanks? Some do – 76th Precinct provided fuel to other agencies. •   Housing Authority not sufficiently communicative. •   Suspend rule against renting out apartment (e.g. Airbnb) – Bloomberg change in position on short-term rentals – same as changing rule to allow multiple fares in one cab. •   Not having a tally or census inventory of affected people could lead to our being shorted on disaster relief. •   Where are displaced people going, and what can be done for them – expropriation of private property (!), eminent domain. •   Some older buildings require parts that are no longer available. •   Could the tunnel entrances have had steel doors welded on?

Christos Tsiamos of EPA starts off by speaking about how he is glad that the EPA finally has an opportunity to meet with Brooklyn CB6.    Results: The risks are above acceptable levels. There is potential toxicity to humans and organisms. Thus, the EPA must act to mitigate the risks. o   The Feasibility Study which is an exploration of how to clean the canal, has also been completed within a year. o   The EPA then put together the mitigation plan, after meeting with some of the Responsible Parties (ex: National Grid, the City of NY), the community, etc. They then presented the plan to Washington. o   Now: The EPA has a draft proposed plan on how to clean the canal. They hope to present it to the community by the end of Dec/early Jan. They are still waiting on the comments from NY State. Big boys of charters – Success and Kips are the ones who can battle community opposition.

Charters have issues with special needs and ESL students but we got the law changed to have targets for special needs and ESL.

CHAIRPERSON’S REPORT………………………………………………………....….DANIEL KUMMER
Chairperson Daniel Kummer began his report by wishing everyone a Happy New Year! He thanked everyone who attended this year’s holiday party. The atmosphere was warm, the food was delicious, and I was especially pleased that Captain Schiff and Community Affairs Officer Vincent Marrone of the 76th Precinct were able to stop by. A very special thanks to the district office staff for handling all of the event logistics – particularly our Assistant District Manager, Leroy Branch, who came to the party even though he was a bit under-the-weather, and to all of our board members who were able to donate items for the raffle.
Chairperson Kummer reported to the Board that our community stands to lose one of our most active members, a woman who has made it her mission to help the downtrodden and fight injustices here at home. Former CB6 Board Member Celia Cacace will be leaving the district on Monday, January 14th and moving in with her son in Wisconsin. She’s not leaving by choice – her building is being sold and she has not been able to find an affordable housing option that meets her fixed budget. A group of her friends in the community have organized a tribute party for Celia for this Sunday, January 13th, 3:30-6:30pm, at Mama Maria’s Restaurant, 307 Court Street. The suggested price is $20 per person, $10 for seniors, for hors d’oeuvres and a cash bar. This tribute party will also signal the kick-off of the “Bring Celia Back from Wisconsin” campaign as many of her friends are unwilling to let her go without exploring every alternative for getting her back to her beloved Brooklyn. After all, you may be able to take Celia out of Brooklyn (and that has yet to be seen) but you can never take the Brooklyn out of Celia Cacace. Please come to her tribute, if you can.
Chairperson Kummer ended his report by informing the Board that the EPA has released their proposed plan for cleaning up the Gowanus Canal as part of the Superfund process. The draft plan is available on their website and comments on the plan will be taken up to March 28, 2013. To help the public understand the proposal better, and answer any questions people may have about it, the EPA has set up 2 public meetings. The first is at 6:30pm on Wednesday, January 23rd at P.S. 58, on Carroll and Smith Streets in Carroll Gardens. Please note the time was changed for this meeting as it was originally announced to start at 7pm. And the second will be held at 7pm on Thursday, January 24th at the Miccio Center here at 110 West 9th Street. We are expecting to comment on the proposal and I am pleased that our Environmental Protection Chair Mark Shames will be working with our District Manager on that effort.
DISTRICT MANAGER’S REPORT………………………………………….…….CRAIG HAMMERMAN
District Manager Craig Hammerman began his report by informing the board that he recently attended, first in December and a follow-up meeting in January, to a meeting in downtown Brooklyn to talk about the formation of a new Business Improvement District (BID) at the edge of our district that would include the Barclays
2
Center, Atlantic Terminal, Atlantic Center and the BAM Cultural District. He has chosen to refer to it as the “Flatlantic” BID, others have come up with different names. This is an initiative that has been spearheaded by the Downtown Brooklyn Partnership to create this new BID in a gap where about 7 different BIDs virtually intersect. The thinking is that this area can benefit from the services of a BID, specifically sanitation, security, marketing and promotion. The group involves the businesses and cultural groups from the area as well as the anchor tenants, i.e. Forest City Ratner. They would like to see this move forward this calendar year if possible and so they set up an aggressive meeting schedule. It will be coming to Community Boards 2, 6, and 8 – since it would overlap different boards – for public review once their district plan has been developed. They will try to address forward thinking, rational policy-driven objectives for how we can best make use of public investment. Seth Pinsky, President of the Economic Development Corporation, will be chairing this initiative for the Administration, even though this is not an EDC project.

Presentation and discussion with representatives for the Department of Transportation on the new commercial bicycling education and enforcement program.
Presentation I - DOT Commercial Bicycle Education and Enforcement Program
DOT will be holding 2 forums, one on 1/23 at St. Francis College and the other on 2/21 at the Brooklyn Arts Exchange (5th Ave, 8th Street). These are geared towards business owners to educate them on the program.
The program has the goal of educating business owners, who will in turn educate their employees who ride bikes as delivery people to follow the requirements for cyclists, which include: helmets, wearing of a visible 3-digit ID number, reflective vest with business name and ID number visible, bell or audible device, front and back lights, reflectors, brakes and business name on cycle.
They also want to make it clear that delivery people must follow all traffic laws, yield to pedestrians, travel with traffic, stop at lights and signs, not travel on sidewalks and signal for turns. They are in the works of designing a course on-line for this as well, but DOT will not be enforcing the laws, that will still fall to NYPD. DOT is educating owners on laws and expecting them to follow.
Q&A
Roger: Where does one obtain a bike ID? Ans: Self-made by the business, just need to have relevant DOT required info on them.
Bill:   Are electric bikes under the program? Ans:    They are currently regulated as bikes, no difference.
Jerry: How will outreach be done? Ans: Working with BIDs, canvassing businesses.
Matt: is this coordinated with NYPD? Ans: NYPD can contact DOT if they have questions, but not directly coordinated.
Gary: Why aren’t e-bikes regulated separately? Ans: Not sure, that is a NYS DMV issue.
Roy:    Are penalties for rider or business? Ans:    Businesses can get a ticket from DOT for not educating their employees but tickets by NYPD are given to individual riders.
Bill:   Are there parking regulations (if not please include in the program)? Ans:    DOT has tried to provide as much bike parking as possible on commercial strips, but we can look into it.
Eric:   When does enforcement start? Ans:    April 1, 2013
Jerry: How are we directed to self-police? Ans: 311
Judith: What are the liability issues on the business? Ans: Not sure about insurance issues.
Committee asked for a report back in a few months to see how the program was going.
Presentation and discussion with representatives for the Department of Transportation on the City’s pedestrian wayfinding initiative.
Presentation II – Pedestrian Wayfinding program
Issue: Many individual BID’s and non-profits city-wide have taken it upon themselves to create wayfinding signage in their specific neighborhoods over the years and they don’t match with each other. DOT has decided to make a universal wayfinding system that will be approved by the PDC and will match citywide. This is the pilot.  The goal is public place-making, not shopping guide. Maps are based on walking distance times (average determined by DOT). Immediate scale shows 5 minute walking distance, pan out shows wider area.  The design follows the subway signage design, white on black
    Map is oriented to show what is front of you, not always “North is Up”     Will be placed mid-block

CHAIRPERSON’S REPORT………………………………………………………....….DANIEL KUMMER
Chairperson Daniel Kummer began his report by extending condolences on behalf of the board to our former Chairperson, Pauline Blake, whose sister Cherry Blake passed away a few days ago. Cherry Blake, like her sister Pauline, was also quite active in the Park Slope community teaching Sunday school at St. Augustine’s R.C. Church on 6th Avenue for the last 3 decades, and serving as the Secretary of the 78th Precinct Community Council. Our hearts go out to the Blake Family. They will be in our thoughts and prayers.
Chairperson Kummer reported to the Board that only 2 years ago Continuum Health Partners had announced their intention of closing down various health care services at Long Island College Hospital. At that time, we immediately heard from LICH, who were transparent and honest in explaining the fiscal challenges that Continuum was facing. Based on intensive lobbying and a great deal of behind-the-scenes action a deal was brokered for Continuum to sell LICH to SUNY-Downstate. When SUNY-Downstate took over, they did so with much fanfare and an announcement that they would be preserving LICH’s spectrum of health care services. Flash forward 2 years later, and we learn that the State Comptroller issued a report in January 2013 detailing the precarious fiscal condition of SUNY-Downstate. With absolutely not a word from anyone at LICH, we learn in the media that SUNY-Downstate is not only considering closing down LICH, but that their Board of Directors has even voted to go ahead with it. What’s most outrageous is that no one at the hospital, or at SUNY-Downstate, or the Governor’s Office, has reached out to let the community know that any of this was going on. We have been trying to get someone to come out to brief our Youth/Human Services/Education Committee, seemingly to no avail. From what we know, even though SUNY-Downstate has as much as written off LICH, they cannot move ahead without the approval of the State Department of Health which has a unit that oversees hospitals. So even though SUNY-Downstate may intend to close down LICH, it is not as yet a fait accompli. And, of course, there is a lawsuit challenging the process. We will keep you posted as we learn more about this most troubling development.
Chairperson Kummer informed the Board that last month he announced that the EPA had released their Potential Remediation Action Plan (or PRAP) for the Gowanus Canal and that the period of comment on the proposal ran through March 28, 2013. We have recently learned that the EPA has extended the period of comment an additional 30 days to April 27, 2013. In the interim there have been a series of meetings, some involving the EPA and some strictly for the Red Hook community, to talk about one element of the PRAP that would potentially involve establishing a processing facility on the Red Hook waterfront to treat some of the dredged materials from the canal and turn it into inert landfill to be used to fill in a section of the private property that would be used. This element has engendered a great deal more curiosity on the part of Red Hook residents who are coming to learn more about it. There will be a meeting at 6:30pm this Wednesday evening, February 13th at P.S. 15, 71 Sullivan Street (between Richards and Van Brunt Streets) with the EPA to answer more questions about this controversial element of the proposal. The EPA has pledged previously that they
2
would not force the community to take on this element if it proves to be too controversial so they are interested in making sure that everyone knows the facts before a judgment is reached.
Chairperson Kummer ended his report by advising the Board that we’ve also seen some alarming headlines about the Brooklyn Public Library’s intention of selling off the Pacific Branch Library at 4th Avenue and Pacific Street in Park Slope. Since 2004 we have been pressuring both the Brooklyn Public Library and the Landmarks Preservation Commission to move forward on a report that would allow the designation of the branch as an individual landmark, as it was the first Carnegie-designed branch library in Brooklyn when it was built in 1904. Both agencies have stymied these efforts over the years for reasons never known to us. Now, it seems, the Brooklyn Public Library intends to use the proceeds of the sale of this property to finance the construction of a new, modern library branch a bit further to the north in the Brooklyn Academy of Music, or BAM, Cultural District. There is currently a ULURP application that has gone to Brooklyn CB2 and the Borough President to approve the BAM South Site development which would include the new library branch. They are projecting that the new branch wouldn’t be open until 2016 at the earliest, and they will not move ahead with the disposition of the Pacific Branch until after the BAM South Site development application is approved. We have been assured that the disposition of the Pacific Branch is subject to ULURP, so there would be a public review process before the property could be sold. But they are clearly dependent on the funds from the sale to finance the new branch, which puts the disposition question well after the fact when it comes to future planning for their system. At this time we are looking to bring representatives of the Brooklyn Public Library out to meet with us in March to reintroduce themselves; it’s been more than a few years since their last visit and obviously there’s a lot going on that they haven’t been proactively sharing.

Presentation and discussion with representatives for the Department of Transportation on a proposal to implement the PARK Smart program along the Court and Smith Street corridors, between Atlantic Avenue and Sackett Street in Cobble Hill.
The presentation was made by Chris Hrones and Manzell Blakeley on the proposal to implement the PARK Smart program. • CB6 has also seen and approved previous versions of the PARK Smart program in Park Slope. • This was brought up by a need for more vehicle turnover – suggested by Charlie Sahadi and Sandy Balboza. DOT also met with over 100 merchants in the study area and has the full support of the Atlantic Avenue BID.
Proposal - to extend meter time limits to 2 hours in entire project area.
-   Provide loading zones -   Begin progressive rates for meters -   Data collected found high usage with very little available parking and long average durations (at times nearly 2 hours…..which means some are parking for 4-5 hours, balancing out those who only park for a few minutes).
Progressive Rate Structure – the longer you stay – the more you pay.
-   Wants to preserve low hourly rate for those who turn over spots often. -   Encourages people to only park as long as they need to rather than hog spots all day. -   2 hour limit: $0.25 for 15 minutes $0.50 for 30 minutes $1.50 for 60 minutes $2.50 for 90 minutes $4.00 for 2 hours
Implement in Spring and will evaluate program over the year and report back to the committee.
Q & A:
Q. Only a few commercial blocks south of Sackett Street on Smith Street – why extend now? A. Rather do it in smaller chunks now, then expand.
Q. Already some people are willing to feed meters, won’t that encourage residential spots being used? A. Yes, but it’s already hard to find spots on residential blocks. In Park Slope, it had little impact.

CHAIRPERSON’S REPORT………………………………………………………....….DANIEL KUMMER
Chairperson Daniel Kummer began his report by congratulating our long-time Landmarks Committee Chair Robert Levine who was recently honored by the Prospect Park Alliance for his invaluable contributions toward their ongoing efforts to archive Prospect Park history. Landmarks Committee Chair Robert Levine has an impressive collection of postcards and ephemera specializing in Brooklyn which is envied by historians, nostalgics and enthusiasts alike and has been loaned to and borrowed by many institutions and businesses. Anyone who visited the Pavilion movie theater in Park Slope, for example, may have noticed that they had poster-sized enlargements of historic postcards of local scenes; those were taken from his collection. He also thanked him for representing us at a recent Landmarks Preservation Commission hearing. Our letters are factored into the decisions made by bodies like the LPC but when someone can actually represent us in person that can often have an even greater impact.
Chairperson Kummer also thanked our Environmental Protection and Permits & Licenses Committee Chairs, Mark Shames and Gary Reilly, who along with myself, our District Manager Craig Hammerman, Hildegaard Link, Glenn Kelly and Bette Stoltz, attended a working session to begin the process of organizing our response to the EPA’s Proposed Remedial Action Plan (PRAP) for the Gowanus Canal as part of the Superfund process. We intend to have a draft to be discussed at their next committee meeting which will take place on April 1st, so anyone wishing to contribute to this effort is welcome and encouraged to attend this upcoming meeting. I announced last month that the EPA had extended the deadline for response to April 27th so it is my intention to have a recommendation coming out of the April 1st committee meeting to be presented to the full board for discussion and adoption at our general meeting next month.
Chairperson Kummer additionally thanked our District Manager Craig Hammerman who hosted the group of 7 students from NYU that attended our general meeting last month in a visit to our district office to field questions about their project on the Gowanus neighborhood. Craig later informed me that he sees at least one class of students every semester at the district office who come from a variety of disciplines but typically representing the fields of urban planning, journalism, political science, and public administration. As I understand it, keeping up with the inquiries from students and researchers is one of the reasons why we initially posted a website 12 years ago and continue to use it as a repository for our minutes and other documents which make it easier for the public to have ready access to the information in our office without having to inconvenience or disrupt our hard-working staff members.
Chairperson Kummer advised the Board that we will have at least one of the two new business improvement districts under formation in our district present at our next Economic/Waterfront/Community Development & Housing Committee meeting on Monday, March 18th. Representatives for the Park Slope 7th Avenue BID which is currently in formation will be joined by representatives of our 3 existing BIDs, namely, Atlantic Avenue, North Flatbush Avenue and Park Slope 5th Avenue. I’d encourage anyone who’s interested in the
2
commercial health of our district to consider attending to hear about all of the exciting programs and services these local business organizations’ offer.
Chairperson Kummer informed the Board that representatives for the Brooklyn Public Library system will be introducing themselves at an upcoming meeting co-sponsored by our Parks/Recreation/Cultural Affairs and Youth/Human Services/Education Committees on March 20th. As I reported last month, the Brooklyn Public Library is looking to dispose of the Pacific Branch Library which could, ultimately, be demolished as it lacks landmarking protection. The building is the first Carnegie-designed branch to open in Brooklyn and dates back to 1904. If you’re interested in speaking directly with the Brooklyn Public Library to find out what’s going on in any of our 4 branches and the BPL system in general please consider attending this meeting.
Chairperson Kummer reported to that our Transportation Committee will be featuring an update from New York City Transit on their ongoing work on the Culver Viaduct, including updates on the Smith-9th Street and 4th Avenue subway stations at their meeting on Thursday, March 21st.
Chairperson Kummer ended his report by wishing everyone a Happy St. Patrick’s Day, Passover, Easter, spring and anything else that may be cause for celebration over the next month.
DISTRICT MANAGER’S REPORT………………………………………….…….CRAIG HAMMERMAN
District Manager Craig Hammerman began his report by advising the board that there have been a few blog and newspaper reports about a dispute taken place between neighbors in our Gowanus neighborhood, the Marriott hotel and Spoke the Hub at the Gowanus Arts building next door. They both reached out to the district office and he held a mediation session with them last week. The first meeting went well and he will be following up with them in the near future. His goal is to at a minimum have both parties figure out a way to peacefully co- exist with one another and, ideally, leverage the others presence in the community. We ended the meeting by agreeing to continue to keep the lines of communication open. Anyone who would like more information should call him at the district office
District Manager Hammerman informed the Board that he has been attending the Mayor’s Special Initiative for Resiliency and Rebuilding Task Force which has been meeting at City Hall on a monthly basis since January. They had a public meeting in Carroll Gardens in which they got some valuable feedback from the community. This initiative is the Bloomberg Administration’s efforts to put together a comprehensive report, largely motivated by Hurricane Sandy but taking a broader view of climate change and the impact that it could potentially have on New York City and how we should best prepare and respond to that. They will be issuing a report by the end of May and we will keep everyone posted as the information becomes available.
District Manager Hammerman reported to the Board that our Gowanus BOA team recently had a meeting with representatives of the State DEC, National Grid and the Parks Department to talk about the three manufacturing gas plant sites in our district; Public Place Site at Smith and 5th Streets, Fulton manufacturing gas plant at Douglass/Degraw Pool, Metropolitan manufacturing gas plant at Lowes/Pathmark. Both the Fulton and Metropolitan sites are in the process of being evaluated for remediation, they are in the feasibility study phases and there will be some testing going on at the Public Place site within the next couple of months. Some of the remedial approaches that will take place at that site will include: securing the bulkheads, installing monitoring wells, remediation of the soil and the installation of barriers to prevent in further migration onto any of the new areas that they would be remediating. The Public Place site is over six acres and before they begin an all-out remediation effort they wanted to do a smaller portion of methodology testing first. We have ask them to come out and brief the community within the next few months so that before any major work is done on the site so we will have an idea of what to expect in terms of the impact to the surrounding area.

Kai Feder, representing Borough President Markowitz, reported to the board that he had received most of the board members’ reappointment applications. For those who have not submitted they are due by February 20th.

The Councilman has set aside $1 million to fund the projects that get the most votes. Voting will be from April 2-7 in locations throughout the district. For more information please visit http://bradlander.com/PB. The Councilman along with his colleagues have called on the Bloomberg Administration to extend Cobble Hill’s existing 50’ height limit to cover the Long Island College Hospital (LICH) campus, in order to help save LICH and protect Cobble Hill. They have asked the Department of City Planning to apply “contextual zoning” to ensure that new construction or additions could not exceed the 50 foot height limit that covers the rest of Cobble Hill, and on the Landmarks Preservation Commission to extend the existing Cobble Hill Historic District to include the LICH campus. The changes will go into effect in April.
Tamar Smith, representing Assembly Member Joan Millman, reported to the Board that the Assemblywoman has been deeply involved with ongoing efforts to make sure that our community's healthcare is not threatened. She stated that a group of hospital advocates led by SEIU 1199, the New York State Nurses Association and a group of LICH doctors filed a lawsuit contending that the Trustees violated New York State's open meeting law. At a hearing on March 8, a Brooklyn Supreme Court judge agreed to extend a temporary restraining order until he could examine all of the facts. We will have information on his final decision when it is rendered. The Assemblywomen has written letters to the Commission of Health and NYC City Planning Commission and Landmarks, and she is urging everyone to contact Governor Cuomo directly to demand that LICH be kept open. flood maps being prepared by FEMA, their implications for future insurance coverage, and what it might mean to property owners rebuilding from Super Storm Sandy.                For more information please visit http://www.nysenate.gov/press-release/senator-montgomery-publishes-guide-new-fema-flood-maps-and- insurance-program-changes.
Zeeshan Ott, representing State Senator Daniel Squadron, stated that the Senator is focusing on legislation that would allow undocumented student to receive state aid and raising the minimum wage to $9 an hour, with future increases indexed to the cost of living. The Senator has asked the Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) to undertake a Full Line Review of the G train. MTA has agreed to review the G by the end of June 2013. In recent years, he has worked with the MTA to create the first-of-their-kind Full Line Reviews of the F train. Presentation and discussion with representatives for the Park Slope Chamber of Commerce on the proposed formation of a new business improvement district for 7th Avenue, from St. Johns Place to 16th Street.
•   Mark Caserta, consultant for the Park Slope Chamber of Commerce and the Park Slope 5th Avenue Business Improvement District (BID), gave a presentation about BIDs and the proposal to create a new BID for 7th Avenue. He explained that BIDs are established by local merchants to improve the business climate and quality of life. They are financed by property owners along the designated street(s) through a special assessment. The intention of the 7th Avenue BID is to improve the cleanliness of streets and sidewalks, beautify and green the area, produce promotional events and guides, and provide additional security. They do not replace regular city-financed services such as sanitation, but supplement them and serve the priorities identified by merchants. The budget for the BID would be approximately $300,000. •   The assessment is based on property size, using a formula that combines frontage (linear feet along the street) and commercial square footage. •   BIDs are nonprofit organizations governed by a District Management Association, which is responsible for delivering services and coordinating with city agencies. •   Irene LoRe, former business owner and current Executive Director of the Fifth Avenue BID, noted that BIDs benefit not only the merchants, but all local residents and people who shop and dine locally. BIDs help keep districts vital and are part of the economy of a neighborhood.
•   The Chamber of Commerce has been reaching out to all merchants and property owners through mail and in-person, although there are challenges in identifying some property owners. A majority of the owners must agree to the formation, and there will be a formal public hearing.
Presentation and discussion with representatives of the existing business improvement districts (BIDs) serving the district.
•   Representatives of the three existing BIDs in Community Board 6 (Atlantic Avenue BID, North Flatbush Avenue BID, and the Park Slope 5th Avenue BID) gave overviews of their activities and how they have been serving merchants and local residents. •   Significant accomplishments and changes along Flatbush and 5th Avenue were highlighted. •   The representative of the Atlantic Avenue BID, which is the newest (formed last year), explained current and planned activities and services being provided.

Chairperson Daniel Kummer began his report by announcing that Board Member Marco Chirico, one of our newer Board Members appointed last year, has resigned from the Community Board citing increased demands on his personal time. DISTRICT MANAGER’S REPORT………………………………………….…….CRAIG HAMMERMAN
District Manager Craig Hammerman began his report by advising the board that the Carroll Street Bridge over the Gowanus Canal will close to all traffic for at least four months starting April 1st. The bridge, one of five along the Gowanus Canal, will be shuttered to cars, bicyclists, and pedestrians while the city's Department of Transportation repairs it. DOT will revamp the bridge, which was first built in 1889, by replacing its deteriorated timber deck, structural steel, and making other upgrades. DOT is directing motorists and cyclists to use the nearby Union Street Bridge as an alternative. The work will take place from 7 am to 4 pm on weekdays and is expected to be finished in August.
District Manager Hammerman informed the Board that after a two-year rehabilitation project, Smith-9th Street Station will reopen on April 26th, restoring and     service to the Red Hook, Gowanus and Carroll Gardens communities. The 79-year-old facility—the world's highest subway station at nearly 88 feet—underwent a ground up renewal over the course of 22 months. The rehabilitation began in May 2011 in conjunction with the rebuilding of the Culver Viaduct.
District Manager Hammerman reported to the Board that following extensive damage caused by Hurricane Sandy, the Red Hook Branch Library re-opened on Tuesday, April 2nd. Joining the re-opening ceremony were Brooklyn Public Library President & CEO Linda E. Johnson, Red Hook community members, Brooklyn Public Library staff and leadership, Borough President Marty Markowitz, Representative Nydia M. Velázquez and Assembly Member Félix Ortiz. When Hurricane Sandy hit New York, the Red Hook Library was covered by 18 inches of water, causing the destruction of roughly 2,500 books and other materials, as well as damaged floors, mechanical equipment, furniture, shelving, and supplies. In total, the library suffered $750,000 worth of damages. Brooklyn Public Library President & CEO Linda E. Johnson also announced that the Red Hook Library will undergo a complete renovation in 2014. Together with the non-profit Spaceworks, they will create
2
two new Spaceworks studios in the library, which will be affordable workspaces available for local performance artists to rent, and collaborate with artists to provide new arts education programming in the branch for patrons.
District Manager Hammerman advised the board that the Department of Transportation along with Brooklyn Borough President Marty Markowitz and the 4th Avenue Task Force will be hosting a Park Slope Open House on April 9th at St Thomas Aquinas Church. At the Open House one would be able to view new design concepts for 4th Avenue between Pacific Street and 15th Street and provide feedback. This open house follows a public workshop in February where community members discussed the future of 4th Avenue. The goals of the project are to reduce speeding, create simpler turns, create safer pedestrian crossings and improve safety for all users of 4th Avenue. DOT will update our Transportation Committee at their May 16th meeting.
District Manager Hammerman informed the board of a new initiative by the 76th Police Precinct, entitled "Spot It To Secure It," in which a team of four police officers will patrol a selected area of the 76th Precinct and look for parked cars where iPhones, iPads, laptops, or wrapped packages are left on the seats. The officers will snap a picture and mail it to the car's owner with a form letter. Precinct Commanding Officer Schiff also said the new task force will also be checking apartment building doors to see if they are locked. If one isn't, the landlord will be getting a letter from the NYPD encouraging him to make sure the door is locked at all time.
District Manager Hammerman reported to the Board that the district office would be hosting an informational meeting on April 30th in an effort to better understand the rules and regulations governing restaurants and bars in our district. Representatives from the State Liquor Authority, City agencies and local precincts will be on hand to answer any questions in respect to noise, smoking, backyard usage, garbage and other related issues.

History of house: Built in 1833 (frame house with clapboards); damage done to building in “great fire” in December 1835; Mansard roof added in 1860’s; stucco placed over clapboards in 1922.
Plans are to remove stucco, replace rotted clapboards with new wood boards (painted grey), and restore doorway, other architectural details, and add/replace shutters (as per original treatment).

CHAIRPERSON’S REPORT………………………………………………………....….DANIEL KUMMER
Chairperson Daniel Kummer began his report by reporting to the board that within the past week we’ve had 2 resignations from the Community Board, bringing our total headcount down to 45 members. Board Member Monique Verret, who has served on the Community Board for at least a decade, has cited competing demands on her personal time which has made attendance difficult. She has asked to remain on the Transportation Committee and will continue to serve out her term as a committee member. Board Member Joni Kletter has also cited competing demands on her time having also been appointed as a trustee at the Park Slope Civic Council and serving as a delegate in Council Member Lander’s Participatory Budgeting initiative. She has also requested to stay on the Parks/Recreation Committee as a committee member. He thanked them both for their selfless service to our communities and for their continued service as active committee members.
Chairperson Kummer reminded the Board that each year the Executive Committee reviews the existing committee structure of the board to see if any changes should be considered for the coming year. While we have all noted the heavy caseload our Permits & Licenses Committee carries we do not have a consensus on how our structure could be changed to better distribute the work. So for our upcoming 2013-14 session we will not be making any changes to the existing committee structure. Applications for committee membership will be out in June, appointments made in August, and the new one-year terms are effective on September 1st.

At our next Transportation Committee meeting at 6:30pm on Thursday, May 16th DOT will be presenting their findings and recommendations to us for review and consideration. The meeting will be held at the Family Reception Center at the corner of 4th Avenue and 9th Street.

District Manager Hammerman reported to the Board that he recently met with the Deputy Director of the Mayor’s Office of Operations. For the last 25 years, the Mayor’s Office of Operations has been taking monthly measurements of street and sidewalk cleanliness throughout the City. He brought to the director’s attention the fact that we have a very substantial and swiftly changing infrastructure on our street and public spaces. The introduction of new elements like bike corrals, the expansion of class 1 bicycle lanes and the roll-out of new bike docking stations to name a few, have an unintended consequence of creating opportunities for litter to collect. The Department of Transportation has a mission to expand these elements and our board has generally been supportive of these types of projects. But at the same time the Department of Sanitation has an obligation to clean our streets and this new infrastructure has made that task much more challenging. If unattended this challenge could result in a diminished quality of life which was not the intention. We have challenged them to come up with a better way to accurately monitor cleanliness in light of the new infrastructure. They acknowledged that this is a growing need and is unsure whether the current administration would be able to do anything in the short amount of time they have left. We did get their attention and their commitment to get the ball rolling.

Warren Cohen, spoke about the importance of including the communities voice in large development, i.e., The Lightstone Group project, in the Gowanus section of our district. Brooklyn CB6 wrote in their letter to City Planning that when Lightstone proposed a minor modification to the project that there was discomfort with the process that the normal land use procedures were not followed. As we all know that since that modification has been withdrawn, one of the largest developments in the Gowanus will go up as an “as-of-right” project with no input from this board, our elected officials or the community. If we had discomfort with the old process we definitely should have it with the way this project is moving forward. Since the last time this project was discussed we have been devastated with Hurricane Sandy which made building this project in its current proposal a game changer. Since then our elected officials have written letters asking that the project be postponed until further studies could be done in regards to the impact on the community and/or what safety measures should be put into place to prevent such devastation as it was after Hurricane Sandy. Presentation and discussion with a representative for the Commission on Human Rights on the mission, programs and services offered by the agency.
The presentation was made by Paula L. Sanders, Deputy Director for the Community Service Center in Brooklyn.
- Each borough has one
- Law enforcement agency under the Mayor
- Strongest human rights laws in the country
- Jurisdiction in housing, employment, public accommodation — anyplace providing goods or services to the public.
Protected Classes: Gender (includes sexual harassment), Color, Race, Creed (religion), Alienage (citizenship), Age, Marital status, Nationality, Partnership status, Disability, Sexual orientation.
Familial Status (children, housing). Arrest and conviction record (employment). Lawful occupation (housing). Lawful source of income (housing). Status of domestic violence victims/survivors.
- Income is not a protected class
- Takes on cases by case basis, not class action suits.
Housing — jurisdiction for apartments of 6 floors or more or 2-3 family homes.
Employers — it is illegal in NYC to ask if you've been arrested. Can ask if you've been convicted, however.
Agency sends out testers to make sure employers and housing authority are being fair.
Judge decides based on merits of complaint.
No jurisdiction over NYPD — no "stop and frisk" control.
No jurisdiction under NYCHA (NYC Housing Authority).
Last year, the City Council added cyber-bullying to the list of protected classes.
Discrimination complaints can be filed either with the city or the state but the city covers more categories.
Commission can go after other city agencies but not NYPD or NYCHA.
As of June 11th, another protected class is being added — Unemployment status. It is illegal for employers to not hire if someone had been unemployed for a year or more.

Chairperson Daniel Kummer began his report by welcoming our newest Community Board members who are joining us tonight for the first time. Chairperson Kummer reminded the Board that application forms for Committee Membership have been sent out and are due next week. It is generally my preference to give our members their top choices so please complete and return them to the district office as quickly as possible. I will rely on the information you provide in your application to make appointments to our committees. Appointments are for a one-year term effective September 1st. We would like to get appointment letters out in early August.
Chairperson Kummer highlighted a couple of important items that will be discussed at our next Transportation/Public Safety committee meeting. At that meeting we will have a brief presentation from representatives for Forest City Ratner Companies on the effectiveness of their Traffic Demand Management initiatives. If you would like to learn more about the actual traffic impacts associated with the opening of the Barclays Center, see the data about how people are arriving and leaving, and have any ideas to offer on how things can be further improved, this would be a good meeting to attend. Also on the agenda that evening, we will have a representative from the Office of Emergency Management who will be briefing us on disaster preparation. They will be unveiling their newest hurricane evacuation plans which are especially relevant to our district since we regularly experience flooding in our Gowanus and Red Hook waterfront communities. District Manager Hammerman reported to the Board that the New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene and the CUNY School of Public Health will randomly select 3,000 New Yorkers in all five boroughs to participate in the New York City Health and Nutrition Examination Survey or NYC HANES. We will ask them to answer questions about their health and to take a brief physical exam that includes free lab tests. Each individual will receive a stipend of $100.00. When NYC HANES was first conducted in 2004, they found out how many New Yorkers were at risk for heart disease, how many had diabetes, and how many of those with diabetes were being effectively treated. They also learned that New Yorkers were breathing in more second- hand smoke than other people around the country, and that some groups had higher levels of mercury in their blood. Sex workers report that they are more likely to be arrested if they carry condoms. Police officers regularly confiscate condoms from people they allege are engaged in prostitution to use as evidence against them at trial. As a result people are hesitant to carry condoms to protect themselves and others; for fear that it will lead to arrest or be held against them in court. NYC Build it back. 4 Pathways Repair, Rebuild, Reimburse, Acquisition
Questions about whether you have to build to building code.
If it wasn’t conforming to building code, need to bring it up to building code. If substantially damaged and in flood zone, need to rebuild to code for flood location. Presentation and discussion with representatives for the Red Hook Initiative (RHI) on the programs and services they provide to our local community. Presentation and discussion with representatives for the Red Hook Community Justice Center on the programs and services they provide to our local community.
RHI discussed their Young Adults Program which began in December 2012.
Presenters included:
Jade Elias – Director of Programs Fabiola – Social worker Tiwan Burros – Digital Steward Carlos Viveros – Program assistant Rebecca Fishburne – Program Coordinator Danny Aiken – Social Justice Fellow
Participants must be between the ages of 18-24 and live in the Red Hook community.
The program offers job training and GED classes. The job training includes resume writing, interviewing and other soft skills, as well as placement at local businesses. They currently have 11 business that have hired graduates with Ikea being having taken the most.
The participants get hired for 8-10 hours a week paid for by RHI. The businesses must provide training as well.
52 young adults have been placed so far with IKEA taking 16 of those, ten of which have become full-time jobs.
They also have a Digital Steward program where they have partnered with OTI, Open Technologies Institute, to provide free wi-fi throughout the Red Hook community. They have covered Coffey Park so far. They also took a trip to Detroit recently to share ideas and best practices as well as learn some new skills
Another program is their Social Justice Fellows. These young adults take on local social justice challenges such as the LICH Closing, Stop Question and Frisk, and housing issues. After meeting with the 76th Precinct several times they have seen a decrease in local stops among kids in the area.
Their education program has taken in 15 students with one having passed the GED already.
They need more meetings with businesses that might be willing to hire interns and tech help regarding learning technology skills.
Red Hook Community Justice Center, information presented by Jessica Colon
Launched in June 2000, the Red Hook Community Justice Center is the nation's first multi- jurisdictional community court. It serves juveniles in family, housing and criminal court for misdemeanor charges. Last year they had over 11,000 cases.
They have increased their treatment services for people coming through the system and that are identified as having drug abuse problems or mental health issues. About 2000 cases went through those programs last year.
They report that crime is low in the area with no murders in the area and no reported gunshots since last November.
A recent innovation that they are piloting in New York State is not sending 16 and 17 year olds through the adult court system as they currently are for certain crimes. Instead they are given a chance to be tried as juveniles and upon successful completion of assigned programs their cases are sealed.
They are also developing new Alternative to Incarceration program. And some other programs include GED classes, Art programs and internships.
In the last year the work with the community and NYCHA after Sandy was a great experience and the recent changes to the age limits for offenders being tried as adults were two of the highlights for the year.
They also always need new business to partner with.

Chairperson Daniel Kummer reported to the Board that the committee reviewed the Department of Transportation's proposal to redesign 4th Avenue traffic corridor.
Motion:        by Committee;
Recommendation to approve a proposal by the Department of Transportation to redesign 4th Avenue traffic corridor (between Atlantic Avenue and 15th Streets) with the following conditions: 1) That the department return to the Community Board with specific proposal(s) to review before any other changes are implemented for 4th Avenue, including but not limited to the addition of loading zones, bicycle corrals, bicycle lanes, metered parking, etc.; 2) That the prohibited southbound left-turns be further reviewed with an eye toward including additional signage and/or other strategies that would minimize the impact of turning traffic that is displaced specifically to 5`h and/or 10`h Streets; 3) That the department return to the Community Board with an evaluative report one-year after the project implementation; 2
4) That the department collects new traffic and pedestrian counts in the vicinity of the Whole Foods Market at 3rd Avenue and 3rd Street, within 6 to 12 months after the store opens; and, 5) That the department further review and develop plans to beautify the 4th Avenue corridor beyond the limited plantings suggested in the revised plan.
Board Member Judith Thompson stated that she has driven on 4th Avenue in Sunset Park and was frustrated because of the painted markings on the ground. DOT should “build up” with cement where the markings are as well as including beautification enhancements for the medians in the proposal.
