DOT is totally right to calm traffic on 4th Avenue. We have heard the numbers of injuries 646 in 5 years; we can have fewer with this plan. We also heard that this plan would be good for drivers too. He does not want anyone else to die on 4th Avenue, so let’s turn 4th Avenue from a deadly speedway into a proper Brooklyn street.
Board Member Gary Reilly stated that the issue is less about what 4th Avenue is and what it could be, but more about what the kind of 4th Avenue we want and deserve and he thinks this plan moves us into that direction.
Board Member James Bernard stated that he has never heard of any disagreement with the thrust of the proposal, people would like to preserve the 3rd Street and 9th Street turns. He wished we had more time to digest the proposal and the stats on the turns. It just does not make any sense, a lot of traffic and angry drivers will be pushed to 5th Avenue and a little more traffic on the side streets like 5th and 10th Streets is still bad. We can ask for other things to happen at 3rd and 9th Streets to make it safer.
Board Member Peter Fleming stated that he agrees with his colleague that he does not disagree with the intent or the majority of the things they want to do in this proposal, there are elements of it that they have not thought enough about and that because they don’t seem to have the tools to think about them they kind of just sort of gloss over them a little bit. He wished that we had the power to be more specific about what we like and what we don’t like, but it is probably not worth it and he will agree with it by and large but there are elements to it that he does not agree with.
Board Member Benjamin Solotaire spoke in favor of the motion stating that 4th Avenue is changing and developing and although he understands the issues of the residents on 10th Street, we need to make it safer for the community overall.
Board Member Suzanne Turet stated that she agrees with the motion but is frustrated that DOT will not reconsider the removal of southbound left turns on 3rd and 9th Streets.
Board Member Elly Spicer spoke out against the motion stating that the removal of the southbound left turn onto 9th Street is ludicrous. In Sunset Park along 4th Avenue there is not the same type of community, i.e. a cemetery-vs.-commercial strip, so it is hard to make the comparison between the two neighborhoods.
Board Member Roger Rigolli stated that the plan sounds good. Like they mentioned they used theory first and then practical application. Why couldn’t they use theory with everything stopped and let pedestrians cross, with one side making a left turn when that goes red the opposite side makes the left turn and see how that works with theory, it might work the other way too. What he dislikes is when Board Members use sensitive feelings and bring that into play here he thinks that is wrong. Emotions should not be a part of these meetings because sympathy should not work here. We should have rules and regulations and stick to the subject without getting emotional and bringing emotional people into this.
3
Board Member James Bernard asked if we could amend the motion to include not removing the southbound left turns from 4th Avenue at 3rd and 9th Streets. Chairperson stated that we already ask DOT to eliminate those elements and they stated no.
Board Member Philip Mindlin stated that the arguments in favor of this proposal, i.e. number of deaths, number of injuries may be relatively small in regards to not allowing the turns on 3rd and 9th Streets, while the arguments for not implementing are based on emotions not data. In his mind the data wins.
Board Member Judith Thompson stated that when making the decision we must also consider the change in the community around 3rd Street, i.e. Whole Foods, and the new residents coming to the neighborhood from new developments in regards to safety on 4th Avenue.
Board Member Gary Reilly stated that DOT has reported that we get the most conflicts, the most accidents and the most injuries from 3rd and 9th Streets.

COMMUNITY DISTRICT MAP CHANGES
Every 10 years, in the year that ends in 3 and by on October 1st, the Mayor proposes a new map to the City Council with possible changes to the Community District maps based on decennial Census and any operational concerns of the City.
-   For us, an area of particular attention is the Barclays Center/Atlantic Yards footprint which straddles Community Boards 2, 6 and 8. -   The Police precinct boundaries have changed because of Barclays Center. -   Community Boards 2 and 8 have been discussing. One concept being considered by CB2 is to keep the Community Boards’ boundaries coterminal with the police precinct boundaries. -   CB8 would like to keep open rail yards and is not suggesting supporting coterminality
District Manager Craig Hammerman presented a series of maps with various community district mapping scenarios (existing conditions, map showing new police precinct boundaries, ideas from CB2 and CB8). The District Manager also prepared a table highlighting the similarities and differences between the various scenarios.
Motion: The Brooklyn CB6 takes a presumptive default position favoring coterminality unless a compelling argument is made to consider something different, and that the boundaries generally respect neighborhood integrity.
After a great deal of discussion and consideration Suzanne Turet withdrew her motion based on consensus that we need more information before making a resolution. What the committee would like specifically is more information related to the resulting population addition and how that would affect Councilmanic apportionment on the Community Board, further input from the Police Department on how the new police precinct boundaries are working, input from the Department of Sanitation and other agencies on what impacts they perceive from a new district boundary.
The committee did recognize that it is possible that our District Manager may be consulted, as the Administration is required to do prior to the release of their proposed map, and did want him to strongly convey the thoughts of the committee even in the absence of a formal resolution of the full board. The committee does intend to take this matter up further, hopefully with additional information to consider and/or in response to any proposals put out by the Administration. This is an important subject and the Community Board will need to ultimately adopt a position in this matter.

*** MINUTES ***
Presentation and review of a proposal to establish a community garden at 503 President Street (Block 440, Lot 45) between Nevins Street and 3rd Avenue).
Summary: Review of two competing proposals for the use of the lot at 503 President Street:
1) HPD proposal to transfer the community garden "A Small Green Patch" (SGP) from 348 Bergen Street to a new location at 503 President Street. There was no representative from HPD at the meeting to explain the transfer process and governing rules. 2) President Street Block Association's counter-proposal to register the site at 503 President Street as new community garden under the NYC GreenThumb program.
A Small Green Patch represented by Tami Johnson. President Street Block Association represented by Ivan Rodrguez and Barbara Quadrello. Paula Segal spoke on behalf of 596 Acres, a public open space/garden advocacy group.
Tami Johnson – liaison for A Small Green Patch: Excerpts from Tami Johnson's reading from a written statement by the participants and members of "A Small Green Patch":
   SGP has always known its lot on Bergen Street would be a temporary space.    SGP contains plants and a green space and is made up of local organizations and individuals from the community who service, attend, and volunteer at the space.    Events and Activities at SGP include: 1. St Lydia’s food kitchen 2. Workshops held by the Textile Arts Center 3. Feedback Farms 4. A beekeeper for pollination of flowers 5. Pot Luck dinners 6. Live Music 7. Flowers, Plants and vegetables 8. Composting 9. Hosted a 1 million tree giveaway event 10. Perennial garden
Development funding for the lot being used for SGP was approved in Spring, 2013. Existing GreenThumb garden license allowed for the relocation of the space within a .5 mile radius. 503 President Street was identified as a potential lot for relocation. Residents of the block were engaged by Tami through knocking on doors and two public meetings held at the lot. 22 people
attended the meetings.
Residents voiced a mix of support and opposition: Vocal opponents of the SGP relocation plan expressed evolving concerns with the project. Initially they expressed a desire to leave the land vacant, then they raised concerns about their lack of control over the space, and most recently they have come forward with their own garden proposal.
Many member of SGP are no longer interested in moving to 503 President Street as a result of the block association’s opposition.
SGP member would support any group effort to turn 503 President Street into a space that is accessible to all in the community.
Questions Q: How long has SGP been in their current location? A: 2 Years Q: What is the size of the Bergen Street lot? A: Three lots, each 20 x 100, totaling 60 x 100 = 6,000 sq.ft. Q: What is the Parks Department role? A: Parks Department issues a GreenThumb license to those that want to tend to a garden in a now vacant lot. The Parks department acts as a liaison between GreenThumb, the Department of Sanitation, and the HPD (city agency for Housing and Public Development.) Q. Does SGP have members? A: Yes, 20-40 members. Q: Are there any other eligible lots located within the .5 mile radius of SGP? A: No. Q: Are you losing all three lots that comprise SGP? A: Yes Q: How big is the President Street lot?
A: 20 x 100 feet Q: Did you state that members of SGP are no longer interested in relocating to President Street location? A: Feedback farms will not relocate, St. Lydia’s will not relocate, the beehive will not relocate. However a small group of members are still interested in building something at a new location.
President Street Block Association represented by Ivan Rodriguez and Barbara Quadrello Excerpts from President Street Block Association (PSBA) statement:  PSBA is committed to making positive productive use of the lot located at 503 President Street as a community park.  Formal Request has been made of HPD for a community sit-down park.  PSBA has the means, structure, and finances to run and operate this land as a park steward.  For 25 years numerous attempts have been made by members of the President Street community to determine the true owner of the lot at 503 President Street.  They have prepared a packet illustrating their proposal for the land to the CB6 Committee.  Members of the PSBA are architects and landscapers able to help develop the lot.  The PSBA does not want any vegetable or food growth on the property.  The PSBA has local support from individuals and neighborhood businesses to develop this lot as a park.
PSBA’s concerns with SGP’s intentions for the lot are as follows: 1) Food growth on the lot 2) Privacy 3) Security 4) Adjacent homeowners’ concerns
Questions Q: Do you have any documentation of the prior attempts made to secure this site? A: No. All questions and solicitations for information were done via telephone. Neighbors previously had an attorney investigate ownership of the land, and attempts were made from residents to purchase the land from the city. The city was not able to identify the true owner of the parcel in these attempts. Q: Did you ever attempt to contact the Parks Department? A: No Q: If this lot is designated to the PSBA, what will be the legal outcome? A: GreenThumb will designate this as an interim park pending the CB6 decision. Committee Member Glenn Kelly clarified that this lot is zoned for manufacturing, however the HPD is willing to turn over the land to the Parks Department. A: The PSBA’s ultimate goal is to become a part of the GreenThumb program. Q: Do you expect to manage and maintain the site? A: The Parks Department will manage park maintenance. Q: Do you have a budget for this work? A: No, but we expect to do fundraising Q: Why was it so difficult to determine the owner of the property when that information is on
ACRIS?
A: We were not given any answers by various city agencies and these inquiries went back 25 years, well before ACRIS.
Glenn Kelly: Tami can you give some insight as to how you started up SGP? Tami: Persistence and it took two years to get the information needed from the city and Jack Hammer. Scott Stringer posted an opinion stating that public land should be turned over to the public, and I used that as leverage to gain support for the community garden project. A private property owner not using his lot gave permission and support for a SGP, and the HPD approved use of the two lots adjacent to the private lot.
Q: How long was the SGP lot empty before SGP? A: 30 years. Q: What are your plans for access of the park? PSBA: Not discussed. Paula Segal: Public park regulations stipulate 30 hours a week. Q: To both parties – 1) Are you incorporated, are you a 501C3, do you have bylaws? PSBA: Not incorporated, not a 501C3. Yes we have by-laws, but we are very new. Tami: Not incorporated, not a 501C3, no bylaws.
Presentation for clarification by Paula Segal, Legal Director of 596 Acres
 596 Acres is a community legal access advocacy to systematize neighbor’s pursuit of taking care of unused land in their neighborhood.  From a liability standpoint, public land is basically the same as the city sidewalk. The city is slowly chipping away at its liability by turning these lots into parks.  You should not incorporate if you plan to steward public land, as this will subject you to liability.  The Giuliani administration took an inventory of surplus land and found 11,000 surplus lots. 600 of those lots had been turned into community gardens. The administration moved to auction off those garden lots. The Trust for Public Land bought some, as well as other organizations.  The Attorney General represented the gardeners against the city and won the decision in 2010  The resulting rules and regulations for using surplus land for public gardens has morphed into what is now known as the GreenThumb program.  One of the rules of the GreenThumb program stipulates that any garden forced to move from its temporary location will be given the option to relocate to a new available lot within a .5 mile radius.  Once relocated, the new garden must be given a more permanent status, and be taken over officially by the Parks Department  The HPD manages many properties - some are too small or difficult to sell off.  The Parks Department does not want to take on any new properties, due to its own budget constraints but in the case of a relocated GreenThumb property, they cannot say “no”.
Q: Tami – what is your vision for the lot at President Street? Tami: Vision will depend on the result of meetings and opinions of members of SGP. It will not contain a vegetable garden or any food growth as Feedback Farms is not interested in the lot and the lot is not conducive to food growth.
Paula: GreenThumb license is not like a lease. The only indication of stewardship of the land is a Garden Contact and a Volunteer List. It is permission, not a right and it is not given to any one person. If the Garden Contact expires, the permission for the lot is still valid.
Q: Who currently has access to the lot at President Street? PSBA: The lot is now completely fenced in, but prior to last year there was access through the rear of the lot by neighbors’ backyards.
Committee Member Ian Dutton voices concern that the PSBA is using language such as “privacy” in their petition for the lot, rather than language such as “access”, indicating their intent to have a private rather than public space.
PSBA: Have spoken to neighbors of the SGP Bergen lot who have complained about rats and about the composting done on site.
Tami: SGP is willing to make the President Street lot an entirely new space, with new bylaws, and new membership.
Norman Cox: I would like to flesh out the requirements for obtaining GreenThumb status
Paula: Bloomberg administration wants to top-down master-plan everything. The City Department of Long Term Planning has put a hold on all new licenses until a new plan is unveiled. Have been waiting for this new plan since October 2012. Some new licenses have however been awarded due to the advocacy work of 596 Acres to push things through. Six new gardens have been approved since May.
Motion was presented by Committee Member Jeff Strabone.
1) Committee to recommend that HPD execute the relocation of A Small Green Patch to 503 President Street. 2) Committee requests that A Small Green Patch work with the President Street Block Association on a mutually desirable outcome for the lot at 503 President Street.
Motion made in the interest of making more likely the outcome of having a permanent park at 503 President Street. Motion seconded by Ian Dutton
Judi Francis: Recognizes Tami’s experience and hard work, but feels that the neighbors closest to the lot should have special consideration in the fate of that lot. Glenn Kelly: As a 23 year volunteer in Carroll Park, recognizes the difficulty in maintaining a volunteer staff, and believes it would be foolish to ignore the help of SGP. Ian Dutton: Agrees with Jeff and appreciates Tami’s demeanor today. Christina Calabrese: We are only hearing two sides of a multi-faceted issue.
Amendment made to motion: 1) Committee requests that A Small Green Patch and the President’s Street Block Association, following their agreement on the plan for the lot at 503 President Street, make a report of that plan to the CB6 Committee.
Motion for Amendment Seconded by Ian Dutton.
John Heyer: Has the committee ever give a space over to another neighborhood? Judi Francis: I am the longest serving committee member and I’ve never seen this happen before.
CALL TO QUESTION on the Motion:

CHAIRPERSON’S REPORT………………………………………………………....….DANIEL KUMMER
Chairperson Daniel Kummer began his report by requesting a moment of silence for Samuel Cohen-Eckstein, a 12 year-old boy who was killed while chasing a ball into the street at the intersection of Third Street and Prospect Park West in Park Slope.
Chairperson Kummer congratulated City Council Member Letitia James on her Primary Run-off election victory for the Democratic line in the Public Advocate’s race. Of course, that means we’ll also continue to be served by State Senator Daniel Squadron’s representation of our district in Albany. This Friday, October 11th, is the last day to register to vote in the General election which will be on November 5th. We have Voter Registration forms here tonight. Please take them to anyone you think could use them. There will also be 6 referendums on the ballot this year so you probably will want to take a few minutes to look them over before heading to the polls. The district office will send out a link to them on the Board of Election’s website.
Chairperson Kummer informed the Board that the Environmental Protection Agency released their Record of Decision (ROD) on September 30th, which effectively spells out the remedial strategy they will be pursuing with regards to the cleanup of the Gowanus Canal Superfund site. In the 105-page decision, with over 3,000 pages of supporting documentation, the EPA outlines the general dredge and cap process they intend to use along the canal. They also said they intend to include aggressive measures to mitigate the Combined Sewer Overflow (CSO) issues, specifically by forcing the City to build tanks at two locations near the highest volume outfalls to retain CSO solids. Lastly, the EPA will not be using Red Hook for a Confined Disposal Facility, one of the other controversial elements of their proposed remedy. Now that the ROD has been issued, they will be spending the next 2 years designing the actual remedies. This is where we’ll actually get into the planning for elements like how the dredged materials will be transported and where they will set up staging and processing areas. The dirty work is still ahead of us. We have encouraged the EPA to work with our district office as a good way for them to obtain insight and help keep the community informed. He thanked Board Member Mark Shames our Environmental Protection Committee Chair and our District Manager Craig Hammerman who were there to represent us, and also acknowledged Board Members Glenn Kelly, Gary Reilly and Ariel Krasnow were also in attendance.
Chairperson Kummer encouraged all of our members to consider attending the upcoming meeting of our Economic/Waterfront/Community Development & Housing Committee where we will be hearing from the consultant who has been working on our Gowanus Brownfield Opportunity Area program grant. At this meeting you’ll have a chance to learn about what we’ve discovered about the Gowanus, why it has become such a hotspot for artisans, craftspeople and artists, new media and new manufacturers, what the challenges are that the area is currently facing, and where there are some strategic sites that could make a difference in the area. The committee is meeting at 6:30pm on Monday, October 21st at PS 58, on Carroll Street at Smith Street in Carroll Gardens.
Chairperson Kummer advised the Board that in July we co-sponsored an Informational Meeting with the Park Slope Civic Council regarding New York Methodist Hospital’s new, state-of-the-art facility on an assemblage of properties they own which front on 5th Street, 8th Avenue and 6th Street. At the meeting Methodist representatives were able to share their concepts with us and gather some early feedback from the community. The hospital returned to our Landmarks/Land Use Committee at their September 26th meeting to present us with the most current version of their project plans which incorporated community feedback. They have redistributed bulk from the building away from the nearby residential uses and eliminated the proposed traffic pass-through from 6th to 5th Streets. We are anticipating receiving their Board of Standards and Appeals application any day now, so we can finalize the planning for a Public Hearing.

Chairperson Kummer reported to the Board that they would hear later from our Budget Chair Rick Luftglass when he presents our Fiscal Year 2015 Capital and Expense budget priorities and in anticipation of that I would like to acknowledge him, along with Board Members Ariel Krasnow and Bob Levine from our Executive Committee who, along with District Manager Craig Hammerman and Assistant District Manager Leroy Branch, attended our annual budget consultations with the City agencies on September 17th. This 5-hour budget marathon session is a real commitment. We are indeed fortunate to have members who are willing and able to represent us and I wanted to single out their efforts and thank them.
Chairperson Kummer ended his report by informing the Board that this year, the Brooklyn CB6 holiday party is going to be on Tuesday, December 17th. The district office is still looking for people to volunteer to help as this is a fundraiser for our non-profit affiliate, Friends of Brooklyn Community Board 6, Inc. If you’ve got some time to spare please call Director of Special Projects Sarah Phillips at the district office and let her know you can help.
DISTRICT MANAGER’S REPORT………………………………………….…….CRAIG HAMMERMAN
District Manager Craig Hammerman began his report by informing the Board that James Proscia, BK6 Superintendent has retired and is being replaced by Superintendent Nando Sala. He further reported that the Department of Sanitation will be instituting their annual shift to night collection hours in mid-November, continuing through mid-April, to ensure that personnel are available around the clock in the event of emergency snow removal. Each year one of the five Sanitation sectors within the district is shifted to nighttime collection. This year Sector 62 which encompasses Cobble Hill, North Carroll Gardens, and the Columbia Street areas of our district will receive night collections. Also, the Commanding officer of the 76th Police Precinct Deputy Inspector Jeff Schiff was transferred to a Queens command and our new commander is Captain Justin Lenz who will be introducing himself and talking about his strategies, priorities and initiatives for the precinct at our October 17th Transportation/Public Safety committee meeting.
District Manager Hammerman informed the board that the district office has been recently awarded a $29,250 grant from the State Archives department. This grant will enable us to take all of our Land Use records, digitize them and put them on microfiche. In a future grant we envision applying for next year we hope to take those records and create an online content management system making it publicly accessible on the Internet.
District Manager Hammerman ended his report by introducing the new Planning Fellow in the district office Mia Brezin. She will be working with us this year on a special project with a cutting-edge firm called Open Plans (the organization that created the DOT crowdsourcing tool that was used to acquire the bike share program docking station location suggestions). They are working with us to develop a Capital budget mapping tool that will allow us to gather information from the public at-large who will be able to make suggestions to us in regards to our budget requests.

Vilma Hermania introduced Lindsay Donnellon, Carroll Gardens Association’s Community Program Coordinator, who described the Columbia Waterfront District Commercial Vision workshop that CGA sponsored on 11/6/13. She reviewed the workshop process and summarized the goals of the effort. CGA distributed a printed summary of the most important topics discussed during the breakout session.
Q:     Why is the organization named Carroll Gardens Association if it is concerned with Columbia Waterfront?
A:    Name was established many years ago; the organization works focuses primarily on the Columbia Waterfront district.
Q:       How did the need for this activity arise? A:       Local business owners have been interested in this for years; a local merchants association exists but is looking to CGA for coordination and guidance.
Q:      Has funding been set aside? A:      CGA is funded through various sources; for this activity CGA will apply for grants from various public sources.
Q:     How will decisions be made about spending funds received? A:     Final decisions will be made by the merchants association.
Q:     Has a boundary for the “commercial corridor” been established? A:     The entire Columbia Waterfront: Atlantic to Hamilton, Hicks to Van Brunt.
Q:     Who is the action plan for? A:     Any local organizations, agencies or entities.
Q:     How many participants have stores? A:     The majority were business owners, some of them have storefront studios.
Q:      Are you expecting resistance to the suggestion to provide parking meters? A:      Not a lot – merchants feel that metered parking will be good for business. Residents don’t want to lose parking spaces. One suggestion was to develop a public parking lot on land at the end of Sackett Street.
Q:     What about the proposal for mixed zoning? A:     There is concern that ground floor space is being used for residential which interrupts and limits the commercial potential. There is interest in determining if commercial ground floor use could be required.
Q:     Is this effort really coming from the commercial community? A:     CGA has been involved in discussions with various local merchants for years, trying to coalesce a workable group.

CHAIRPERSON’S REPORT………………………………………………………....….DANIEL KUMMER
Chairperson Daniel Kummer began his report by congratulating our Public Safety Committee Chair Matthew Silverman and his wife, Rachel, who gave birth to a son – Adam Jay Silverman – on November 24th.
Chairperson Kummer informed the Board that on Tuesday, December 3rd District Manager Hammerman and I attended a neighborhood forum on Street Safety in Park Slope, the kick-off meeting of a new group called Park Slope Street Safety Partnership which includes the neighborhood’s elected officials, DOT, 78th Precinct, the Community Board, Park Slope Civic Council and Park Slope Neighbors. The group’s purpose is to capture information about unsafe street conditions in the neighborhood and to lobby for increased safety measures called for by Mayor-elect de Blasio in his “Vision Zero” campaign which envisions reducing if not eliminating fatalities and injuries caused by crashes. I’d like to commend the group, particularly Council Member Brad Lander who played an important organizing role, for raising awareness and engaging the community. The Park Slope United Methodist Church was a packed house demonstrating that this issue is foremost on people’s minds.
Chairperson Kummer advised the board that Council Member Lander held his first public meeting called “Bridging Gowanus” which invited all of the people and groups having an interest in the Gowanus Canal corridor into a room for an open and honest discussion about the future of the neighborhood. The process has been facilitated by Pratt, which has a long history of involvement in the area, and is intended to produce a current position paper to present to the new Administration so they will have a good roadmap for the issues and concerns related to the Gowanus. Rather than run from controversy, this group is confronting some very tough questions, not with the expectation that they will all be resolved, but so they could be framed out and presented to the new Administration.
Chairperson Kummer reminded everyone that the holiday party is going to be from 6-9pm on Tuesday, December 17th at The Red Rose Restaurant, 315 Smith Street in Carroll Gardens. We’ve already lined up some generous sponsorship from IKEA, Astoria Federal Savings Bank, and the Law Office of Sclar Adler LLP, but we are still looking for prize donations for the raffle. Small, easy-to-carry items like gift certificates, tend to work well. I’m encouraging all of our members to either solicit or donate a prize so we’ll have lots of prizes to give away. Also, I’m told that our guests who prepay will greatly speed up the entry process at the door so if you have a check with you tonight, feel free to give it to Craig or Leroy so we can add you to the list. As a reminder, we’re asking everyone to pay what they can, typically somewhere in the $40-100 range, but more is even better. Checks made out to Friends of Brooklyn CB6, Inc. are tax deductible to the extent allowed by law.
Chairperson Kummer reported to the Board that we have received a resignation from Board Member Greg O’Connell Jr. He wished him well and thanked him for his selfless service to the Community Board.
Chairperson Kummer ended his report by updating the board on the status of the variance application of New York Methodist Hospital which is before them. The hospital has made an application to the BSA to build an ambulatory care facility on 5th Street-8th Avenue-6th Street. There are actually 3 sets of zoning rules that are involved in this application. When the rezoning of Park Slope was done in 2003 the hospital’s campus was largely carved out causing it to retain mostly its R6 zoning status. The hospital is proposing to build a U-shaped building in which the bottom half is within the R6 zoning and the upper two arms of the building are in R6B and R7B zoning areas. At the November 21st Transportation/Public Safety and Landmarks/Land Use Public Hearing, hospital representatives made a presentation in which they stated that it was exploring possible changes to the design in the R6B and R7B sections on the building. Unfortunately, they did not provide details on the proposed changes that night. As a result the committees did not have complete clarity on what they were 2
asked to vote on that night. There were many residents at the meeting speaking for and against the proposal, most were against, with concerns about the bulk and general appropriateness of the proposed building in the Park Slope neighborhood. They also were concerned about traffic and environmental impact. Those speaking in favor of the application included a number of our elected officials and their representatives, as well as several local clergy members all of whom stressed the hospital’s need to expand in order to survive. After the hearing the committee asked the hospital representatives if they were willing to withdraw or delay its application to allow for provision of more information to the community board and further discussion of the design changes that the hospital had alluded to in its presentation. The hospital was unwilling that evening to withdraw or delay its application. The Landmarks/Land Use Committee did pass the following motion as a recommendation to the board which is before us tonight. The motion is that Brooklyn CB6 disapproves the New York Methodist Hospital's Center for Community Health application since the proposed building would alter the essential character of the neighborhood and is not the minimum relief that could be requested. Further, that New York Methodist work with the Park Slope residents, the area's elected officials and the Community Board to amend the variance request in such a way that would reduce the bulk in the R6B and R7B portions much closer to compliance with the zoning limitations, if not fully into compliance. Following the hearing there were communications between the hospital, Community Board 6 and Councilman Lander in which the hospital agreed to do the following: 1. The hospital would return to the committee in early January to make a further presentation on the following three subjects:  A detailed explanation of the need for a building of the configuration that makes necessary the proposed variances. This would include a description of the functions in the building, their current locations and the projected growth in the near future. The hospital would present the relevant standards and guidelines with respect to size and adjacency for the new facility. The community board requested that they provide us with the information that led them to conclude not to build over the parking lot behind the Rite Aid.  The traffic impact of the development as compared to the present traffic conditions with traffic counts and statistics.  Detailed changes to the building in the R6B and R7B sections.
2. The hospital would write a letter to BSA concerning the fact that extending the community board process would result in our not getting our recommendation to BSA within the normal 60-day allotted period. The BSA does have discretion under its rules explicitly to include late filed recommendations from community boards in its hearing record on an application. The hospitals letter would specifically ask BSA to exercise that discretion in this case to allow our recommendation to be included in the record even if we get it in after the 60 days.
Since the hospital agreed to the above in writing, Chairperson Kummer asked for a motion to recommit.
Motion:                       by Board Member Peter Fleming, seconded by Board Member Roger Rigolli; To recommit matter to Committee.

***MINUTES***
Continued review and discussion of an application (BSA Calendar No. 289-13-BZ) submitted to the Board of Standards and Appeals on behalf of New York Methodist Hospital for a variance pursuant to Section 72-21 of the Zoning Resolution to permit construction of a new ambulatory care facility (Center for Community Health) on the campus of New York Methodist Hospital at 473-541 6th Street, 502-522 8th Avenue, 480-496 & 542-548 5th Street and 249-267 7th Avenue aka 505-525 6th Street (Block 1084, Lots 25, 26, 28, 39-44, 46, 48, 50-59, 164, 1001 and 1002).
Meeting opened with introductory remarks by Executive Committee Chair Daniel Kummer who provided background and context for tonight’s meeting before handing over the chair to Land Use Committee Chair Peter Fleming who ran the rest of the meeting.
Various representatives for New York Methodist Hospital presented information requested from prior meetings, and revised renderings showing reduced bulk, height and setback of portions of the proposed new building that fall in the R7B and R6B zoning districts.
Following the hospital’s presentation Land Use Chair Fleming took many questions and comments from committee members and the public.
A motion was offered by Jerry Armer, seconded by Robert Levine. After discussion of the proposed motion, including the insertion of two additional friendly amendments and further specifications related to the formation of the Construction Task Force, the motion that was ultimately adopted read:
In light of the new information and additional proposed design changes presented by New York Methodist (NYM) following the public hearing on November 21, 2013 and the Landmark/Land Use Committee’s vote to provisionally recommend disapproval of the requested variances, the Committee now moves for a resolution that Brooklyn Community Board 6 (CB6) recommend to Board of Standards and Appeals (BSA) that the variances be conditionally approved and granted, subject to the following conditions:
1) R6 Zoning District: In the R6 zoning district (on 6th St), that the variances for front wall height, setbacks, sky exposure planes, rear yard equivalents, rear setbacks and lot coverage be
granted only if the final building design limits the building height to no greater than the height of a complying development in that district.
2) R7B Zoning District: In the R7B zoning district (corner of 8th Ave and 5th St), that the variances for lot coverage, rear yard setbacks and floor area distribution across district lines be granted only if the final building design is in compliance with the height and setback limitations for the district, as shown in the new renderings presented on January 6, 2014.
3) R6B Zoning District: In the R6B zoning district (mid-block on 5th St), that the variances for lot coverage, rear yard equivalents, rear setbacks and floor area distribution across district lines be granted only if the final building design (i) further reduces the base/streetwall height and building height in that district to significantly lower levels than presented, and (ii) maintains at least the additional setback shown in the new renderings presented on January 6, 2014. In this connection, CB6 commends NYM for its good faith steps to reduce the bulk of the building in the portion that covers that zoning district. However, CB6 does not believe NYM has fully met its burden with respect to the variance factors of impact on the essential character of the neighborhood and minimum necessary variance as they pertain to the upper floors of the proposed building within the R6B district, when those factors are considered in the context of the 2003 Rezoning of Park Slope that imposed R6B limitations for mid-block residential districts in order to preserve the built form of the residential community.
4) Certificate of Need: That NYM commits to providing notice to CB6 of their future NYSDOH Certificate of Need (CON) application at the time that it is filed, along with a copy of the application and a letter summarizing how the CON specifically demonstrates that the granting of these variances will provide the minimum necessary for an efficient and effective ambulatory care facility as designed and envisioned by NYM.
5) Long Range Plan: That NYM commits to the development of a long-range plan which considers the long term needs and objectives of the hospital over the next 20 years at a minimum, and how the hospital intends to meet those needs and objectives in a manner that is both inclusive and respectful of the Park Slope community.
6) Signage: That any variance relating to signage be limited to the square footage specified for each sign in the revised plans submitted to BSA on December 20, 2013 rather than the larger square footage amounts in the original application.
7) 8th Avenue Entrance: That NYM confirm its commitment to limit the usage of the entrance at 8th Avenue and 6th Street in the manner described at the public hearing on November 21, i.e., only for employee use and emergency egress, plus entrance to the Urgent Care facility only during late afternoon and evening hours, and commits that this restriction will take the form of a restrictive covenant.
8) Parking: That NYM follows through on its commitment to reduce the total number of parking spaces in the combined existing and proposed parking facilities by at least 189 spaces, while leaving some margin over current projected demand to absorb future growth. CB6 further urges that NYM commit to use some or all of the savings from such reduction to fund programs that
will reduce hospital staff commutation by auto, such as free or subsidized transit passes and shuttle service from transit hubs and off-site parking facilities.
9) Traffic Task Force: That NYM commits to continue its participation on an open-ended basis in the Traffic Task Force organized by Councilmember Lander’s office, and to collaborate with the community, CB6, and relevant City agencies to address transportation impacts on the community, including further consideration and implementation of measures designed to significantly reduce the amount of vehicular traffic generated by the new facility and/or by existing hospital programs. NYM should further commit to conduct a full scale traffic study as well as a redo of the relevant transportation and environmental portions of the Environmental Assessment Study (EAS) with respect to the final approved development, one (1) year after the new building(s) are in full operation, to determine how traffic is flowing to the new building and whether any problems need to be corrected.
10) Design Discussions: That NYM commits to continue participating in design discussions with the Park Slope Civic Council, CB6, and other concerned members of the community as a means to work toward consensus-building on building design issues, including facade designs, exterior materials and treatments, landscaping and signage, with the goal of achieving a design that is less imposing and blends in better with the lower rise nature of the Park Slope area. Resumption of such discussions should occur immediately and should not await completion of the BSA process.
11) Construction Task Force: That NYM commits to participate fully in, and to direct its contractor to participate fully in, a community advisory task force hosted/chaired by CB6 concerning impacts of the demolition and construction phase of the project, which would meet on a monthly basis and more frequently as needed, until the completion of the project. Furthermore, that NYM should provide a letter to CB6 affirming their commitment to this prior to the general meeting on January 8, 2014.
(LANDMARKS/LAND USE COMMITTEE)
VOTE: 10…..YEAS 5…..NAYS 1…..ABSTENTION
MOTION PASSED.

Board Member Daniel Kummer stated that the most important context for this motion comes from the 2003 rezoning of Park Slope, which dramatically lowered the height and bulk limitations in the residential areas of the neighborhood. The chief concern that drove the rezoning effort was to prevent the proliferation of high-rise development amid the generally low-rise residential blocks of Park Slope. In our letter in 2003 to City Planning the Board overwhelming supported the rezoning plan. In that zoning plan New York Methodist’s campus was specifically carved out of the rezoning, and the hospital retained the more permissive "R6" designation for most of the property they owned on the blocks bounded by 7th and 8th Avenues and by 5th and 7th Streets. However, the remaining quarter of the block between 5th and 6th Streets, on the south side of 5th Street, which included building lots then owned by the hospital, was not included in this carve-out, and was specifically down-zoned to R6B and R7B zoning to match the other nearby residential areas. The result is that there are three different sets of zoning rules that cover the hospital's expansion plan. What this motion says, is that we want this project to stay essentially within the height limits that were put in place as a result of the rezoning, along with some
6
additional conditions. It further states that CB6 is willing to give the hospital some flexibility in the R6B area that was carved out, to make the building bulkier on the 6th street side facing the hospital and in the interior rear yard areas, as long as they don't go any higher in that zone than they could as-of-right. But on the other hand, we do not believe they have met their burden with respect to getting more height flexibility for the portions of the building in the rezoned areas that front on 5th street. In the area on the corner of 8th avenue and 5th Street, which is covered by R7B zoning rules, their latest design has voluntarily knocked a floor off of the building to bring it down to complying height and setbacks. So, the motion states that they have to keep it that way if they want the other variances for aspects of the design that pertain to the interior portion of the lot. In the R6B area at mid-block and 5th Street they have pulled back the setback portion in the upper floors by another 10 ft. This is where the motion specifically says that they have not met their burden under the applicable variance factors for permission to go anywhere near as high as they still want to go. I want to stress that we gave the hospital multiple opportunities to meet that burden of showing that these variances were the minimum necessary to meet their needs. Unfortunately, at the presentation they made to our committee they failed again to make a detailed, data-driven presentation regarding those projected needs. I was personally as disappointed and frustrated as many of our committee members and members of the public who spoke at the meeting and asked questions of the hospital only to receive unsatisfactory answers. But that does not mean that we should, as many have urged, just throw up our hands and say "no,” That brings me to the issue of how this motion is framed, which I would describe as a "yes, but only if you do x, y and z" motion, as opposed to a "no, unless you do x, y and z" motion. There are at least two reasons why I believe the approach this motion takes is the right one. The first reason is institutional. Community boards are often regarded as essentially NIMBY (not in my backyard) organizations that don't give careful well-informed consideration of issues and that can therefore easily be disregarded. This board has long prided itself on not taking a NIMBY approach to issues that come before us. The second reason is practical and situational. This is one of those situations, like many one encounters in life, where it's important to be careful what you wish for. If we say "no, unless...," and that were to actually result in a complete denial of the variances, the hospital owns enough land on this block and has more than enough remaining F.A.R. to build a very large as-of-right building that would be worse both for the neighborhood and the hospital. Finally, I should add that this approach has already yielded a letter from the hospital accepting virtually all of the conditions in this motion and pledging to reexamine the design in the R6B area.
Board Member Robert Levine spoke in favor of the motion stating that the original presentation was not in context with the character of the neighborhood. But we have to look at the larger historic look of the neighborhood which is that the hospital has been there since 1881 and has been a part of the neighborhood as a larger building then the row houses around it since it was built. It was seen then and is seen now as a needed institution. A vote of yes will allow the hospital to sit down with BSA and figure out where the bulk should be and hopefully they will not need as much as originally presented.
Board Member Glenn Kelly stated that he wants to support the Hospital and would like to see them expand but we as a Board are not doing what we should be doing in terms of the 4 findings. If we look to those 4 findings I don’t feel that the Hospital has provided us with enough information for me to feel comfortable that we are doing the right thing here.
Board Member Lou Sones stated that he vote no in the committee, but after hearing the comments tonight he was going to change his vote in favor of the motion. Committee Member Roy Slone made a point that needs to be mentioned. He stated that we need a borough-wide plan. He thinks that when you are building a bigger place and two others are going out of business it puts undue burdens on the neighborhood because that hospital becomes the center of all medical needs instead of evenly distributing throughout the community. Presentation and discussion with representatives for the Fire Department on fire safety.
The presentation was made by Lt. Mario Vasconi and Firefighter George Tabeek. Their office does fire safety presentations at schools, churches and for civic groups.  They give out CO detectors and smoke detectors.  Education on fire risks. They investigate fatal fires and why fire resulted in a fatality.  New smoke alarms have 10 year built-in non-reusable batteries.  Program with DHS (Federal) money for Sandy communities to install CO & fire alarms in homes. Trying to expand it to all of NYC.
To access program for fire safety and to get free alarms, batteries and assistance contact Lt. Vasconi or Firefighter Tabeek.
-   CO alarms are legally mandated and many people do not have them. -   Hot water heaters in boilers produce CO and if the chimney is not clean it can back up into the building. -   20 staff members in this FDNY unit do education and training on safety. -   They have a mobile smoke house. It is a simulated apartment with theatrical smoke for people to learn how to escape a fire. -   Fire extinguishers last for 10 years or until used, whichever is first. -   Discussed requirement to have bars that open. Can’t have residences with locked bars. -   The Department of Buildings enforces the gates on windows.
-   Discussed blocked fire hydrants by Barclay center and other areas. Per the FDNY it is mostly an NYPD enforcement issue – go to Community Affairs officer. NYFD will enforce it if they come across it but not their focus. -   FDNY does hydrant testing. If you see a white circle on a hydrant, it’s out of service. Call 311/NYFD if it’s been out a long time. The Water Department fixes them. -   NYFD started a new program to do outreach to 800,000 NYers who are deaf or hard of hearing. CHAIRPERSON’S REPORT………………………………………………………....….DANIEL KUMMER
Chairperson Daniel Kummer began his report by informing the Board that he, along with District Manager Craig Hammerman and Assistant District Manager Leroy Branch, had a chance to sit down with our new City Council Member Carlos Menchaca to talk about some of our outstanding concerns for Red Hook and offer our support for helping to get him and his staff up-to-speed on the issues affecting the Red Hook community that we’ve been involved in over the years. The Chair expressed optimism about working closely with him and his eager staff who already are making quite an impression on the community.
Chairperson Kummer reported to the Board that yesterday, he appeared and testified before the Board of Standards and Appeals (BSA) at their public hearing on New York Methodist Hospital’s (NYM) proposed new Center for Community Health building which we had voted on last month. This Board resolution and his testimony had a strong effect on BSA and NYM was asked to submit additional materials by March 4th. The community will have until March 25th to comment on those materials.
Chairperson Kummer advised the Board that we had several town hall meetings followed by site visits to our public housing properties in our district as we began to pull together a comprehensive list of our outstanding issues, programs and policies which we intended to bring to the attention of the New York City Housing Authority. Of course, our efforts were interrupted by the impacts of Hurricane Sandy which, itself, became yet another learning experience for us. We have managed to schedule a follow-up meeting with the Presidents of all of our respective tenant associations which will be happening later this month so we should be in a good position to reenergize our advocacy efforts very shortly. The Chair thanked Housing Chair Ariel Krasnow for staying with this important subject. As a sense of scale, we have over 4,500 units of public housing in our district which, according to NYCHA statistics, accounts for more than 10,750 residents. More than 10% of our district lives in public housing. It is essential that we continue to play an active role in the life of our public housing residents and, through our advocacy, work to make conditions better for everyone in our district.
Chairperson Kummer encouraged everyone to consider attending The City Club of New York and Pratt Institute’s Breakfast Panel Discussion called, “Acting Local: Community Boards and Neighborhood Planning” which will include our District Manager as a panelist next Friday, February 21st from 8:30-10:00am. With the substantial turnover in leadership in local government taking place we have a chance to contribute and influence many agendas. Discussions like these are opportunities to explore ideas – old and new ones – and really be a part of the change that’s happening around us.
Chairperson Kummer thanked Board Member Mark Shames and District Manager Hammerman for attending the City Law Borough Presidents Breakfast Panel Discussion held last week with the City’s 5 Borough Presidents. I’m told that we could be very proud of our Borough President Eric Adams for offering some strong
2
opinions on issues important to us, like preserving libraries, strengthening Community Boards, and taking advantage of new technologies but not dehumanizing government in the process.
Chairperson Kummer ended his report by informing the Board that the office of Assembly Members Jim Brennan and Joan Millman, together with other local elected officials, New York Methodist Hospital, and CB’s 6, 7 and 14 will be hosting a Volunteer Fair the evening of Thursday, May 29th. District Manager Craig Hammerman began his report by informing the board that he and Assistant District Manager Branch attended a meeting with the Deputy Borough President Diana Reyna and other District Managers from Brooklyn. We discussed submitting to Borough Hall items that we felt needed to be addressed through the Borough Service Cabinet agenda. The Borough Service Cabinet, chaired by the Borough President or a member of his staff and composed of the district managers of Brooklyn’s community boards and representatives from city agencies, focuses on city service delivery and agency responsiveness across the borough. Since the meeting Borough Hall has addressed at least 3 items on the list we jointly submitted. We look forward to working with the new Borough Hall staff in the future.
District Manager Hammerman advised the board that the annual Youth Acknowledgement Awards application is now available on our website at www.BrooklynCB6.org/Announcements. The awards seek to honor youth who have made a substantial contribution to improving the quality of life in our neighborhoods through direct action or by serving as a positive role model for others. Also available on our website is the Robert Acito Award for Youth Involvement application which will be given to an adult member of the CB6 community who has demonstrated a commitment to young people and has proven to be a positive force in their lives. The awards will be given out at our May Board meeting.

Presentation and discussion with representatives from the Department of Transportation on a proposal to install a new bicycle lane on Bond Street between 3rd Street and Schermerhorn Street. The new bike lane would be a Class III shared lane between 3 rd-Douglass, a Class II bike lane between Douglass-Wyckoff and a Class III shared lane between Wyckoff-Schermerhorn. (Note: The segment of Bond Street between 3rd-Wyckoff is in Brooklyn CB6, and will be the subject of review.)
Approximately 400 bicyclists use northbound Bond Street each weekday, and they make up about 8% of the traffic volume during the morning rush and 16% of the traffic volume in the evening. The new lane will be a Class III shared lane between Third Street and Douglass Street, a Class II lane between Douglass Street and Wyckoff Street and a Class III shared bike lane north of Wyckoff Street. The part of Bond Street north of Wyckoff Street is in CB2. CB2's Transportation Committee approved the plan two days prior to this meeting. Bond Street is not wide enough for a Class I bike lane. Also you lose parking in the turning lanes if there is a Class I protected bike lane. There will be no loss of parking spaces with this plan. The DOT does not believe that Bond Street is the kind of street that has a lot of double parking.
Jerry Armer made a recommendation seconded by Gary Reilly that the DOT go ahead with the plan as
presented. The motion passed unanimously.
Presentation by and discussion with Chris Hrones on Prospect Park West traffic changes, Vision Zero and Bicycle Deliverymen
Prospect Park West
The maximum speed on Prospect Park West has been reduced to 25 MPH. Signage has been posted and traffic signal progression has been changed to reflect the new 25 MPH speed limit. Cars are driving more slowly.
Vision Zero
The new Vision Zero plan has been posted and is discussed in detail on the DOT's website. It is a multi- agency initiative that envisions high level coordination among the DOT, the Police Department and the TLC, with regular meetings, especially between the Police Department and the DOT.
Vision Zero identifies that 1. speeding and 2. failure to yield are the elements that most contribute to serious injury and death and contemplates that the police will aggressively enforce the laws in this regard. Additionally, Corridor Slow Zones with traffic signal progression appropriate to the new lower speeds will be implemented, making it harder to speed.
The DOT will also look to do more with neighborhood slow zones. In Boerum Hill, preliminary reports show the slow zone has had the effect of reducing the 85th percentile speed to just over 20 MPH from closer to 25 MPH. The gateway slow zone signs have not been particularly effective, however, in reducing turning speeds. A number of the signs have been struck by vehicles and moved to the sidewalk.
As part of Vision Zero, the DOT will be looking for community input in a systematic way and will combine this input with its extensive traffic and accident data to make the streets safer for everyone. Reducing the general citywide speed from 30 MPH to 25 MPH will require state approval.
Commercial Bike Deliverymen
Commercial bike deliverymen are required to wear reflective vests and helmets and to obey traffic laws. The vests and the bikes are supposed to have identification signs with the name of the establishment and a number to call. The DOT can give summonses and warnings to business owners but does not ticket the deliverymen.
There being no further business to come before the committee, the meeting was adjourned.

URH does not need Community Board approval, but is required by OASAS to inform the community. They came to speak with YHSE Committee Chairs, Benjamin Solotaire and Paige Bellenbaum over two months ago, and then presented at two community meetings prior to tonight’s joint committee meeting.

Michael Mosberg of URH said they have agreed to come to every community meeting even though they do not require CB6 approval. He confirmed that the OASAS application requires that they let the community know, but URH stated that they are also interested in working with the community and being fully part of the neighborhood.
Mr. Mosberg stated that he lives within a mile of Red Hook, and that through a personal experience he discovered that there is not a single pay-for-services drug rehab in NYC, only non-profit businesses. If someone wants to pay for their rehabilitation, they must leave New York and he feels that there is a market for a business to provide this type of service locally.
Questions were taken: 1. In answer to the question of whether the development makes use of the Community Facility bonus for additional space, the answer was that they are taking no bonus and it is not a designated community facility. The development is in an M1-2, it is being represented as an as-of-right project and does not require a variance.
2. In answer to the question of why a Hotel designation was issued by the DOB, Ms. Mosberg stated that they met with the DOB official (a name was given) who was not sure how to qualify the use, but decided that since it is part medical and part hotel it fell into two use groups. The DOB decided to go with Hotel designation a. The question was asked if the reason for the 28-day treatment stay was because 29 days is considered to be the maximum stay for a transient hotel by the DOB. The answer was that 28 days is a standard treatment length.
3. URH was asked why this location, where else they had looked, for how long, and why a Red Hook manufacturing zone was chosen. Mr. Mosberg stated that he was told that this use type can only be placed in a manufacturing zone and he spent two years looking at locations, all of which were along the Brooklyn waterfront M zones (Red Hook, Gowanus, Williamsburg). He was asked why only in this part of Brooklyn, why not further out where property values and zoning codes might be more flexible. Mr. Mosberg stated that he lives nearby and he would like his business nearby.
4. A request was made for greater detail about the development plan and the size of the facility. The partner, Cal Nathan stated that it is situated on a 100,000 SF lot, on which 200,000 SF can be built, and that the URH is only building a total of 20,000 SF. Mr. Mosberg explained further that the building will be five stories, with a footprint of 5000 SF. There will be four habitable floors raised above a ground floor of parking to account for potential future flooding. A. Krasnow noted that 110 Beard Street is listed as a 58,500 SF lot. Mr. Nathan clarified that the developer owns more than just Lot 16, and can combine his lots for a total of 100,000 SF. Therefore, the 20,000 SF building is completely as-of-right.
5. Mr. Mosberg was asked by the committee to learn more about the building and business plans. URH has gone before the DOB and OASAS with their proposal, so must be more information available on which to judge the merits of the project. Mr. Nathan gave the name of the consultant who prepared the drawings and the application, and then stated that the picture of the building was in a powerpoint that had been shown at an earlier meeting. He displayed the proposed rendering of the building on his tablet. The building is a solid, handsome 5-story brick structure with large loft-like windows and architectural detailing resembling turn of the century industrial buildings. There was no information given about specifications that an intensive drug-rehab facility might require and how that might impact the size or requirements of the building. a. In response to the question about the rent that the URH will be charged and how that might inflate other rents in M1 zone, given that the M1 zone and IBZ status are intended to protect land for industrial use, Mr. Mosberg stated that he did not have to share his business plan.
6. Question was asked regarding how many jobs the business will generate, and how many will be available to local residents. Mr. Mosberg began to describe the types of jobs and number of positions, and said that certainly they would draw from the neighborhood whenever they can, most readily for the unskilled jobs.
7. Concern was expressed about the long-term plans of the owner. Mr. Mosberg was asked how long a lease URH expects to sign. URH has no assurance about the length of the lease and has no agreement in place with the owner. Committee member suggested that URH is only a tenant, and that this substantial building conveys the look of a loft residential building or hotel, therefore, the concern about the long-term plans of the owner.
8. There was a comment that the business is being represented as as-of-right, and that the line of questioning should stay on the business of URH. Will URH consider doing outpatient services in the future if it is successful? Mr. Mosberg replied that it is only in-patient now, and will remain in- patient.
Non CB6 members were invited to ask questions: 9. Jobs: What guarantee is there of jobs for the community. The response above was restated. (how, or is, this included in the benefits agreement?)
10. Quality of life: “How can you be sure that people from URH will not come out and go into the projects for drugs? We spent 40 years getting the drugs out of the neighborhood. When those patients get out they will come right over looking for drugs in the projects.” Mr. Mosberg answered that patients have no money, wallets, credit cards or phones while they are in the facility. They would have nothing to go buy drugs with. When they are released they will be driven out of the neighborhood to a hotel or back to their home.
11. Outreach: Question was raised about outreach to the neighborhood for this and previous community meetings. Frances Brown of Red Hook East said that she was not notified and did not see any posters. Mr. Carter said that he had contacted Ms. Marshall (RHWest) and someone from RHEast. URH have met with Red Hook Civic Association, Red Hook Initiative, Council Member Menchaca’s office and CB6.
12. Community Benefits? Mr. Mosberg stated that URH will have open classes for the community, educational courses and free assessments and referrals. Other community benefits are being worked out with CB6, RHI, and Council member’s office.
13. Will there be an Advisory Committee? Mr. Mosberg stated that there will be an advisory committee that includes community members. It was discussed that the inclusion of community members on this committee will help to keep the Community Benefits agreement active and used.
Discussion continued after the meeting, without URH present. There was agreement on the main issues, but disagreement on which issue was more critical: the Urban Recovery House – a rental business, or whether the owner/developer is using the URH as part of a longer range plan. A discussion ensued regarding the lack of criteria or community plan by which to make a decision on land use. With IKEA and Fairway on either side, why shouldn’t a small building/business like this be built? The 197A plan seemed to support this development, but it is almost 20 years old, and in the current climate, should there be a real effort to maintain an industrial waterfront. Or with the BASIS School and URH, should the uses be allowed to change. It was agreed that the Economic & Waterfront Development should start to look more pro-actively about how CB6 would like to see the waterfront evolve.
In support of the Urban Recovery House: URH seems to honestly care about including the neighborhood and have come each time they were asked even though they do not need CB6 approval. It was commented that the URH team seems a little new to this, and that this may be their first business venture. Mr. Mosberg seems to have given a lot of effort to the Community Benefit agreement. The free assessments and referrals is a huge benefit and he may not even realize how much he offered. Comments were made that a healthy business is better than no business on the site, and that the business
presents itself as being independent without needing any financial subsidies.
Against support of the land use: There is tremendous concern about the owner’s long-term plan. Mr. Nathan mentioned that the owner has acquired more than the just the 110 Beard St. lot. There is distrust among EWCDH committee members about the larger motives of the development. It was felt that more clarification is needed regarding how a 20,000 SF building gets built for one potential tenant, who has no track record in the business that he is providing, and without an agreement in place between them.
A decision was made that the Y/HS/E Committee, who support the URH as a viable business for Red Hook, and the EWCDH Committee, who do not wish to support the land owner’s development plan without more information, will present separate motions.
Y/HS/E made a motion to support the Urban Recovery House EWCDH will prepare a motion identifying the concerns that they would like to have on record
The Motion put forth by the YHSE Committee is as follows:
The Youth/Human Services/Education committee supports the efforts of Urban Recovery House, a private pay, methadone free, substance abuse treatment center serving 25-30 patients to open a facility at 110 Beard St in Red Hook with the conditions stipulated in, but not limited to, the Community Benefits Agreement, attached, with the addition of the formation of a Community Advisory Board to be in place prior to the opening of the facility.
There was not a quorum, but the motion passed 6 in favor, 0 against, and 0 abstentions.
Presentation and discussion with representative for the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene on Take Care New York: A Policy Agenda to Improve the Health of All New Yorkers.
In addition to the URH the committee heard a presentation from Heidi Exline from the DOHMH regarding their Take Care New York: A policy agenda to improve the health of all New Yorkers program.
Developed in 2004 with new goals laid out every four years this is a program to enlist communities around NY to help improve the health of all New Yorkers. They have over 600 community partners, including schools, CBOs, and faith based organizations, working on ten priority areas: Tobacco free living, Healthy Eating, Active living, Heart Health, HIV Prevention, Mental Health Promotion, Alcohol and Substance abuse reduction, Cancer prevention, Healthy outdoor and indoor air, and Quality Preventative Care.
They have many ways for community engagement including of course a website which will be launching in spring 2014 that anyone can register at and track their own progress in over 70 indicators.
There being no further business to come before the Committee, the meeting was adjourned.
Minutes were submitted by Ariel Krasnow.

CHAIRPERSON’S REPORT………………………………………………………....….DANIEL KUMMER
Chairperson Daniel Kummer began his report by informing the Board that two housing police officers, Officers Rosa Rodriguez and Dennis Guerra from PSA 1 the police service area that covers our district, responded to a deliberately set fire this past Sunday, April 6th. Both officers were severely injured after rushing into the fire at a Brooklyn housing development in Coney Island. Officer Rodriguez is in the hospital recuperating from her injuries. Officer Guerra succumbed to his injuries at 6:50am this morning. We mourn this loss of life and extend our condolences to Officer Guerra’s family and the police department for this senseless tragedy. The Chair then asked for a moment of silence to commemorate the life of this brave officer who ran towards danger to protect the lives in his charge, the mark of a true hero.
Chairperson Kummer also extended condolences on behalf of the Board to our Treasurer and fellow Board Member Gary Reilly whose brother Aaron passed away on Saturday, April 5th. A memorial service was held yesterday in Tuckerton, NJ where he lived. We are not aware of any other local commemorations. If you would like to extend your personal condolences to Board Member Gary Reilly, please see District Manager Craig Hammerman to obtain his contact information.
Chairperson Kummer reported to the Board that we have received a resignation from Board Member Christina Calabrese, who recently moved out of the district and whose mounting work demands have exceeded her capacity to volunteer at this time. With her resignation we currently have 44 Board Members.
Chairperson Kummer informed the Board that in recent news we have learned that SUNY received 9 responses to their re-issued Request for Proposals for an operator for LICH and, of the 9 responses many of them included maintaining a full-service hospital as part of their proposal. The highest scoring proposal was announced last week by SUNY and it was the proposal submitted by Brooklyn Health Partners, one of the responses that propose maintaining LICH as a full-service hospital. The CEO of Brooklyn Health Partners has already reached out to us to express their interest in being not only good neighbors, but actively engaged in the community. They are furiously working to close the deal and have until May 22nd under the terms of the Court-ordered schedule. This would appear to be good news for us, but until the deal is closed and perhaps even afterwards, there are still more hurdles in the process. Meanwhile, things appear to be on a much better trajectory which is a good reason to celebrate this milestone in the process.
Chairperson Kummer advised the Board that he is really proud of the work that the Youth/Human Services/Education Committee has been doing by getting involved in a wider variety of issues then they have traditionally, which is expanding our board into areas that we have not admittedly been very influential in the past. Their recent initiative to act as a catalyst and bring together tech-savvy organizations with our local schools to teach students to code will enrich our local curriculum by offering students the opportunity to learn a very marketable and sought-after skill. Further to that end, I want to highlight a very special event that our Human Services Co-Chairs Paige Bellenbaum and Benjamin Solotaire have put together for next month. Our 2
committee, along with an impressive variety of elected officials will be sponsoring a professional panel discussion called “Shining a Light on Postpartum Depression: The Role of Programs, Policy and Public Health.” This panel discussion includes some of the top service providers and leading advocates in the field along with legislators who are working on ways to expand access to services for women and families who suffer from this disorder. The panel discussion will take place from 7-9pm on Thursday, May 29th at the Congregation Beth Elohim on 8th Avenue and Garfield Place in Park Slope and will take the place of their regular committee meeting in May. The district office will be forwarding the announcement, and has already created an event on our Facebook page.
DISTRICT MANAGER’S REPORT………………………………………….…….CRAIG HAMMERMAN
District Manager Hammerman began his report by informing the Board that the district office would be hosting an informational meeting on April 14th in an effort to better understand the rules and regulations governing restaurants and bars in our district. Representatives from City agencies and the local precinct will be on hand to answer any questions in respect to noise, smoking, backyard usage, garbage and other related issues.
District Manager Hammerman advised the board that he was invited to a meeting along with Congress Members Nydia Velázquez and Jerry Nadler with the Federal Aviation Administration and their Regional Administrator to talk about the impact of helicopters on our district, particularly over Red Hook. Last year there were 40,000 helicopter flights over New York harbor. These flights in their general pattern take off from the Wall Street Heliport in Downtown Manhattan and as part of their climb they are ordered to fly over the Buttermilk Channel between Governors Island and Red Hook. New York City Economic Development Corporation participated in the meeting making claims about how important helicopters are to the New York City tourism industry. Of course, their numbers were suspect and questionable in terms of how much was actually a result of being induced by the ability to fly in a helicopter. Much of that money, we believe, would have been spent on tourism in NYC anyway even if helicopter rides were not available. At the end of the day the results of the meeting were not very encouraging, as there was no intent to even consider reducing or further regulating the number of flights that impact our district. And so there is no relief in sight.
District Manager Craig Hammerman informed the Board that on March 25th the Board of Standards and Appeals voted unanimously to approve the application by Basis Independent School. Remember, this was an item that the Land Use Committee was recommending conditional approval of, which the Community Board overturned and ultimately voted to disapprove. The Basis school is planning to open its doors on September 15th. This will be a K-12 school with 1,000 students. It is a private school that will charge $23,500 year tuition. At this point we do not know whether they intend to hold to any of the previous commitments they made to our Land Use Committee while they were reviewing it such as, but not limited to: A. Commitment to hire local businesses where possible; 1. To provide pupil transportation 2. Cafeteria services 3. Security B. Hire local teachers; C. To make their auditorium, gymnasium and other facilities available to the community during off hours when the school was not using them; D. To make scholarships available starting in year two.
District Manager Hammerman reported that the district office will be shortly launching a new crowdsourcing tool, which will solicit ideas from the public for where we could be thinking about future capital budget projects that we would advocate for as part of the Community Board’s role in the City’s budget process. This is not “Participatory Budgeting”. It is a part of the Community Board’s annual attempt to gather input from the public so as to provide informed and supported suggestions to our elected officials that ultimately creates the City’s budget. We are call it “Put Your Money Where Your Map Is” and we will be sending out the link soon. 3
