*** M I N U T E S ***
A motion to adopt the minutes of the last meeting held on March 10, 2014 was made by Rick Luftglass and seconded by Glen Kelly.
Brief report by Daniel Kummer about demarcation between CB2, CB8 and CB6 around the Barclay Center, and the conflict on the community district map.
Updates from our District Manager Craig Hammermant:
1) Our Community Budget Suggestions mapping project is being looked at and people are finding it useful. Other Community Boards have requested the tool for their own use.
2) Winding down of Gowanus BOA project which, among other byproducts is transitioning into to an Industrial BID feasibility study for the Gowanus area.
Discussion of the possibility of making changes to the committee structure. Chairman Kummer reminded Executive Committee members that our bylaws requires us to take a look at our existing committee structure on an annual basis to determine whether there should be any changes for the upcoming year. New committee session begins on September 1 st of each year, with applications for committee requests going out in June.
Glenn Kelly brought up question of why Landmarks/Land Use starts at 6:00pm and not 6:30pm, now that their load is lighter. The District Manager offered that the earlier start time was viewed as necessary when the committee had a much more substantial caseload, a good portion of which has been shifted to the Permits & Licenses Committee. Since neither committee chair was present, it was the sense of the group that this should be pursued with them after the meeting and,
if they were in agreement, we could move the start time to 6:30pm at this time to be consistent with all other committees.
Discussion of Public Notification and Outreach Standards and Rules.
District Manager Hammerman said that it is good and healthy for us from time-to-time to review our procedures for consistency, efficiency and efficacy. The district office and individual board members have observed and suggested some ways in which we could strengthen our public notification and outreach standards and rules to ensure that the public has convenient and ample access to information about the Community Board for actions coming before us which may impact the community. The District Manager prepared and distributed a list of problems and proposals for discussion purposes.
Suggestion that many of the newer public notice procedures used in liquor licenses be used in other committees so we have one consistent set of rules.
Glenn Kelly suggested that we incorporate a checklist of the various forms of notification and outreach procedures that applicants can use.
Discussion of whether to use perjury language on our certification form to make people more responsible (with words) like swear or affirm.
We propose a single issue standard notification format for other non-hearing items so the applicant and public would not be confused.
Suggestion to have different templates for different kinds of notifications (i.e., liquor licenses, sidewalk cafes, landmarks, land use, etc.) as opposed to one-size-fits-all. District Manager expressed a preference to condense and simplify to the extent practical.
We should include a requirement that notice be posted on subject property, using the same notification format that the applicant distributed.
Need to research legality to see if it is legal to put on street hardware with our official CB6 letterhead and a disclaimer at the bottom of the notice. Just take this as far as what other Community Boards do. District Manager and others also cautioned that we do not want to create a new source of litter or visual clutter in the community. We will only research the legality at this point and will not implement without further consideration.
Suggestion that additional use social media, neighborhood blogs, neighborhood list servers, etc. could be used but basic distribution of flyer condition would still required.
The 500-foot requirement might not reach all people impacted, as was clearly the case with the Basis Independent School proposal. One suggestion was to include a condition that required applicants to contact local civic group(s), lists of which are available on our website. Another suggestion by Glenn Kelly was that if there are no residents within 500 feet that the applicant should be required to contact district office to discuss additional requirements.
On a related topic, Ariel Krasnow suggested that we require appropriate visuals for applicants at a public hearing and also a list of what they have to show. Richard Bashner suggested that we build from our liquor license application format for a different use for land use items. District Manager said that we could begin work on that over the summer.
Lastly, related to committee caseload management, the Permits & Licenses Committee reviews a significant number of unenclosed sidewalk café permit renewals. We have not had any issues that have arisen during the renewal process which has necessitated that the committee take any action other than to approve the renewals as presented. It was suggested by our District Manager that we then use the same policy we do for liquor license renewals, that is, unless the district office has a reason for putting an unenclosed sidewalk café permit before the committee for a renewal (which would generally be due to persistent, chronic and founded complaints), or unless the community petitions us to hear a particular unenclosed sidewalk café renewal application, that we no longer routinely place these applications on the Permits & Licenses Committee docket. After some discussion it was agreed by consensus to adopt this as the new operating policy for the committee.
Motion to adjourn.
Minutes were submitted by Lou Sones.

CHAIRPERSON’S REPORT………………………………………………………....….DANIEL KUMMER
Chairperson Daniel Kummer began his report by informing the Board that he has received a resignation from Board Member Elizabeth Shipley, who recently moved outside of our district. Citing escalating work demands coupled with this change of residence, she felt that the best option for her was to resign at this time. With Elizabeth’s resignation we currently have 43 Board Members. While membership terms technically expire on March 31st for those of us who are up for reappointment, anyone who is currently serving as a board member automatically continues to serve until new appointments are made which could happen at any time.
Chairperson Kummer reminded the Board that each year in June we begin the process of applying for membership to our standing committees for the yearlong term that begins on September 1st. At our Executive Committee meeting on Monday night it was the consensus of the committee that our existing committee structure is working well so it will remain in place for the 2014-2015 session. The district office will send out new Committee Membership Request forms next month, which I urge you all to complete and return to them as quickly as possible. Even if you think we have your resume on file, please provide us with your most up-to- date version, and especially let us know if any of your personal contact information like phone numbers or email addresses has changed. Please keep in mind that I do make every effort to give board members their top choices when possible.
Chairperson Kummer also reported to the Board that the Executive Committee reviewed and discussed changes which we believe will strengthen our public notification and outreach standards and rules to ensure that the public has convenient and ample access to information about actions coming before us which may impact the community. Some changes to our requirements for applicants will be incorporated into our existing rules over the summer, which will be in place in time for our new committee session in September. One special new policy was also discussed and adopted which I will share with you now. As you all are very well aware, our Permits & Licenses Committee often has a significant caseload dealing with all of the new applicants coming to us for liquor licenses and sidewalk café permits. While we have not routinely reviewed liquor license renewals, we have been automatically reviewing sidewalk café permit renewals which, by and large, have not surfaced any problems with these operations or produced any further changes to any conditions we may have imposed when we first reviewed them as new applications. Therefore, we will now apply the same rule for sidewalk café permit renewals that we use for liquor license renewals – unless the district office has a reason to put a
2
sidewalk café permit renewal before the committee, which would typically be because of a persistent, chronic and founded complaint history, or if the community petitions us to hear it, we will no longer be automatically hearing sidewalk café permit renewal applications before our Permits & Licenses Committee. I believe this will allow us to continue to intervene in situations where reviews are warranted, and not bog down our committee and board with mindless automatic reviews that have not added value to the City’s overall permitting process.
Chairperson Kummer ended by invited all interested parties to the Transportation Committee meeting on May 15th, where they will be discussing with our elected officials an act to amend the vehicle and traffic law and administrative code of the City of New York, in relation to reducing the speed limit to 20 miles per hour.
DISTRICT MANAGER’S REPORT………………………………………….…….CRAIG HAMMERMAN
District Manager Craig Hammerman began his report by informing the Board that he was invited to be a presenter at a Brownfield conference that was given by New Partners for Community Revitalization (NPCR). In the discussion he proposed an idea that the City as well as the State could create a dedicated earmark of funding stream for environmental remediation programs from environmental violation penalties that they collect, especially since the theme of the conference was how the future of brownfield funding is uncertain in New York State. NPCR stated that they would include the concept in their final report to Albany.
District Manager Hammerman advised the board that we have submitted a draft of the Gowanus Brownfields Opportunity Area (BOA) report to the State which is currently under review. As soon as they sign off on it, we will share the final report more broadly. One of the recommendations of the report is to study the feasibility of creating an Industrial Business Improvement District (iBID) somewhere in the Gowanus. We have applied for discretionary funds from our local city council members so we can bring together the area’s indigenous manufacturers, artist, designers and business advocates to see whether an iBID is something that would suit their needs.
District Manager Hammerman informed the board that DOT will be resurfacing the segments of Bond Street that needs it before they install the new bike lanes and markings. This is in response to what the board had recommended in its conditional approval of the bike lanes. The other section of Bond Street that does not need resurfacing, the bike lanes will be installed imminently. DOT has agreed to come to our June Transportation Committee meeting to make a presentation and discuss how roadways get resurfaced. They are also in the process of installing pervious pavers at the 4th Street cul-de-sac, per the plan they presented to Transportation Committee last year.
District Manager Hammerman reported that the Department of Sanitation is in the process of distributing the new brown bins for the organic waste recycling collection that will begin next month in portions of our district. They will begin with the east/west streets from Union to 15th Streets and move from the canal to Prospect Park west to the east, before doing the north/south Avenues. We will be including reminders the Gowanus and Park Slope communities.
District Manager Hammerman advised the board that the Department of Design and Construction will be finishing their work on Henry Street in Cobble Hill and will restore the trench by the end of the week. The sidewalks are being done by National Grid, who is still working on Warren Street, and will be completed by the end of June. Any bluestone or tinted concrete that was disturbed will be restored or replaced in-kind.
District Manager Hammerman ended his report by announcing that the Reconstruction of Columbia Street is nearly completed. The contractor at this point is working on the various odds-and-ends or “punch list” items. If anyone sees anything that they believe should have been done, let the district office know as soon as possible so we can see if it can be added to the list before the City signs-off and releases the final payment. As a byproduct of their completion the community and city agencies have already begun the construction of new, interim open

space on the west side of Columbia Street between Kane and Degraw Streets, a little project we are referring to as Diverter Park.

Stacy Passmore, Department of City Planning, Project Manager introduced the Open Industrial Uses study. She reviewed the study objectives and different phases. Open Industrial Uses are important services, especially in a growing City, but they must be run well to be good neighbors. They include such things as construction and demolition transfer stations, scrap metal yards, automobile disassembly yards, asphalt and concrete yards, etc.
Introduced the notion that zoning performance standards must be updated and DCP wants to put forward site design standards instead, then key performance standards to other specialist agencies (i.e., noise standard tied to DEP, etc.).
Businesses would have 5 years to comply with new recommendations or they would be shut down. They could apply through the BSA for extensions if they need more time to come into compliance.

Q. Eric Anderson – What’s the level of proscriptiveness? How detailed? A. DCP – will be developed in greater detail by other specialist agencies.

Q. Craig Hammerman – how will enforcement work? Is there a way to tie enforcement records from disparate agencies together so they are a cumulative record reflective of the operator’s fitness? A. DCP – we haven’t considered that. Enforcement is always the most challenging component.

Chairperson Daniel Kummer reported that on the morning of Monday, June 2, a 14-year old boy named Nicholas Soto who was rushing toward his school bus was struck and killed by a car while he was crossing Lorraine Street at the Hicks Street intersection in Red Hook. CHAIRPERSON’S REPORT………………………………………………………....….DANIEL KUMMER
Chairperson Daniel Kummer began his report by announcing that over the summer we received a letter of resignation from long-time Red Hook Board Member and 2nd Vice Chair Lou Sones. Board Member Sones cited competing work demands and some personal health issues as his reason for leaving the board. We will miss him, and his representative voice, and we wish him good health and all good things moving forward as we thank him for his many years of selfless service on behalf of our community.
Chairperson Kummer reported to the Board that owing to the loss of Board Members Elizabeth Shipley, our former Secretary, and more recently Lou Sones, our former Second Vice Chair, our bylaws states that it falls upon the Chairperson to appoint replacements to fill out the remainder of the term until the next regular election, subject to the ratification of our Executive Committee. The committee met this past Monday evening so we have 2 new officers to welcome to our dais. I’m pleased to welcome Board Member Pauline Blake as CB6’s new Second Vice Chair and our Housing Committee Chair Board Members Ariel Krasnow who joins us as Secretary. Both Board Members have proven their commitment to the Community Board many times over, and we are most fortunate to have such high caliber talent joining the ranks of our officers.
Chairperson Kummer advised the Board that he is now in the process of appointing an Election Committee to oversee our nominations and election process over the next few months. He has asked Peter Fleming to continue as Chair of our Election Committee since he has done such an outstanding job in this role. This year three of our officers including myself as Chair, Board Members Tom Miskel as First Vice Chair, and Gary Reilly as Secretary, will be term limited, thus preventing us from running for our current offices on next year’s slate of officers. Chairperson Kummer took a moment to spotlight some upcoming meetings which some or all of you may be interested in attending and participating in:  On Monday, September 15, 2014 at 6:30pm at the 78th Precinct, 65 6th Avenue, three of our committees are co-hosting a meeting, being co-sponsored by State Senator Velmanette Montgomery and City Council Member Brad Lander, where representatives for the New York State Department of Corrections and Community Service will be presenting us with plans to open a borough wide parolee 2
reporting center at 15 2nd Avenue at the Gowanus Canal. When we first found out about this back in July, District Manager Hammerman immediate wrote to the DOCCS Commissioner in Albany to try to find out more about what this project entailed. In the absence of a response from the agency, State Senator Montgomery’s office intervened and arranged for the representatives to attend. DEP is under order by the EPA to address the CSO issues as part of the Gowanus Superfund listing, and the department has been looking at all of the properties in the Gowanus corridor to determine where these retention tanks can be built. The tanks will have the capacity to hold the mixture of sanitary sewage and storm water during and after rain events to prevent it from discharging untreated into the canal itself. The mixture will then be slowly released back into the sewer system where it is sent to the water pollution control plant for processing.    On Wednesday, September 17th at 6:30pm at the Miccio Center, 110 West 9th Street, our Parks/Recreation/Cultural Affairs Committee will be hearing two presentations related to the Columbia Waterfront and Red Hook waterfront. The fact sheet is available on our website calendar listed under the committee’s September 17th meeting. The second item on their agenda is a presentation from the Park Department on a $2mil Capital project to construct a comfort station – bathroom – at the Louis Valentino Jr. Park & Pier. Council Member Carlos Menchaca and Borough President Adams each contributed $250,000 to a pre-existing $1.5mil budget, and the department is beginning the process of talking to the community by presenting their initial thoughts on how that money can be used.
Chairperson Kummer ended by reminding the Board that every October the Community Board reviews and adopts its annual Capital and Expense budget priorities for the next City fiscal year. I’d invite everyone to visit www.BKCB6budget.org to put your suggestions on the map so that was can consider them next month, and in the future. Presentation and discussion with representatives for the Department of Parks &
Recreation on the proposed scope of work and preliminary design for a Capital project at Valentino Park & Pier in Red Hook.
Kevin Jeffrey, Brooklyn Borough Parks Commissioner, introduced the need to harden facilities after Sandy. $2.4 million allocated for this project. He introduced Kevin Quinn, Parks’ chief architect of the capital project to design a new comfort station at Valentino Pier.
Mr. Quinn: Problems/considerations: Can’t build too close to water (tidal), must be 13 feet above sea level, keep views of Statue of Liberty, small footprint, vandal-resistant, welcoming, ADA accessible.
Architect: Proposed location for the comfort station at the foot of the pier makes it part of pier and street grid. It adds a second entry to the park, which highlights the comfort station. It will have two rooms with two toilets each. It is made out of corrugated metal and brick, with two tall windows in each for natural light, and effort to be as sustainable as possible (plumbing), size is 650 sq. ft.
Q: Roof drainage? Door material? A: Roof pitches towards bioswale with plants that absorb water. Doors and door frame are stainless steel.
Q: Why not rent bathroom space nearby? A: City doesn’t like to rent space because it will be for a long time. Comm. Jeffrey: This comfort station addresses a community concern.
Q: Will it be insulated and heated? A: It is insulated and has natural cross ventilation.
C: The station should be located in the back of the park. A: It needs to connect to the existing entry and be visible from the pier.
Q: Buy pre-fab bathroom? A: Pre-fab is cheaper, but harder to transport and install.
Q: Comfort station should be against adjacent building. Water feature? A: Do not want to abut neighboring building, fire code issues. Water feature was not requested. This is not a playground.
C: This is a highly utilized part of the park, with the largest open space area. Put the station in the corner. Vote: Who doesn’t want any comfort station? 4 votes for no comfort station.
C: We do not want a big bathroom. We want benches and play space for kids. C: How was the need for a comfort station decided? A: Comm. Jeffrey: Councilwoman Sarah Gonzalez submitted a proposal based on community desires.
C: Price too high. $4,000/sq. ft. is outrageous. This can be done cheaper. A: We all want it cheaper.
C: We can get a line item breakdown of the cost.
C: Vladimir, aide for Councilmember Menchaca present to take questions.
Q: Amount of toilets seems excessive. Is this bathroom needed? Safety may be a concern. How long will it take to build? A: 16 months
C: Parents are either comfortable letting their kids go to the bathroom, or else they would accompany them. Q: Are there alternative proposals? A: Yes.
Q: Will the station be open year round? A: Yes. Longer hours in summer.
C: Smaller footprint is desirable, less pavement.
Q: What is interior design? A: Tile, concrete. Resilient materials. $2.4 million is the price for the entire project, not just the room.
Q: Will the equipment be raised? A: Yes, 13 feet above sea level.
Q: Solar or thermal heater instead of a boiler? A: Not enough space for solar, and batteries are much harder to maintain.
C: The need for, and location of the comfort station has been sufficiently questioned to warrant further discussion.
Comm. Jeffrey: Talk with your Council Member and further community input will be invited.
Presentation and discussion with representatives for the Port Authority of NY&NJ, Red Hook Container Terminal and Escape Music Festival organizer regarding an upcoming music festival event planned at the Red Hook Container Terminal, Pier 9A (roughly at Kane Street) for the weekend of October 11-12.
Greg Brayman, owner of Red Hook Container Terminal, operated on behalf of Port Authority. “There will be no more events without community board discussion.”
Q: Are any events – public or private – planned before October? A: No.
C: Concert ended late and left a huge mess and was very noisy. There were drones in the sky A: An NYC film agency might have been responsible for the drones. We (owner) did not permit drones. We can establish guidelines governing future events.
C: Great party, but the event was not respectful of the neighborhood.
C: The permits for events should be open for review.
A: The container facility is subject to Port Authority jurisdiction, which did a risk assessment and issued a permit for the event. Discussion can continue, but the security thresholds at this site are higher than most places. All events are vetted for safety.
Q: Have events been held elsewhere on Port Authority property? A: Yes, for filming.
Q: How does a promoter do an event at Red Hook Container Terminal? A: They approached us. This was the first public special event at the site.
C: Events are great, but not raves. The music could be heard all over Red Hook. A: The concerts end at 11 pm each night. These events are very rare. We are mindful of the community. Things got away from us the last two events. We were just trying it out.
Q: Hannah Holland, aide from Councilman Lander’s office: why hold events at the port? A: We want the port to be profitable. We can run it successfully with minimal need for subsidies. We want the container terminal to stay here. It may move to Sunset Park.
C: We will reach an understanding before there are more concerts like this one last Friday, which surprised the community.
Neil Ryan and Merritt Quirk, the concert promoters, talk and take questions.
We started the search for a space for this festival 2 years ago. We wanted it to be a new and interesting cultural event in the Columbia Waterfront District featuring local vendors. We see it as an opportunity for Red Hook.
Q: How did you find the container terminal as a possible location for the event? A: Searching on Google Maps, and a broker suggested it. Music will be 1pm-11pm on Oct. 11 and 12.
Q: Speaker placement? A: It is a waterfront space, so sound travels and wind affects it. We will distribute sounds to try to ameliorate nuisance. Festivals make noise. We try to juggle between community and artists’ desires. Sound is subjective. We will make every effort. Environmental study can incorporate acoustical testing.
Q: Transportation to the event? A: Designated Uber pick-up spot, NY Waterways ferries from Manhattan, increased B61 bus, discouraging car use. A temporary barge is being installed to accommodate ferry passengers.
Q: Any nonprofits involved? A: A portion of proceeds will go to two nonprofits; The Brooklyn Greenway Initiative and PortsideNewYork.
Q: Need additional security and police.
A: We suggested building a container wall but Coast Guard disapproved. There will be ample security and police. This event is happening.
C: Community feedback will be required after this concert.
C: The sound maps that you make should be available to the public A: We will share the sound plan with the community board.
Q: Bathrooms? Garbage? A: Friday night was a learning experience. We have a security plan being written. Port-o-johns at the entrance/exit.
Q: What kind of music will the concert feature? A: It will be like a smaller Governors Ball. Indie Rock and electronic music. The average age of concertgoers will be around 25. 20s-30s is our target audience. The lineup has been released.
Q: What will be for sale? A: Food lineup, beer (with security), water, energy drinks, VIP tent with liquor.
Q: Why here? This is Red Hook, not Williamsburg. A: We like the view here. It is a very unique space for events. We want to be the first to use this space. It is very versatile.
C: The container terminal offers union jobs, which are hard to find these days. We want to preserve a working waterfront. A: Will continue to be a working waterfront. We can arrange a community site visit for interested parties. We do not want to be a concert venue every week. We want to be good neighbors. We welcome feedback after this event. We can then reassess whether this is a good idea.
C: We want the port more open to the public. A: This is a good idea. We can arrange for a tour, within the restrictions of the site. Red Hook Container Terminal is unique because it is the last port in a residential neighborhood. The promoters have been very successful and professional.
Q: What is selection process for events? A: It is very expensive for a promoter to hold events here. It is a for-profit venture. It cannot happen every day because it is prohibitively expensive.
Q: Does the Port Authority get money from the event? A: Yes, to cover all of the costs. The costs for the October event went up from last Friday’s event to address bathroom and garbage concerns.
C: You should display signs urging concertgoers to respect neighbors. A: We can consider that. The 76th Precinct will have plenty of police and security on hand.
C: The community does not like when events like this happen without any notice. A: No future events without community involvement.
Q: How will you notify the community in advance? A: We do not want any issues. We will formulate how to discuss with community.
Q: Is there re-entry into the event if you leave? Can you support local businesses? A: No re-entry. We can direct outgoing traffic towards local businesses. We have medical facilities and staff on site.
Q: How do people leave? Lots of people will have to walk really far to the subway. A: We expect 5,000-6,000 people, who will use a mix of public transportation. Driving is discouraged. There is bike parking at the event. Last event we only had one month of planning.
Q: Permit process? A: Saw the space in January, got approval for use in July. Very time consuming process.

CHAIRPERSON’S REPORT………………………………………………………....….DANIEL KUMMER
Chairperson Daniel Kummer began his report by announcing that we received a letter of resignation from former Youth Committee Chair Mark Kolman. We wish him good health and all good things moving forward, and we thank him for his many years of selfless service on behalf of our community. That brings our total down to 45 board members.
Chairperson Kummer reported to the Board that last month three of our committees co-hosted a meeting where representatives for the New York State Department of Corrections and Community Supervision (DOCCS) appeared to talk about their plans to open a borough-wide parolee reporting center at 15 2nd Avenue at the Gowanus Canal. Since then, the community organized another meeting which was facilitated by District Manager Craig Hammerman and Matthew Silverman our Public Safety Chair, and attended by our Human Service Co-Chairs Benjamin Solotaire and Paige Bellenbaum as well. At that meeting several community groups and elected officials made statements regarding their concerns about this project, which we still having nothing in writing about. At our committee meeting the State representatives committed to responding to our questions in writing, and also to return to us for a follow-up meeting. So we assembled all the questions from our meeting and the community’s meeting, and District Manager Hammerman and I wrote to the DOCCS Commissioner asking for a response by the end of this month. We also told them that we would like to reconvene and host the follow-up meeting sometime in November, assuming of course that we have their written responses in hand. Lastly, it was suggested by the community groups that we offer to give them a walking tour of the area around the new facility, which we also offered to do in our letter. We will share their response broadly when we receive it.
Chairperson Kummer advised the board that last month the Port Authority and Red Hook Container Terminal Operator were in the process of permitting a third party event organizer to hold an event at Pier 9 in the containerport. The event was billed as a weekend music festival, designed to attract roughly 8,000 people per day over the Saturday and Sunday of Columbus Day weekend, October 11-12. We have since found out indirectly that the event organizer has moved their venue from the containerport to Governors Island instead.
Chairperson Kummer ended by informing the Board that we have a new Commanding Officer here at the 78th Precinct, Captain Frank DiGiacomo, who took over command a couple of months ago. Our next Public Safety Committee meeting is going to be held in this very room at 6:30pm on October 16th and Captain DiGiacomo will be in attendance to introduce himself more formally. Presentation by representatives for the Brooklyn Public Library on the upcoming

(not in the CB6 district) • What is the money to be gotten from the “sell-off” of almost 40% of the Red Hook branch to SpaceWorks and where are those funds going? • To expand hours at night – one branch in each neighborhood.

CHAIRPERSON’S REPORT………………………………………………………....….DANIEL KUMMER
Chairperson Daniel Kummer began his report by congratulating all of our local elected officials who won their bids for re-election on November 4th, and would like to especially congratulate both State Senator-elect Jesse Hamilton who will be taking over the Senate seat that was vacated by Eric Adams when he became our Borough President, and a special congratulations to Jo Anne Simon, who will be taking over Assemblywoman Joan Millman’s seat since she has opted not to run for re-election. We are fortunate that neither State Senator- elect Hamilton nor Assemblywoman-elect Simon are unfamiliar faces to us; they have both been regular attendees of our meetings. Of course, we will be extending ourselves to them to offer any support they might need to help get them up-to-speed on all of the active issues we are currently engaged in.
Chairperson Kummer advised the Board that this year the Brooklyn CB6 holiday party is going to be from 6- 9pm on Monday, December 15th at The Bahche at 191 7th Street between 2nd/3rd Avenues in Gowanus. I’d like to thank Board Member Glenn Kelly for immediately stepping up again this year to help coordinate the raffle prize donations. Remember, if every Board Member were to get us one raffle prize, we would have 45 prizes to raffle off. If everyone could make an effort to get their favorite restaurant, boutique, nail salon, or coffee shop to consider giving us a modest gift certificate, or other similar prizes that represent the best wares our merchants have to offer, we could really turn this party into a fundraiser as intended. Please let Board Member Kelly know what stores you’ll be approaching so we don’t inadvertently make repeated requests of the same merchant by different board members. Cost of the event is $40 again, but this year we are also offering a $35 early incentive to buy tickets in advance so that we can plan better and have less work to do at the door. Anyone interested in buying advanced tickets (or making a donation) can go directly to www.FBCB6.org/holiday-party-2014.
Chairperson Kummer reported that we were expecting the NYS Department of Corrections and Community Supervision to come to a follow-up meeting in November, as they had promised to do when they attended our committee meeting on September 15th. We were also expecting a second written response to our unanswered inquiries which they also said they would provide to us. The community-based group that has coalesced around this issue called Gowanus United, filed a lawsuit against New York State so the agency on the advice of their lawyers, at this time will not commit to either returning to us for that meeting, nor will they release any additional written material, on account of the pending suit. Of course, with no injunction in place the construction continues at the site at 15 2nd Avenue and will continue with no further discussion with the agency. We will remain optimistic that we will have an opportunity to talk more with the State and possibly influence what happens at the site, although that seems unlikely at this time.
Chairperson Kummer ended by acknowledging and thanking Council Member Brad Lander for coming to our Executive Committee meeting this past Monday evening to give us a briefing on the preliminary draft of the “Bridging Gowanus” initiative’s findings, offering us an early opportunity to reflect on it and to help develop a strategy for moving forward with all of the complex issues related to the Gowanus. For those of you who were unable to join us, the Council Member is setting up a series of meetings with various stakeholder groups and will be having a public meeting from 6:30-8:30pm on Monday, November 24th at PS 32, at Hoyt and Union Streets.

***MINUTES***
Review and discussion of information related to the development of a New York State Department of Corrections and Community Supervision (DOCCS) borough-wide parolee reporting center at 15 2nd Avenue (between 6th Street/Gowanus Canal).
Matthew Silverman: Learned of DOCCS borough-wide Parolee Reporting Center several months ago. Had an initial meeting with DOCCS and sent about 60 questions to follow up. DOCCS has declined to answer questions or attend this meeting on advice of counsel because of lawsuit by Gowanus United.  May concerns around safety, traffic, etc. and wisdom of concentrating all parolee reporting in one somewhat inaccessible location.  Most troubling aspect is that CB6 learned about the project from a third party, not from government actors.
Benjamin Solotaire: Draft motion is not official, just a starting point for discussion outlined by Matt Silverman.
M. Silverman: DOCCS has said they are going ahead with the project regardless of CB6 input.  Goal is to have something in front of the full board in December, go on record with CB opinion before its opening.  No opportunities for public comment.
David Mazzucca: Did we invite DOCCS back? Did they decline?
M. Silverman: They were invited, not returning due to lawsuit.
Noel Berk-Rauch: Do we know what elected officials’ positions are?
M. Silverman: Borough President Eric Adams opposed. Other electeds expressing concerns.
Benjamin Solotaire: Did anyone attend rally?
Andrea: SWBIC – attended 11/19 protest. BP Eric Adams, AM Felix Ortiz, CM Brad Lander representative were present. Fair number of residents. Kept it short due to the cold weather.
M. Silverman: the press reported about 100 people.
Joanne Smith: Is this unprecedented? Has DOCCS ever built a borough-wide center?
B. Solotaire: This is the new model. There were three related facilities in downtown Brooklyn. But not a new model.
J. Smith: Do we know what social effects have been in other areas?
B. Solotaire: We don’t really know.
Paige Bellenbaum: There was a shooting in Brooklyn outside of one of their reporting centers, but we do not know if it was related to the center.
Adine Pusey, with Gowanus United: There were a lot of electeds represented. AM-elect Joanne Simon, Comptroller Scott Stringer, etc. City hasn’t weighed in very much – that’s next step. Mayor DeBlasio is named in the lawsuit. Stringer may be interested in.
Eric McClure: What’s the parking situation?
M. Silverman: A couple of dozen spots for staff.
B. Solotaire: Part of the controversy is that 96 spots or so were waived.
Douglas Gordon: Any request to DOCCS for shuttle service to transit, a la Methodist Hospital?
M. Silverman: Believe that was previously asked to DCCS. No response.
Adine: Rumor is that there will be shuttles.
M. Silverman: The fact that we’re dealing with rumors is at root of problem.
Rachel Freeman: There is precedent for state offices (DUMBO) to provide shuttles for staff.
Adine: Neither of the nearby subway stations (Smith-9th St and 4th Ave) are handicap accessible.
Bill Blum: Total frustration with lack of information and terrible process. We’re going to be stuck with this facility. All we can really do is express our anger. Agree with some aspects of the motion. Not productive to deal with rumors.
M. Silverman: No motion yet. These are just areas of concern that need to be further explored.
R. Freeman: Where do things stand on an advisory group?
P. Bellenbaum: DOCCS agrees in principle on a CAG.
R. Freeman: Are they going to wait for facility to open before answering questions?
Adine: December 12th is the hearing date on the lawsuit.
J. Smith: What’s the distance to subways?
P. Bellenbaum: 7 minute walk from Smith-9th Street.
D. Gordon: Issue is its just F, G and R trains.
T. Jackson: Do the parolees have a voice in this? Is location a problem?
B. Solotaire: Vocal NY has been talking to parolees. They’re concerned with accessibility. No statement yet.
T. Jackson: Does it make sense to work with affected client community?
P. Bellenbaum: City has tried through best practices to locate within communities of parolees. Less recidivism when parolees are more connected to their communities.
T. Jackson: Can we bring those points into the motion?
B. Blum: Motion – DK. Community Board should write to Governor Cuomo and appropriate officials expressing the board’s and community’s dismay with the process. Legislation decentralizing siting of parole facilities in NYC.
The motion was seconded by Eric McClure.
P. Bellenbaum: There should be a target elected for intro of legislation.
Ariel Krasnow: Most potent part is the recommendation for a CAG. Trying to change legislation may be a step too far. I like the points the way they were written.
B. Solitaire: I’d prefer we refer to “people on parole” rather than parolees.
B. Blum: I do think we should call for legislation. The Board has taken positions on wars.
B. Solitaire: Amend to “policy or legislation” agreed to by Bill.
M. Silverman: Legislation for community notice good; on decentralization maybe should be a conversation with elected.
J. Smith: We need numbers on recidivism rates to make informed decisions (diffuse centers vs. centralized).
B. Solitaire: When board discussed recovery center in Red Hook.
B. Blum: Restated motion, accepted all friendly amendments.
M. Silverman: Friendly amendment – add sentence stating that scope of facility raises concerns of public safety, traffic and IBZ.
A. Krasnow: Takes issue with wording. Board approved Whole Foods with much greater traffic concerns. Issues raised reflect nature of people, not the number of people.
M. Silverman: I think it’s important that we state our concerns.
Suzanne Turet: What we wanted was for DOCCS to come and address our concerns and they haven’t.
Lisa Collins: I know a ton of people who live and work there and their concerns are very much about public safety.
M. Silverman: We don’t know what public safety issues are in other areas.
D. Gordon: We should be careful about language. People coming to parolee appointments are trying to go straight. Focus should be on process.
D. Mazzucca: It all comes down to lack of accessibility. That’s what we should address.
E. McClure: The issue is, because of absence of process and lack of communication, we don’t know enough to know what to be concerned about, including public safety, traffic, accessibility, and effect on industrial business zone.
A. Krasnow: We should ask for follow up study on traffic – a la Whole Foods. To make the motion strong, I think we should look for actionable items.
B. Solotaire: Parking waiver was a key item. We need to follow that up.
J. Smith: We need an on-site ombudsman.
Robert Underwood: Yes, we need someone acceptable on the ground.
B. Solotaire: Re-evaluate traffic and parking analysis and report back to the Board within six months of opening.
Daniel Ramos: Why not ask for a community member to be at the facility to be community’s eyes and ears?
R. Freeman: Most such facilities have security teams.
M. Silverman: There will be metal detectors and cameras.
T. Jackson: Should we include language about accessibility?
E. McClure: Call the question. Unanimous assent.
Bill Blum: Motion read again
CB6 should write to Governor Cuomo and appropriate State Representatives and DOCCS, expressing the Board’s and community’s dismay with the process leading up to the placement and opening of this facility, and ask that.
1. A community advisory group be assembled and meet before parolees begin reporting to the facility. This group should include DOCCS, NYPD, CB6, people on parole, elected officials and representatives of local organizations and other interested members of the community.
2. As legislators to take all actions possible to obtain further info about this facility including traffic, environmental issues, accessibility, public safety and zoning and to disseminate that information as broadly as possible and as publicly as possible so that the community can be fully aware of the impact that the proposed facility will have.
3. The state should reconsider and fully assess through policy and legislation whether serving all people on parole in Brooklyn at this facility benefits the state, the community and people on parole.
4. Legislation be introduced to require DOCCS to obtain community input prior to locating and opening such facilities in the future.
5. DOCCS should reevaluate the traffic and parking analysis and report the results to CB6 six months after opening.
MOTION APPROVED: UNANIMOUSLY

Chairperson Kummer briefly spoke about the recent tragedies of Eric Garner and Akai Gurly from New York City, Michael Brown from Ferguson, Missouri and Tamir Rice from Cleveland, Ohio. The question is what we are going to do about the clearly impaired, some would say broken, relationship between our community as a whole and particularly our communities of color and the police forces that exist to protect and maintain order in our communities. Many others in our community have tried to advance this conversation about this difficult subject in recent days, most notably or Brooklyn Borough President Eric Adams and Civil Rights Attorney Constance Rice. For him it boils down to a simple social contract of mutual trust and respect between our communities and the police forces around the country. He has developed an enormous respect for the responsibility and risk that our police offices take on in fulfilling their duties to keep of safe and maintain order. When they carry out those duties lawfully and with integrity, he strongly believes that they need and deserve our respect. We also need to show respect to the authority they have been given as a necessary tool in carrying out their jobs. We are entitled to insist in return that they maintain the highest respect not just for our legal rights but more fundamentally for the equal value for all of our lives and our physical safety; “All Lives Matter.” There is obviously much more to be said and discussed as we move forward to heal the pain from these tragedies, to build and repair a foundation of mutual trust and respect. Chairperson Gary Reilly began his report by welcoming the board officers to the dais including Sayar Lonial our new First Vice Chair; Pauline Blake, returning as Second Vice Chair; Jerry Armer, our new Treasurer, and; Ariel Krasnow, returning as Secretary.
Chairperson Reilly reported to the Board that by virtue of being our Treasurer, Board Member Jerry Armer also now has the distinction of becoming Chair of our Finance/Personnel & Law Committee. He has asked Eric McClure to take over the Co-Chair seat for our Transportation Committee, relieving Sayar Lonial. Also, since he is no longer the Chair of the Permits & Licenses Committee, he has asked Mike Racioppo to take over the Chair for that committee. Board Members Eric McClure and Mike Racioppo will therefore be joining our Executive Committee. I’m also quite pleased that Richard Bashner has agreed to continue to serve as our delegate to the Brooklyn Bridge Park Community Advisory Committee where he will continue to represent us. And, lastly, I’d like to thank Daniel Kummer for agreeing to continue to represent us on the New York Methodist Hospital’s Design Group, which is finishing up its work on their new Center for Community Health as they prepare to transition from design to construction.
Chairperson Reilly informed the Board that one of the first things he will be doing as Chair is to meet with all of the local elected officials whose districts overlap with ours, beginning with the Borough President and our Council Members. It is important for me to get to know them all so that we can call upon them as needed to continue to provide the level of support and leadership we have always relied upon to advance the Community Board’s and our community’s goals.
Chairperson Reilly advised the Board that he has also asked our Finance/Personnel & Law Committee to begin a comprehensive by-laws review process which, he’s hoping, will culminate in a vote on any proposed revisions to the by-laws at our June board meeting. More information will be sent out to the full board shortly by our Finance/Personnel & Law Committee soliciting your ideas, explaining how you can become more involved and providing a good road map of the process between now and June.
Chairperson Reilly ended his report by congratulating our District Manager for reaching an important milestone. On January 8th he celebrated his 25th anniversary working for Brooklyn CB6. Tonight marks his 248th consecutive CB6 general meeting—he has never been absent from a single general meeting. On behalf of the members and staff, please accept our sincere thanks and congratulations on this impressive achievement.
DISTRICT MANAGER’S REPORT………………………………………….…….CRAIG HAMMERMAN
2
District Manager Craig Hammerman informed the Board that the Department of Corrections and Community Supervision (DOCCS), the Attorney General's Office, which provided legal assistance to DOCCS, and Gowanus United, a community-based coalition of area residents and business owners, have reached a legal settlement regarding the operation of a parole facility at 15 Second Avenue. Under the agreement, the number of parolees reporting to the Gowanus facility will be reduced from 6,000 to 2,000 for a minimum of two years. To serve people on parole who will not be reporting to the Gowanus facility, DOCCS will introduce a program to decentralize reporting locations in Brooklyn. This program will establish DOCCS community reporting sites in neighborhoods throughout the borough, making it easier for parolees to meet the conditions of their parole. Further, NYS DOCCS has agreed to meet on a regular basis with representatives from Gowanus United, Brooklyn CB6, 78th Police Precinct, and the Gowanus Alliance. These meetings will provide a forum for discussing any issues pertaining to DOCCS's ongoing operation of the facility. DOCCS has also agreed to provide statistics on an ongoing basis regarding the number of parolees assigned to report to the facility.
Chairperson Reilly recognized New York City Criminal Court Judge Michael Gerstein who update the Board on the number of cases in the Kings County Criminal Court. He stated that it has been reported in the news that the NYPD has had a “Police Slow Down” in terms of arrests. He further stated that interns of the number of cases in criminal court the reports in the news are accurate. Criminal court ordinarily has one arraignment part everyday doing mostly felony arraignments and a second arraignment part doing mostly misdemeanor arraignments. We have the same thing at night between the hours of 5pm and 1am. Over the past several weeks we have been able to combine the two daytime parts as well as the two nighttime parts. Most of the decrease has been in misdemeanor arrest. Felony arrest also drop by only 20-25%. In the news this week it has been reported that arrests are back up. So today for the first time in weeks we had two arraignment parts in the daytime and I suspect we will have two in the evening. So what ever happened in the past to decrease arrests has since gone back to normal.
Chairperson Reilly also recognized State Senator Daniel Squadron who began by congratulating Chairperson Reilly and all of the new Executive Officers. Senator Squadron then stated that he has pushed for Full-Line Reviews throughout the MTA subway system. These reviews have led to newer, cleaner cars for the F, and improved service along the L and G. Recently, the MTA has agreed to perform a Full-Line Review on the A and C. He has recently joined the Riders Alliance in convening a working group to bring public input into the Full-Line Review process. He also stated that he is opposed to housing on Pier 6. He has been pushing to get Brooklyn Bridge Park completed and make sure it’s financially self-sustaining. You may have notice on Pier 1 the developer has broken the rules by building the luxury housing to high. He would like to prevent that or anything like it on Pier 6. He believes that if there is housing on Pier 6 it should be affordable housing. He ended by stating that he along with his colleagues have introduced the Community Healthcare (LICH) Act, which would establish a clear, transparent, and community-oriented process when hospitals are threatened. The LICH Act would allow the Commissioner of the State Department of Health (DOH) to only approve a hospital closure application if the needs of the community and impacted stakeholders, including access to emergency medical care, can be adequately met. And, under the proposal, the Commissioner would not be allowed to close a hospital without a significant and thorough community input process dictated by a statutorily imposed timeline. The LICH ACT would, following the application for closure of a general hospital, require the Commissioner of the State Department of Health to: 1. Explain in a report within 30 days of an application for closure:  The anticipated impact of closure on the surrounding community’s access to care, including the uninsured and underserved.  What measures DOH and others have taken or plan to take to lessen any negative impacts.  Why the State cannot assume financial responsibility for the hospital or identify an alternate operator.
2. Hold a community forum within six weeks of application, giving community members and local elected officials the chance to raise questions, voice concerns, and offer alternatives.
3
3. Respond to community input by:  Answering, in summary, comments received from community members and local elected officials  Explaining why significant alternatives were or were not incorporated into a final closure plan.  Identifying any changes to the plan resulting from community concerns or suggestions.
4. Only approve the application if needs of the community and impacted stakeholders, including access to emergency medical care, can be adequately met.
5. Explain options for transitional medical services to impacted communities, including arrangements for continuity of care.

Other Business
Elected officials were slated to speak at the end of the last General Board meeting.      No objections or complaints have been received about the change.
Why is Public comment always at the end of the meetings?
District Manager explained the two prevailing arguments for it:
1) Community is encouraged to actively participate at committee meetings which are set up specifically to be local and interactive. Permitting community comment right before the board
votes could effectively short-circuit the committee structure.
2) The primary purpose of a general meeting is to vote on recommendations referred out of committee. Allowing public comment at the front-end of the meeting could jeopardize a quorum which is needed for the board to conduct business.
It was added that applicants are expected to attend the committee meetings where they have an opportunity to share information, answer questions, respond to comments, etc. but no such opportunity would exist at a general meeting. Comments from the public at a general meeting would, therefore, essentially be one-sided.
Jerry Armer remarked that for both Landmarks/Land Use and Permits & Licenses, the applicant has a specific responsibility to do outreach, which drives a lot of people to the committee meetings. Having the applicant assume this responsibility works quite well in terms of getting notice out and encouraging participation.
The District Manager added that in addition to the written guidelines we provide to applicants for LM/LU and P&L, we do a great deal of outreach from the district office as well (notices, emails, social media, etc.) and we could always do better. If anyone has any specific ideas for how we could improve our outreach they should please let him know.
Benjamin Solotaire posited that we could consider moving the Community Session up to the beginning of the meeting for a specific length of time, then continue it at the end of the meeting. He also wondered if we could help the people who sign up to speak if, for example, they have a service delivery item which would be referred to the district office for follow-up. In that case, why should someone have to sit through an entire meeting just to be able to report something?
By-laws Review Process
We are in the process of kicking-off a by-laws review process. Jerry Armer, Chair of our Finance/Personnel & Law Committee, has already met with our District Manager to discuss it.
Some of the initial issues to consider included:
   Elections: What if no one has been nominated to fill a position? The nomination procedure, in general, should be reviewed.    Standing committees: Must be reviewed yearly.    Chairman “Emeritus” position: Possible spot on the Executive Committee for past Chairs.
Jerry reminded everyone that by-laws changes are a process spelled out in the by-laws. They must be presented at two consecutive meetings, then voted on at the second meeting. To get a vote in June, they would have to be first presented in May. And there are no provisions for making changes on the floor. By-laws changes must be voted up or down.
   Would there be attendance review for committees? (Committee Chair can appoint or dismiss).
   There are Board Members who do not go to committee meetings – but there is no rule about it.
There will be an audit of committee attendance by the First Vice Chair. For attendance, make a yearly grid to see immediately who is showing up.

Presentation and review of New York State Senate Bill 2500-2015, an act to amend the public health law, in relation to the closure of hospitals.
Presentation and discussion on bill known as LICH act (“Local Input for Community Health") led by staff from the offices of State Senator Daniel Squadron and State Assembly Member Jo Anne Simon.  LICH act was created after a lengthy debate surrounding the recent closing of Long Island College Hospital in Brooklyn. Officials saw that the current public health law didn’t include any specific procedures pertaining to the closing of hospitals.  Under the old law the Commissioner of the State Dept. of Health was only required to notify the public within 30 days after a hospital was closed.  Sen. Squadron’s staff took language from a piece of legislation that then-Assembly Member, Scott Stringer put together in the 1990s, and used it to establish a timeline (as detailed in the Bill 2500- 2015) for notifying the appropriate elected officials and members of the public as soon as the Commissioner receives an application to close a hospital.  Details of the proposed bill were reviewed--language that establishes a specific process and a timeline that allows communities a chance to respond (and have their responses acknowledged) when notified of an application to close.  The proposed process also serves to create a body of evidence by requiring documents and reports from the Commissioner and the entity applying to close a hospital; and allows the public to formally respond in writing.
   The LICH act was announced in December 2014 and is presently assigned to the senate’s Health Committee.    Sen. Squadron’s staff are cautiously optimistic about it passing; somewhat concerned about it being “an uphill battle” since they are in the senate minority. They also noted that at the moment bill drafting is really backed up--partly due to the recent upheaval in the assembly.    The bill has the support of 1199SEIU and NYSNA and nonpartisan support is expected from several assembly members; Staff is also getting support from various Community Boards.
Question posed by a YHSE committee member:  Is there a city or state mandate that a hospital must exist to serve X number of people within a certain radius? (Sen. Squadron’s COS said she could look into that.)
Discussion moved to other issues around health care needs & additional legislation.  Assembly Member Simon is working on a bill that would address the need to gather data re: response time and emergency needs.  Overall sense by YHSE committee and Assembly staff is that the LICH act is too short to address such complex issues and that additional legislation may be needed. Focus now is getting the LICH bill passed and signed by Governor Cuomo.
Comment by a YHSE committee member:  One concern is that the LICH act just deals with the closing of hospitals but does not address a transfer of management; perhaps that can be reformed in a future piece of legislation.
Questions posed by YHSE committee members:  Q: Who is responsible for managing the “continuity of care” as outlined in the LICH bill?    A: Sen. staff answered that the rulemaking process means that the Commissioner of the State DOH has to figure out how to comply with the details of the law.
   Q: How are “surrounding communities” defined?    A: a lot of debate about how specific to be in the bill, and decided it’s in the public’s best interest to be vague; so the language is meant to be broad and open to interpretation for the communities involved.
   Q: Is it still possible to make changes to the bill?    A: No, they are no longer accepting input (other than a critical typo pointed out by Benjamin Solotaire, Chair) because if they try to amend it now they may lose the ability to use a motion to get the bill out of committee (a result of parliamentary rules imposed by Senate majority.)
General sense of YHSE committee after discussing LICH bill is that it’s a good idea to have the goal of getting it passed and then add on to it with additional legislation. The bill provides an opportunity for communities to have input when a hospital is under consideration for closure.
Suzanne Turet, Chair, motioned that we actively support the LICH bill. Paige Bellenbaum, Chair, seconds the motion.

***MINUTES***
Presentation and discussion with representatives for Move NY, a region-wide grassroots coalition promoting a Fair Tolling and Transportation Reinvestment plan.
Jonathan Matz of Move NY made the presentation. - CB2 and CB8 voted to endorse the plan already - CB6 helped sponsor a Move NY town hall last month. - Goal is to push forward this plan and get legislation introduced this session within the next three months. - Congestion grinds us to a halt now - Fares go up on driving tolls and subway and bus fares - But, looking at the map, city charges money where there are no transit options and it’s free where there is plentiful transit. System is lopsided and induces toll shopping and unneeded congestion. - Architect of plan is former DOT commissioner, Sam Schwartz.
Plan is to:  Improve road infrastructure such as the BQE  Fill transit gaps  Restore 2010 service cuts  Provide more express buses and subways  Subway station rehabs  Replace MetroCard
   Expand countdown clocks    More and faster subway trains (technology is 100 years old)    Targeted areas expand ferries    Increase suburban transit options    Expand transit system    New subway lines
Strategy:  Wipe slate clean  Redo tolling structure based on: 1. Charge more where there’s more traffic and better transit 2. Lower tolls everywhere else – reductions of 39-45% on outer borough bridges by charging CBD (Central Business District) below 60th Street. 100% charge would electronic via EZ Pass and cameras. 97% of all trips will pay the same fares as now, or pay less.
Plan generates $1.5 Billion net on top of current funding when bonded that fills gap in MTA capital plan.
Revenue Use – 25% roads and bridges Some to operating cost of system Bulk to transit improvement
Protect Revenue – New financial authority collects it and it’s not subject to budgeting process. Set aside $1.5 Billion for local transportation needs chosen by local elected and communities.
Other options to make some money: - Increase gas tax 46% - Increase sales tax a full point - Double payroll mobility tax - Issue even more debt and give current drivers and straphangers 15% increase
Discussion: Q. How do we guarantee MTA will use money correctly? A. MTA is talking to Move NY. Realizes it is best chance to get money and relying on legislators to work ironclad language into legislation. Jerry Armer wants to see legislation so it’s not a boondoggle like the Lottery system.
Q. What is the cost of implementing the system and how is that paid? A. Involves initial $100 Million to build – taken out of current capital program
Q. Fares on Staten Island ferry? A. Not yet. It’s operated by EDC not MTA. Port Authority is also not yet part of this complex plan.
Q. Lower fares on outer bridges encourages more traffic? A. Yes, slightly. But those are transit deserts with no other options.
Q. Are all bridges in 5 boroughs? A. Yes
Q. Will this go forward without two-way toll reinstatement on Verrazano Bridge? A. Yes. Plan will still work though not as well. Hoping Federal Government will undue the one-way legislation.
Q. Madelaine Murphy – Verrazano Bridge problem is commercial traffic coming into NYC via VZB and exiting through Manhattan – they pay nothing. A. That’s true. Exactly the point of Move NY plan – skewed incentives are the issue.
Q. Not thrilled about new authority. A. It’s only a financial authority.
Q. Why 60th Street? A. More than ½ of traffic is coming from the North.
Q. Who supports? A. Cautiously optimistic. Focused on a short timetable. Jose Peralta, Mark Weprin were congestion pricing opponents but support this plan. CM Lander, AM Simon, AM Brennan and Sen Squadron are all enthusiastic about the plan. The Governor is staying out of it and has not slammed the door on this.
Q. George Fiala asked- why not go after VZB two-way issue instead of “regressive taxes”? A. It’s not regressive. Used census data. Benefits people of lower incomes and also this is a regional transportation solution.
Q. Appreciate how this reduces cut-through traffic. Show it in a slide! A. Charles Komonoff did the numbers and they’ll dig into the numbers. The plan is synergistic with Vision Zero.
Q. Why not ask cab passengers to pay the tolls rather than surcharge? A. Goal is to discourage segmenting fleets of cabs. It’d create lots of congestion but surcharge avoids that.
Q. Time of day pricing? A. Support it but it is a negotiable part of it that would need to be worked on during implementation.
A motion was made by Dave Abraham that CB6 support the Move NY plan as presented. Bill Blum seconds.
VOTE: 10…..YEAS            0…..NAYS       1…..ABSTENTION
MOTION PASSED

CHAIRPERSON’S REPORT……………………………………………………….................GARY REILLY
Chairperson Gary Reilly began his report by congratulating Mark Shames, who recently received an Honorary Mention award by the New York State Press Association for Best Column in the Red Hook Star-Revue, one of our local newspapers which generally covers our waterfront communities of Red Hook, Columbia Waterfront District and Gowanus. Board Member Shames writes their political column, which is always peppered with just the right amount of information and wit. I’d also like to congratulate the Red Hook Star-Revue itself for receiving two awards this year—one for Board Member Shames’ column, and also a First Place award for Best Picture Story.
Chairperson Reilly also congratulated our Council Member Steve Levin who announced via his Twitter account yesterday that he is now engaged to his longtime girlfriend Ann Carroll. On behalf of the board I’d like to wish a lifetime of blessings to the happy couple.
Chairperson Reilly thanked Board Member Glenn Kelly for representing the board at a meeting two weeks ago with Parks Commissioner Mitchell Silver. The Commissioner was interested in meeting with representatives from the Brooklyn Community Boards to talk more about Parks equity issues and how the department can do a better job of responding to our communities’ needs.
Chairperson Reilly informed the board that our Finance/Personnel & Law Committee had their second meeting to review our by-laws and that the revisions that were discussed are in the process of being drafted for circulation to the board. The process, as currently outlined in the by-laws, requires that revisions be sponsored by at least twenty-five percent of the board in order to be acted upon. They must also appear on the agenda of two successive regular meetings, and voted on at the second meeting. So the process moving forward will be as follows. The FPL Committee will have a draft document that will be circulated to the full board very soon. It will be reviewed and discussed at our next Executive Committee meeting on May 11th where all board members will be invited to comment and/or attend the meeting to participate in the discussion. We will be prepared to make any final adjustments to the draft document then solicit sponsors at the Executive Committee meeting—twenty-five percent means 11 board members need to agree to sponsor the revisions to put it before the board. The final document will be transmitted to all board members and the item will appear on our May general meeting agenda. Finally, the item will appear for a second time on our June general meeting agenda at which time we’ll vote on them. We will not be able to make changes to the document after it appears on the May agenda, so the May Executive Committee meeting will be the last time and place we’ll be able to incorporate any revisions. I’m hopeful that you will all take the time to read over the document when you first receive it and if you see anything that concerns you that you will speak up right away. It’s my goal to have this 2
done before our summer hiatus. Meanwhile, I’d like to thank the members of the FPL Committee who have really put some tremendous, thoughtful effort into this exercise, specifically, it’s Chair Jerry Armer, Board Members Daniel Kummer, Richard Bashner, Mark Shames, Rick Luftglass and, while he’s not on the committee, he thanked, Board Member Glenn Kelly for going to both meetings and being a part of the ongoing discussions.
Chairperson Reilly advised the board that on April 3rd the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation issued a Potential Remedial Action Plan (or PRAP) for the Fulton Manufactured Gas Plant which generally shares a footprint with the Thomas J. Greene Playground and Douglass-Degraw Pool, and surrounding blocks generally in the vicinity of the canal to 3rd Avenue and Douglass to Sackett Streets. Since the site extends to the bulkhead of the Gowanus Canal, it is imperative that NYSDEC have an approved action plan in place in order for the EPA to move forward with its Superfund clean-up activities at the north end of the canal, which is the first phase they intend to address. Friends of Brooklyn CB6 had received a Technical Assistance Grant from NYSDEC years ago and has been working closely with the State’s project manager as we’ve moved from milestone to milestone in this process. This latest step in the critical path to remedial involves the public review and comment on the PRAP which was issued on April 3rd and is open for comment through May 3rd. NYSDEC has committed to hosting a public meeting to present the PRAP and answer questions from the public on April 16th, 7-9pm at the Wyckoff Gardens Community Center, 280 Wyckoff Street. I would encourage anyone interested in the park and/or the clean-up of the canal to consider attending, and submitting comment to the State. We intend to resubmit the relevant parts of our prior comments on the EPA’s Superfund PRAP to NYSDEC so they would be aware of the previous positions our board has taken on this matter. Meanwhile, I’ve asked District Manager Craig Hammerman to send out links to the PRAP and other pertinent documents, together with the public meeting information—which was briefly referenced in our April newsletter—to help get word out and encourage broader participation by the community.
Chairperson Reilly reminded the board that last year the Brooklyn Public Library had presented a plan to us for the redesign of the Red Hook branch library that would have repurposed a portion of the interior space for more programming by local cultural organizations. The plan was for the non-profit group called SpaceWorks to come in and manage the space in partnership with the library. After hearing a resounding message from the Red Hook community that there were concerns about this plan, most notably the fact that few people in the community had been consulted as it was developed, the Brooklyn Public Library backed off and agreed to re-engage the community in a discussion about how best to use this vital but chronically underutilized public facility. In fulfillment of that commitment, the Brooklyn Public Library has hired an outside facilitator called NY public to run an all-day visioning session next Saturday, April 18th for Red Hook stakeholders. It is hoped that the Brooklyn Public Library and Red Hook community will both emerge with a better, clearer idea of what people want from this library so that ultimately it can be better used by the community. The library does have some Capital money set aside from the prior project which it intends to use down the line, once the community and library have a better idea of what it would like to see there.
Chairperson Reilly reported to the board that in response to one of the conditions we stipulated as part of our conditional approval for the New York Methodist Hospital’s Center for Community Health facility, the hospital is beginning to form a construction task force with us and other local stakeholders to help coordinate and monitor the impact of the construction activities during the construction of the facility. The hospital does intend to start demolition and excavation in the coming months, and the task force is expected to have its first meeting this month. The hospital will produce newsletters and periodic reports to keep the community informed, which we of course will also help promote and distribute on a broader scale.

DISTRICT MANAGER’S REPORT………………………………………….…….CRAIG HAMMERMAN
District Manager Craig Hammerman began his report by informing the board that a few weeks ago, we had a meeting with the Department of Transportation, CB7 and the offices of Council Member Brad Lander and Carlos Manchaca to begin the discussion of the 4th Avenue Median Redesign Project. The good news is that there is money in the budget for the project and they are planning on installing raised planted medians with irrigation systems. This project will begin at 8th Street and proceed southward. North of 8th Street will not be included in the project. We will have to continue to request these medians for north of 8th Street until it is included.
District Manager Hammerman advised the Board that we had our first quarterly BID management meeting with 5th Avenue, Atlantic Avenue and Flatbush Avenue to discuss projects, programs and policies. We came to realize that all 3 of the BIDs converge at the Barclays Center. One of the shared concerns of all the BIDs was the need for more “wayfinding” signage which help pedestrians navigate to points of interest and other attractions in the area. Unfortunately, at $20,000.00 per sign, it would be very difficult for the BIDs to pay for them. We will be putting our heads together with the BIDs to see if we can find creative ways to raise funds and obtain resources to pay for the signs.
District Manager Hammerman reported to the board that this past month we had the second meeting of the Community Advisory Group that was formed around the NYS Department of Corrections at Second Avenue and 6th Street. Overall, the residential and business neighbors have developed a healthy dialogue with the facility managers. The center is seeing 100-200 parolees a day. Some of the parolees are having trouble finding the center because of its location at the end of Second Avenue. One of the businessmen at the meeting offered to design and manufacture a sign to help people find the center faster and more efficiently. At the request of the community, the center manager requested that Lowes provide them with parking. Lowes has provided them with 27 parking spaces for staff vehicles. Also, the 78th Police Precinct has reported that since the center has opened, overall crime is down in the area.
District Manager Hammerman ended his report by updating the board on the Solarize Brooklyn CB6 Campaign where we’re working with EDC and Sustainable CUNY to enlist solar installers who could effectively sign up interested property owners, both business and residential, to convert their rooftops to solar systems. Within the last few months, New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) had issued an RFP to make available up to $40 Million Dollars to support the development of community micro-grids. The objective is to promote the design and build of community grids that improve local, electrical distribution system performance and resiliency in both a normal operating configuration as well as during times of electrical grid outages. We have been approached by two different groups; one looking at Park Slope/Gowanus and one looking exclusively at Red Hook. We have provided both with non-exclusive letters of support to accompany their application. We have since been approached by the Red Hook group who would like to engage the Community Board further in the planning process. They have asked The Friends of Community Board Six, our

non-profit group, to sponsor the application as a fiscal conduit. The first stage of the grid competition would award winning groups $100,000.00 to conduct feasibility studies. The second step, NYSERDA will give $1 Million Dollars for further engineering studies. The third step would award winners with $7 Million Dollars for construction. The RFP calls for applications to be submitted by May 15th and we should be notified by the summer if any of the applications from our district have been chosen.
