Presentation and consideration of a proposal by the North Flatbush BID to install planters along Flatbush Avenue between Pacific Street and 8th Avenue.
Presentation from North Flatbush BID by executive director of BID.
BID seeks to install approximately 70 planters along Flatbush Avenue. Approximately 40 will be within CB6 boundaries.
Sidewalks on Flatbush are 15 – 20 feet wide, many with subway grates, limiting opportunities to add new street trees. Planters are the only opportunity to increase greenery outside of triangle parks.
Coincides with $60M DDC infrastructure project to improve pedestrian space and expand 12 curbs.
BID has worked with DOT and Parks and Recreation to identify preferred planter styles and plantings. BID will add perennials and annuals. 2 – 3 plantings per year depending on conditions. Has collaborated with DOT on siting locations, taking into consideration crosswalks, subway entrances. Has received support from businesses/residents on Flatbush Ave.
BID will work with 3rd party vendor to maintain planters, water and weed, and keep area clean.
Timeline: Present to CB6 and CB8 in Jan/Feb. Submit application to Public Design Commission in March. Install Phase 1 (approximately 35 planters) in March 2018. Phase 2 in April 2019 to allow DDC project to finish.
Public questions:
Why were neighbors not notified? Why is this meeting held here and not near Flatbush? Answer from Eric McClure: Public sidewalks do not require neighborhood-wide notification. Verified by DOT.
Is BID working with Brooklyn Botanic Garden? BID is working with Horticultural Society of NY on appropriate planters. Will work with vendors to use environmentally friendly materials, fertilizers, etc.
Jerry Armer: Is BID planning to increase assessment or take money from somewhere else, if so where? BID: Budget is $150K/year total. For pilot program, council members are supporting with discretionary spending. More sponsorships will come from events.
Joanne Brown: Will planters narrow sidewalks? BID: Will be placed along curb. BID has worked with DOT to identify proper siting. Also making room for coming Union Market and is not putting planters there to facilitate deliveries.
Ian Dutton: Thanks BID for current planters on pedestrian triangles. Is pedestrian safety part of the plan? Defense from out-of-control drivers? BID: Not framing this as bollards, but are creating demarcated space in pedestrian triangles and bump- outs. Will not be there once pedestrian spaces are built out by DDC.
Pauline Blake: Triangle parks are the last piece of project? BID: Yes.
Pauline Blake: Is Barclays Center excluded? BID: Yes. Nothing around arena, nothing in front of Modell’s. Nothing in the triangles, since they already have greenery. Barclays Center also already has bollards, which would be too cluttered with planters.
Bahij Chancey: Urges BID to consider native plantings. Will BID do periodic check to make sure nothing is moved? BID: Yes. Will do periodic maintenance, which will include checks. Site locations also aren’t 100% set in stone and can change based on business feedback. Can be moved as needed.
Q: Will planters be on subway grates? BID: No. Regulations do not allow this. DOT has 8-foot clearance guidelines and Flatbush has wide sidewalks. Even with these there, Flatbush will have excess clearance.
Q: Has BID considered safety from terrorism? BID: BID isn’t trying to frame this as a safety measure, but that is a collateral benefit.
BID estimates $15K/year for plantings watering, budget can sustain that.
Joanna Oltman Smith: Are there seasonal requirements for vendors? BID: Three-season plantings are planned for now. Will add mulch for winter.
MOTION PUT FORTH BY Jerry Armer:
We recommend to the Public Design Commission, DOT and other agencies our wholehearted support of this proposal. The sooner we get to Phase 2 the better. The motion was seconded by Bahij Chancey.

ITEM 2: Presentation and consideration of NYC Department of Transportation’s proposed locations for implementation of the NYC Carshare Pilot Program.
No motion required tonight as this was a mandated City Council program. No vote on the project.
Presented by: Laura MacNeil, DOT. Leroy Branch, DOT.
Branch: DOT is soliciting feedback on locations related to safety, business. “Just because you don’t want it there is not a good reason.”
Eric McClure: DOT came in June to present to committee. Online portal was open to take feedback. CB6 sent out info in July.
Branch: Brad Lander’s portal was open.
MacNeil: Carshare presentation.
Full presentation on DOT website: http://nycdotcarshare.info/sites/default/files/2018-01/BK6_carshare_01.18.18_website.pdf
-   Challenge of continued growth. Congestion. Sustainable means of transportation. -   DOT sees carshare as one of those ways of increasing sustainable modes of transportation. -   Carshare is a service providing access to automobiles for short periods of time. Includes insurance, gas, maintenance, and place to park. -   Currently, most carshare is limited to where there is off-street parking/garages. Leaves voids in map. -   Car2Go offers on-street placement, can be dropped off anywhere in home area. -   NYC is number one market for carshare in country. -   DOT consulted other cities for best practices. -   Members of round-trip carshare companies – up to 32% report giving up a car. One-way programs: 5%. Others put off purchase of personal vehicle. -   Reduction in Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT). -   Offers low-cost, low-hassle way for non-car owners to access cars when needed. -   City Council Local Law 47 and Local Law 50 passed to establish pilot program. Signed into law in March by Mayor de Blasio. -   DOT is proposing two-year pilot program to use permits for carshare parking spaces. Benefits: fast implementation, flexibility. Locations can be moved. Companies that don’t comply with program can have permit revoked.
-   14 zones citywide based on mobility benefits and reduced parking demands. -   Companies required to provide ADA accommodations, incentives for discounted rates for low- income NYers. -   Two parking spaces per site. Designated by sign with curbside regulations and pedestrian-level signs explaining the program. DOT provides spaces, but not the carshare service. That is provided by the carshare companies themselves. -   Carshare companies are responsible for maintenance. Alternate-side parking (ASP) regulations do not apply to carshare spaces. Companies must clean at same frequency of adjacent ASP regulations. -   Companies may relocate cars that do not have permit privileges for the spot. Same process as film shoots. No expense to car owner. NYPD can ticket and tow. -   Park Slope: DOT will site 15 locations (30 spaces) for pilot. -   Red Hook: 5 locations (10 spaces) -   Carroll Gardens: 15 locations (30 spaces) -   Boerum Hill: 10 locations (20 spaces) -   Implementation: Spring 2018. -   Info: nycdotcarshare.info
Discussion:
Elena Santogade: Excited about program, has spoken with neighborhood association, lots of interest among people who have smaller uses for cars.
Q: We double park our cars for ASP, but if that car doesn’t move for ASP, cleaner cannot get around. DOT: We will evaluate during pilot. Corner locations will help allow sanitation to move around cars.
Q: Will DOT be responsible for damage to sidewalk for installation of new signs. DOT: Hoping to use existing pole locations to consolidate signage.
Assembly Member Robert Carroll: concern with giving public property to private corporations. DOT: This will reduce parking demand.
Q: Do you own a car? How did you reach out to those without computers? Is there a time limit to how long someone can use a car? Our block has lost parking spaces to driveways.
Ty Beatty, CB6: Summer outreach, sent to full email list in district. Includes 13,000 people, block associations, electeds. Portal was hosted on website from summer through Thanksgiving. Did more than typical outreach.
Q: Where do you live? CB6: Not something you have to answer.
Comment: Parking has become a challenge. They park everywhere. Put the spots on Court and Smith in metered spots. 2nd Place spots seem too close together. DOT: We will look at 2nd Place.
Q: We are happy to give up spots to those who want it. We have such terror about parking and people being rude. Clinton and Hicks are filled with traffic. We don’t need this. Car2Go is at least fair.
Q: What are measurables that will be put in place so that DOT and public knows it’s working? Do other cities have those specific? Do those other cities have robust transportation systems? DOT: We will evaluate by working with UC Berkeley Transportation Research unit to do surveys of carshare members before and during program. We’re mandating data-sharing. Will look at parking analysis. We believe bringing the pilot will be a valuable service and benefit. Legislation mandates annual data reports.
Q: Is there a vote at end of two-year pilot? DOT: Yes, we will definitely be coming back.
Q: Cheever Place has 8 driveways and 2 hydrants. Would you consider Hicks Street or other locations?
Q: Two spots of concern: Nelson/Clinton is not ideal as spots are already lost to private garages and lots. 4th Place has many driveways. Roughly 10. Will DOT consider relocating those spots? DOT: Will consider these locations. Those spots, however, were suggested through online portal but we will take into consideration.
Q: What measurement is used for spots? DOT: DOT standard of 20 feet per space, 40 total. Car2Go is transitioning out of SmartCars and to larger vehicles. Will be using bigger Mercedes Benz models.
Q: Will Enterprise get to use spots? It already has spots in lots. How is this determined? DOT: Criteria: locations are shared with carshare companies. Companies must meet 20% equity – low- income areas that don’t have existing carshare. Companies can give preferences of locations. No guarantee that Enterprise would get the spot near their existing garage. May have higher preference for it, however.
Q: Why do companies get particular spots? Why not leave it open to all? DOT: Users want to know what you’re getting, who is responsible for providing the service. Provides name recognition, reliability, and accountability. Eric McClure: Adds identifiable responsibility for maintenance.
Rita Lynn: In Barclays Center impact zone people park anywhere. Who is responsible? How quickly will cars be moved? How will they be ticketed? How will people get around double-parked cars during
ASP?
DOT: We will work with NYPD and carshare companies. People can call companies and ask them to relocate the car or call NYPD. DOT will be watching how these options work. We think sizeable percent of people who have cars for occasional use will reconsider transportation options.
Q: I’m looking forward to getting rid of my car and giving a spot to someone who needs it more than me. Can DOT come to CB6 once you have data? Do companies pay for permits? DOT: Yes. OMB will collect a nominal fee from the carshare companies. Just for the issuance of the permit and evaluation of permit application. DOT can assess with data how to better address curbside demand. DOT will come back to CB6.
Jerry Armer: Concern re: signage. You’re establishing territories for these companies plus free advertising. If we’re providing spots, it shouldn’t matter what company. DOT: No one company will have zone.
J. Armer: But even individual spots will be given over to one company.
DOT: We considered this. In other cities opening spots to every company creates confusion, lack of accountability. Comes from best practice of other companies.
J. Armer: Concern that this is fiat designating public space to private company. DOT: In Park Slope we could have six companies competing for spots.
J. Armer: It should be carshare spots period.
Q: My concern is density. If cars are not available and with six companies and 12 – 15 locations, there’s no density. We want to see program succeed but it needs to be substantial. DOT: That is one of the things we hope to learn through this pilot. If we’ll be a victim of our own success. We are using this two-year pilot to assess and learn, and perhaps after a year we will see what’s working and what’s not, we will be coming back to give you more information.
Pauline Blake: When you install these carshare services they will be limited to X number of cars per location? DOT: 40 feet. If carshare company uses SmartCars and can fit three cars in space, they can do that. But most will use two. We will limit the space.
Q: Degraw/Cheever. Where Cheever runs into DeGraw, there is no parking because of Key Food trucks, plus seven houses with recessed carports designed for two cars each. Plus there are three hydrants. This specific site may need to be revisited. DOT: Thank you. We will note that.
Q: I would like to see that we’re taking trips that would otherwise be taken by private car be switched to carshare and not trips that would otherwise be taken on transit or bike. At program level we should not chase transit riders as customers. Also, cleanliness of spots and parking enforcement – can 311 system and app accept carshare space complaints? DOT: We are working with 311. Plan to put in place means of reporting poorly maintained spaces. Blocked space notification. DOT will look at 311 data. We are also interested in seeing if this increases VMT in city or provides decreases.
Joanna Oltman Smith: This will reduce the number of car trips in NYC. Will make cost of car use very apparent to users. Wondering about exclusivity of spaces. Any discussion with EDC of making interim spots accessible to all companies? Possible benefits to making it more generic. Could maintenance responsibilities be assigned by size of fleet?
Q: Concern re: DeGraw Street, Cheever Place. Another issue is the 76th Precinct on Union between Henry and Hicks. Concern with three [Citi] bike locations in two-block radius. Carroll between Henry and Hicks has heavy parking demand. Why don’t you have all these spots on Hicks when there are so many of them? DOT: Hicks is right by the BQE, so you only have one side of the street next to where people live. The highway takes away half the people who might find that location convenient. Did not meet the requirement to be an accessible location.
Q: What about homeowners who do renovations and need a dumpster. DOT: Contractors, utilities must work with DOT permitting office. DOT can make alternate arrangement with carshare companies to suspend or move location. We also have emergency contingency plans.
Q: Do signs have contact info? Phone number for company? DOT: Yes. On pedestrian-level signage they will have information, how to sign up, 800 numbers, etc.

Consideration of a request for expeditious historic landmark designation for two buildings located at 236 and 238 President Street (between Court/Clinton Streets), Carroll Gardens Historic District.
The residence at 236 President Street has sold to a developer with the intention of demolishing it and erecting a 6 story building. Concern that rezoning 238 President to a R6A will cause future development problems. City Planning set a 74 foot height in 2009. Nine years later fears have materialized. Application has been sent to FDC that both buildings be considered for individual Landmark status.
The Community Board cannot take a vote on this. A request should be made to Landmarks to look into the situation. If Landmarks Preservation Commission decides to designate or calendar the properties it will come back to the committee as a ULURP. The timing is critical as the closing on the property is due to take place on March 1. If LPC supports, the Department of Buildings can hold off on demolition until LPC makes a decision
The historic significance of the properties: Both properties were bought in 1897 by Elmira Christian. 238 President Street, the larger of the two properties became a Home for Deaconesses. The smaller of the properties, 236 President Street became a memorial to her husband as the Hans Christian Kindergarten. Until 1974 they were a single property, at which time, they were split and sold separately to different owners. 236 became the first Spanish Methodist Church.
The Coop President agreed that it made sense to hold off on the closing as there is value to individual landmark status. He is sending a letter of support to the Landmarks Preservation Committee asking for their review.
The Landmarks/Land Use committee of CB6 agreed unanimously to the request for review of the properties by the Landmarks Preservation Commission.

Presenter: Melissa Ortiz, Congresswoman Nydia M. Velasquez’s office.
This new bill is intended to bring back the “Superfund Tax”, repealed in 1995, which allows for government to tax industrial polluters (some industries had been dropped from the initial 1980 list) to fund remediation of “orphaned” sites. In addition, the bill would create assistance through SBA for loans and tax deductions, to assist businesses forced to relocate due to superfund cleanup.    PUBLIC HEARING regarding an application to the Department of City Planning by PHD Summit LLC pursuant to Sections 197-c and 201 of the New York City Charter for an amendment to the Zoning Map, Section No. 16a, changing Lots 48-52 on Block 352 (AKA 55-63 Summit Street) from an M1-1 District to an R6B District to permit development of a 5-story, 14- unit residential building. Department of City Planning ULURP No. C 170047 ZMK.
The Attorney for the owners of the property presented on their behalf and, as he explained, they regretted that could not attend as they had to attend a funeral in California.
The applicants attorney stated that the intent was to rezone a M1-1 District to an R6B District to permit development of a 5-story, 14 unit residential building and that it was a typo that the notice read “12 Unit”.
This property had been left out of previous re-zonings in 2007 & 2009 and that the applicant felt that had left it as an in anomalous and incompatible zoning for the lots.
To comply with Mandatory Inclusionary Housing (MIH)1 this property will include 25% of the square footage to be affordable which amounts to 3 to 4 affordable units.
The applicant stated that they had also considered adding community space but that option was not financially viable and the building envelop would be limited to 50 feet in height.
For the affordable rates- based on the Area Median Income (AMI) would be as follows:
-    At 40% of the AMI a studio would have a monthly rent of $475, a 1- bedroom $600, 2 bedroom $736 and a 3 bedroom would cost $843. -    At 60% of the AMI a studio would have a monthly rent of $760, a 1- bedroom $962, 2 bedroom $1165 and a 3 bedroom would cost $1338.
The applicant also stated that there was, in the unlikely event that they do not build the affordable housing on site they have agreed to a "community benefit agreement" in which they would make a $3 million donation to the Brooklyn Community Foundation.
One member of the community came to speak to this application and was opposed to it.
Daniel Ordower who lives at 53 Summit Street also stated he spoke on behalf of 51 & 49 summit Street as well.
The community resident said that there is support for something being built in the currently unoccupied space but that he, and his neighbors, believed it should not be, what they see as, an out of context development. He also stated that his interactions & responsiveness with the developer have not been satisfactory with issues such as cracked sidewalks. He also mentioned the concern for too much shade being cast over the low rise Columbia Waterfront district.
There were some question about the placement of the utilities and whether they’d be placed on the roof due to its proximity to the flood zone.
Councilman Brad Lander arrived and spoke in favor of this application and the MIH component of the deal and, in the unlikely event they are unable to build the affordable, that 3 million would go to a non-profit organization in the community.
Committee Chair Peter Fleming then explained that after the next item, also a land use public hearing, the committee and public would be allowed to gives its opinion and ask questions of the applicant.
1 Refers to zoning text changes made in 2016 that requires   zoning actions include various levels depending on unique factors, that a share of new housing to be permanently affordable.

PUBLIC HEARING regarding an application to the Department of City Planning by the New York Police Department and the New York City Department of Citywide Administrative Services, pursuant to Section 197-a of the New York City Charter, for the acquisition of property located at Lot 250 of Block 612 (AKA 700 Columbia Street for continued used as a vehicular evidence storage facility. The committee also asked about community facilities in the surrounding area to which the applicant was not sure of their locations but cited that this can include private businesses such as doctors’ offices.
Along with this, the committee asked about whether or not this would be LEED2 would it be a “passive”3 development?
The applicant stated that this may not be possible but was certain every possible effort to be environmentally sound will be made.
2 Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED) is a rating system devised by the United States Green Building Council (USGBC) to evaluate the environmental performance of a building and encourage market transformation towards sustainable design.
3 “A Passive House is a building, for which thermal comfort (ISO 7730) can be achieved solely by post-heating or post-cooling of the fresh air mass, which is required to achieve sufficient indoor air quality conditions – without the need for additional recirculation of air.”
The committee then asked about the developer’s history of redevelopment as opposed to ground up building. The applicants’ attorney indicated that they have been involved with both through New York City and Brooklyn.

January 27, 2025
OPENING REMARKS
The meeting began with an introduction, confirming quorum, and welcoming committee members both in person and via Zoom. A document prepared by the Red Hook Business Alliance was shared, aimed at assisting businesses in preparing for ICE-related incidents and ensuring the safety of workers and customers. This document, created in collaboration with the ACLU, was made available for circulation.
524 COURT STREET — NEW GREEK RESTAURANT (APPLICANT: ANTONIA VITALIUS)
Antonia Vitalius, along with her sister, presented their application for a new on-premise liquor license for a Greek restaurant at the location previously occupied by another business for 16 years. The restaurant will serve Greek cuisine with a family-friendly atmosphere, offering lunch, dinner, and weekend brunch. They plan to have 16 seats on a sidewalk cafe, which is currently in the permitting process.
The applicants emphasized their intention to create a neighborhood restaurant with a focus on quality food and reasonable prices. A suggestion was made by the committee to reduce the number of seats to comply with building code regulations. The applicants agreed to review the floor plan and make adjustments as needed.
The applicants outlined their hours of operation, mentioning a proposed closing time around midnight on weekends. They agreed to revise the hours to ensure compliance and will send an updated version via email. The bar program will feature high-end liquors and Greek wines, with a focus on sophisticated cocktails paired with the restaurant's food offerings. The applicants shared their experience in managing a hotel restaurant in Long Island City and explained the reason for staying open later, to provide customers with an alternative to fast food after hours.
A motion to approve the application was made. It was seconded, and all committee members present voted in favor.
ALSO HEARD
117 Columbia Street, 497 5th Avenue and 210 Flatbush Avenue were also on the agenda. The minutes on file do not record the presentations, discussion or motions for these three applications.
CLOSING REMARKS
The committee thanked the applicants for their presentations and noted the importance of ensuring all businesses comply with relevant regulations regarding liquor licenses, seating capacity, and hours of operation. The committee also reminded applicants to submit any necessary amendments or updates to their applications.
Meeting adjourned.

1. 5th Ave Safety plan
No resolution, since it was just a presentation in the early stages from DOT.
We did ask DOT to:
- conduct direct intercept studies of people on 5th Ave asking them how they arrived on the avenue (mode share: walking, biking, transit, driving) so that DOT isn't solely asking merchants for how they think customers arrive. - drop the speed limit on 5th Ave to 15 or 20 mph in accordance with Sammy's Law. - study how much of the automobile and truck traffic on 5th Ave originates or ends within the neighborhood and how much is cut-through traffic - do vehicular and bike counts in multiple months, not just november. (personally, I didn't feel this was necessary, but one community member, not a committee member, asked for it) - explore additional loading zones away from corners so as to preserve hardened daylighting and pedestrian safety.
2. GAP Sidewalk plan
Motion: Jerry
Second: Mandi: The transportation committee of Community Board 6 highly supports the renovation of the sidewalk and the installation of a grass ribbon on Plaza Street East and urge DOT to complete the project as soon as possible.
3. Court Street:
Motion: Jerry
2nd: Madeline
The transportation committee of Community Board 6 thanks DOT for its plan for Court Street. We support the project and urge DOT to put the new design into effect this summer. Additionally, we ask that DOT include additional improvements: - The installation of hard infrastructure (bike corrals, planters, boulders) on pedestrian islands to prevent illegal parking, blocked crosswalks and blocked sightlines. - Additional daylighting on side streets with hard infrastructure. - Harder bike lane barriers such as low concrete curbs instead of plastic Kwik Curbs. - A lower speed limit of 15 - 20 mph on the corridor in accordance with Sammy's Law. - Leading Pedestrian Intervals (LPI's) at all intersections where they don't already exist.
- Extended loading zone hours until at least 8 PM to accommodate Amazon, FedEx, UPS and other later deliveries.
We also ask that: - DOT follow up with NYPD for additional parking enforcement in the period immediately post installation. - DOT study the potential for speed cushions on Court Street after project installation. - DOT study and come back to the committee with a plan for a northbound projected bike lane on Clinton Street.
4. Flatbush Ave Bus Lane
Motion: Jerry
2nd: Anna
Motion to approve the the plan as presented with the urging that it be installed as quickly as possible.
A recommendation:
The Transportation Committee of Community Board 6 calls on Mayor Adams and NYPD Commissioner Tisch to end the crackdown on cyclists. Issuing criminal summonses to cyclists — for infractions that would earn motorists a mere traffic ticket — is not only unfair, but risks exposing the largely immigrant delivery cyclist workforce to law enforcement in ways that could result in deportation without due process. At a time when immigrants are under threat from the federal government and due process rights are being denied, the police should not target essential workers and our fellow New Yorkers, no matter when they arrived in the city. While not condoning illegal or dangerous behavior, we do not believe that such infractions should be subject to criminal summonses.
In addition to calling on the city to end this practice, we ask that the mayor work with the City Council to advance existing proposals to regulate app companies so that they are forced to classify delivery cyclists not as independent contractors but as employees with full benefits and standardized, legal equipment and vehicles for doing their jobs.

addition of a rear deck and modifications to rear windows, with limited visibility from the public way. The application was approved unanimously. A similar approval at 30 Sterling Place was cited as precedent.

Elected Officials & Representatives Council Member Shahana Hanif addressed the Board regarding a recent power outage that affected approximately 2,000 residents, some of whom were without heat for up to five days. Noted that 3K and Pre-K application deadline is February 27, and a survey is available regarding the Nelson Street rezoning in Red Hook.
Daniel Abramson, representing Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso, reported that more than 50 new applicants applied to CB6 this cycle. Capital funding applications are due February

A representative for Assembly Member Robert Carroll announced a Department of Finance assistance event on March 5 focused on property tax assistance and SCRIE/DRIE benefits. NYC Connects senior services resources are available through the district office.
A representative for State Senator Andrew Gounardes reported that the CREEP Act, addressing online harassment, passed in the Senate and that advocacy continues for the NY for All Act. Tax preparation services are available through the office.
A representative for U.S. Representative Dan Goldman reported on a recent ICE oversight hearing, updates to Stonewall National Monument legislation, and the securing of World Trade Center Health Program funding through 2040.
State Senator Zellnor Myrie announced a February 15 event at Weeksville Heritage Center, including a screening of the documentary “Everlasting.”
A representative for NYC Comptroller Mark Levine summarized findings from the annual MWBE report, noting that five percent of city contracts were awarded to minority- and women-owned businesses and that certified MWBEs receive smaller average contract values compared to non-certified firms.
A representative for Assembly Member Jo Anne Simon reported that a community discussion regarding the Court Street bike lane has concluded and that requests have been submitted to NYCDOT for traffic studies.

Andrea, local business owner, expressed concerns about customer access and economic impacts associated with the Court Street bike lane. The speaker stated that multiple businesses have reduced staff and that customers have reported difficulty accessing stores due to parking and traffic conditions. The speaker also described a recent NYCDOT meeting as productive and raised concerns regarding funding sources of Transportation Alternatives.
Michelle raised safety concerns about the placement of an electric vehicle charging station in relation to the new bike lane, noting that its current location could obstruct cyclists. NYCDOT is reportedly evaluating relocation options.
Aurelia announced that applications for the Summer Youth Employment Program are open through February 27 for youth ages 14 to 24. The program includes project-based learning for younger participants and paid employment opportunities for older youth, as well as mentorship and workforce development programming.

LANDMARKS/LAND USE/HOUSING COMMITTEE
March 7,2026@ 250 Baltic Street
Attendees
Dave Jerry Lena (remote) Kathleen Daniel Maddie Laurie Quorum streak continues,
Landmarks 152 Atlantic Avenue – Application for a Certificate of Appropriateness for a Rooftop Addition in the Cobble Hill Historic District
Presented by Richard Grisaru, the project architect. New skylights, stair bulkhead, deck, and railings are being added at the building roof. The height of the rear building wall is being extended upwards to accommodate the new supporting roof structure.
Questions were asked about the visibility of the proposed work from Clinton Street, north of Atlantic Avenue (Brooklyn Heights Historic District). Discussion about the setback distance of front railing and FDNY access. The property owner pointed out that the portion of deck closest to Atlantic Avenue affords a view of Manhattan.
Community members who live on Union Street expressed support of the project since visibility from Clinton Street is primarily of only55 railing.
Jerry: Motion to conditionally approve if railing facing Atlantic is set back an additional 2’. Maddie: Seconded.
Five votes in favor. Two abstentions.
Motion passes.
Land Use 175 Third Street - GSD-175 Third Street Certification & Authorization to modify bulk, Certification of a Waterfront Public Access Area (WPAA), and Authorization to modify WPAA requirements to facilitate a new 28-story, 869,000 sf (6.2 FAR) mixed-use development, including 740,000 sf residential use (1,071 Dwelling Units); 129,600 sf of commercial uses, and 28,000 sf of WPAA on property.
Presented by Tavros Charney development team; BIG, the design architect; and Field Operations, the landscape architect. The focus of the presentation was on widening 2nd Street access, park amenities, architectural features, courtyard, and anchor retail space. 85,000 sf of zoning floor area [ZFA] is being acquired from Powerhouse Arts to add 100 dwelling units; this requires modification of bulk as per City of Yes guidelines.
Lengthy discussion with committee, which included the following comments: - Presentation neglected to distinguish between “as-of-right” bulk and proposed bulk modifications due to proposed acquisition of PHA ZFA. - In previous discussions, developers presented that the total number of units would be 1,000, including 100 added by acquiring PHA ZFA. - In previous discussions and emails dating back to last summer, the committee requested that for its support, the developer must provide public bathrooms, all additional units meet affordability requirements, and that it leverage its purchase of the ZFA from PHA to ensure that the non-profit’s promenade is opened to the public. The developer has declined each of these requests, and repeatedly referenced the limitations placed on it by underwriting. - When asked if there could be any increase in the number of affordable units beyond the 25% MIH threshold at 60% AMI, the developer said due to underwriting no additional units could be affordable. - Committee expressed frustration with minimal apparent effort made to negotiate public access of the promenade with PHA. - The developer confirmed that no money has been paid yet to PHA. - The committee suggested an option where the developer could pay for required upgrades to the promenade to meet WPAA requirements. PHA could use a portion of its incoming funds to amend its DOB paperwork and file for a change of use, initiating the indemnification it has publicly indicated was a sticking point. - Developer was told by PHA that if its current use, as listed on its TCO (Temp. Certificate of Occupancy) was changed, the current programs would not be allowed. The committee disagreed with this since its current primary use is industrial and manufacturing, while its programming is legal under other uses as defined in the resolution. - A committee member expressed reservations on the quality of construction at Union Channel, another property developed by Tavros Charney, raising concerns with the accuracy of the 3rd Street presentation and verbal representations. The developer objected to this characterization of its building. - Given the large sum that the developer will be paying to PHA for its floor area, the committee advised the developer to use its financial leverage to negotiate with PHA on behalf of the community to open its promenade.
Community members asked about access to public transit and a mix of affordable units. The bus stop on the corner of Third Avenue will remain and the mix is required to meet the mix of market rate units. One community member expressed support of the project since it adds more housing.
Daniel: Motion to conditionally approve authorization if, a) the PHA promenade is opened to the public as a direct result of the ZFA acquisition, and b) 30% of the 1,071 units meet the affordability requirements for 60% AMI. Jerry: Seconded.
Six votes in favor. One abstention.
Motion passes.
End of meeting.

I. Adoption of Minutes The meeting was called to order at 6:43 p.m. upon confirmation of quorum. Minutes from the February 11, 2026,  meeting were approved unanimously. It was noted that Peter Fleming’s name was missing from the minutes.
II. Chairperson’s Report Chairperson Eric McClure was not present at the meeting. 1st Vice Chair David Briggs led the meeting in his absence.
III. District Manager’s Report District Manager Mike Racioppo announced the following upcoming meetings: Human Services, Sustainability – Tuesday, March 17th, 6:30 pm @ Principles GI Coffee House Transportation, Parks & Public Infrastructure – Wednesday, March 18th, 6:30 pm @ 250 Baltic Street Business Affairs & Licenses – Monday, March 23rd, 6:30 pm @ 250 Baltic Street Land Use, Landmarks & Housing – Thursday, March 26th, 6:30 pm @ 250 Baltic Street Full Board – Wednesday, April 8th, 6:30 pm @ Van Alen Institute Mike presented an analysis of the 14,000 lots within Community District 6 and announced that this information is now available on the CB6 website. Mike also explained that the CB6 Land Use Guide (available on the website) now includes a glossary of land use terminology. Finally, Mike presented an analysis of 311 complaints in the district focused on February 2026. During this time period, the top complaint category was “illegal parking” (with 31.8% of approximately 4,000 complaints). A six-year trend report is now available on the website. IV. Committee Reports
A. Landmarks, Land Use & Housing 152 Atlantic Avenue David Briggs presented an application for a Certificate of Appropriateness for a rooftop addition. A motion to approve the application with the condition that the railing facing Atlantic Avenue be set back an additional two feet was approved by the committee with two abstentions. The committee had a quorum, so no floor motion was required. The motion was approved by the board, with Daniel Kummer and David Briggs abstaining. 175 3rd Street David Briggs presented a motion to approve the certification to transfer development rights at 175 3rd Street. He explained that this project involves 971 units permitted as-of-right. Additionally, Charney Companies and Tavros plan to acquire zoning floor area (ZFA) from the neighboring Powerhouse Arts, which would enable construction of 100 additional units. This transfer of floor area from a landmarked building is allowed under the City of Yes zoning changes and the request before the Community Board concerns modifications to building bulk. Under City of Yes changes, this application will go directly to the City Planning Commission (CPC), bypassing the local council member and Borough President, with a CPC hearing scheduled for March 17. David explained that the developer did not clearly indicate the difference between the as-of-right envelope and the requested modifications, but noted that one of the two proposed towers would exceed the zoning envelope. The project includes a waterfront park as required under the Waterfront Access Guidelines. The proposal also includes widening “2nd Street” (an unmapped street between the building and Powerhouse Arts). No parking is included in the proposal, which is permissible under City of Yes rules. The committee has made three requests to the developer: 1) 100% affordability for new units, 2) inclusion of public bathrooms, and 3) negotiation with Powerhouse Arts to improve promenade access along the Gowanus Canal. David noted that the developer is paying Powerhouse Arts approximately $15-20 million for the ZFA, which he argued should allow funds for Powerhouse Arts to build a public promenade. He also argued that a change in use designation would allow Powerhouse Arts to benefit from city indemnification for the promenade, which should make the effort feasible. After six months of discussions initiated by the committee, the developer has not acted on these requests and has not engaged Powerhouse Arts in discussions of promenade accessibility or improvements. During the committee discussion, members opposed rejecting a project that would include 230 affordable units. As a result, the committee moved to approve the certification to transfer development rights and bulk modification, with the conditions that 1) the Powerhouse Arts promenade be opened to the public as a direct result of the ZFA and 2) 30% of the 1,071 units meet affordability requirements, averaging at 60% AMI (under Mandatory Inclusionary Housing Option 1). The committee approved the motion unanimously, with a quorum present and one abstention. During the full board discussion, Mandi Spishak-Thomas asked what the impact of a no vote would be, and Pauline Blake asked whether the motion would slow the project to allow more time for discussion. While project approvals are expedited under City of Yes, CB6 will submit their resolution and can argue their case before the CPC vote. Catherine Vaughan expressed support for this approach to avoid standing in the way of housing development. She argued that the board could include an addendum to the resolution showing the developer the value of investing in the promenade. Daniel Kummer confirmed that these points can be communicated in the letter to the agency characterizing our vote. The full board vote approved the motion with Karyn Broughton, Mandi Spishak-Thomas, and Reema Sharma voting no and Pauline Blake and Tiffany Reid abstaining. B. The Business Permits and Licenses Committee
47 5th Avenue (former site of “That Bar”) Mandi Spishak-Thomas presented this liquor license application establishment for a new women’s sports-themed bar at 47 5th Avenue with no outdoor space proposed. The motion was approved unanimously in committee with a quorum. The motion was passed by the full board with no abstentions.
C. The Transportation, Parks & Public Infrastructure Resolution to Introduce a District-Wide 20 MPH Slow Zone Tony Melone presented the following resolution: Recognizing CB6’s commitment to safer streets and support for Sammy’s Law, we recommend that NYC DOT institute a district-wide 20 MPH slow zone on all applicable streets, and adjust signal timing to reflect the new limit, with camera enforcement. We also call for the adoption of a citywide speed limit of 20mph on all applicable streets. Tony explained that Safe Streets and Make McGuinness Safe were presented at the last committee meeting. He explained that the district-wide speed limit would apply only to streets with no more than two lanes in one direction, and that similar motions have been passed by Brooklyn Community Board 1 and Queens Community Board 2. The committee passed the resolution unanimously with one abstention for cause. Marc Torrence noted that while the reduction from 25 MPH to 20 MPH seems small, it significantly improves survivability in crashes. Tony noted that enforcement typically begins 10 MPH over the limit, meaning tickets would start at 30 MPH. The resolution passed unanimously, with Pauline Blake abstaining. Tony also highlighted that the CB6 website now has a traffic safety request form for specific improvements. He explained that the next committee meeting includes a discussion with NYCDOT on unsafe driving on Columbia Street, reopening the Carroll Street Bridge, daylighting initiatives, slow zones, and a northbound bike route to complement the Court Street bike lane. V.New/Other Business Daniel Kummer noted that the Atlantic Yards redevelopment public engagement process will hold its fourth and final workshop on March 19th, including a report on the process and a presentation from the new development team. Scott Middleton noted that Prospect Park Alliance invited CB6 representatives to attend the groundbreaking ceremony for the Vale restoration on March 16th. VI. Updates from Elected Officials and their Representatives
Dan Abramson (Office of Brooklyn Borough President Reynoso) thanked those who participated in CB interviews and noted that CB6 had 75 new applicants this year, plus reapplicants. He encouraged those not selected to serve on the board to remain engaged. Sean Gurl (Office of Assemblymember Carroll) noted that the State Assembly passed its one-house budget, which included an increase in library construction funding from $34M to $71M statewide, as well as a proposed $200M to assist the New York Power Authority in meeting Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act goals. Talia Hoch (Office Assemblymember Jo Anne Simon) also presented a one-house budget update, noting that it includes a $4M student loan forgiveness program for public interest lawyers and Foundation Aid reforms to better account for students in the shelter system and non-English speakers. She noted that representatives of the Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings were available through her office to discuss outstanding tickets and violations. Maia Yedin (Office of Senator Andrew Gounardes) noted upcoming services from the Senator’s office, including tax preparation assistance, an unclaimed funds event (March 25th at the Gowanus office), a visit from the OMNY van on March 30th, and a document shredding & e-recycling event on May 9th in the Bay Ridge office. Krista Reilly (Office of Senator Zellnor Myrie) invited constituents to an all-girls basketball clinic on March 21st hosted with Brooklyn Basketball Training Center. Melanie Kruvelis (Office of Councilmember Avilés) informed the board about a NYC Know Your Rights Act heard in committee on Monday that requires city agencies to post sanctuary policies publicly. She also noted upcoming budget hearings on sanitation, economic Development, environmental protection, waterfronts, and parks. Paul Leguerre (Office of Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez) noted an event on March 23rd at the Brooklyn Public Library Central Branch highlighting women in sustainable fashion. Jacqueline Nieschmidt (Office of Councilmember Hanif) highlighted a hearing with DOT pushing for pedestrian signals and daylighting, and celebrated the installation of a new traffic signal installed at Smith & Douglass.

Presenter: Derek Walker, Brooklyn Borough Commissioner's Office Deck: PEC Overview 2026 09 17 BK CB 6.pdf, sent 9/17
Since 2022, lithium-ion batteries in NYC have resulted in more than:
- 900 fires
- 400 injuries
- 30 deaths
DOT pilot tested battery-swapping cabinets in 2024 with delivery workers who rely on e-bikes (100+ delivery workers)
- Popular, improved fire safety, reduced at-home charging
- Willingness to pay for service
Solution: $3 million in state grant funding to put 25 battery charging cabinets
Bike swapping cabinets are a safer alternative to charge e-bike batteries
- Certified to UL Standards, weather- and theft-proof with fire safety features
- Vendor will charge fee and be responsible for site maintenance and cleanliness
Sites were identified where the most deliveries are taking place and took into account congregation, clear path, fire safety, and appearance issues
CB6 locations:
- Dean St and 5th Ave, NW Corner
- Court St and 1st Pl, NE Corner

1.  Are we racing against private sector with this (e.g., do private charging docks already exist)?

3.  Will there be a DOT representative to remove an old battery and if it's replaced is it given to that particular delivery person for nothing?
1.  Answer: You do not have to be a delivery person to be a part of this program. If there's a bad battery, the company will take the battery out and replace it. No one owns anything, but it's a rental service.

1.  Answer: We see some people already using these vendors and they do have two batteries. We want to continue to expand the network so they don't need to rely on the extra spare at home. Eventually, there will be so many they won't have to charge a spare at home.

3. Low Traffic Neighborhoods [notes from August meeting]
6th Ave cut-through traffic; school-based pilot approach. - Catherine Vaughan (absent) proposed the blocks west of PS 282 and west of PS 39, using the Open Plans Neighborhood Needs Assessment Dashboard
From Catherine Vaughan - I've had a few conversations with David Scatterday, who built this amazing new tool for Open Plans, the Neighborhood Needs Assessment Dashboard. I highly recommend you check it out—it allows you to look at Census tracts across the city and filter on different variables to determine where a low-traffic neighborhood (or any types of street redesigns/treatments, etc.) might be needed. For example, you might toggle the filters to look for neighborhoods under a certain median income, over a certain pollutant level, with a higher than X percentage of people who commute by public transit, etc. — and it will show you which specific neighborhoods fit these criteria. You can overlay data on schools, crashes, Community Boards, etc.
I gave him some context on the 6th Ave cut-through traffic, and we used his tool to identify a few areas where we might pilot LTNs or, at the least, a few diverters. We should speak more with Open Plans about this (curious what Jackson Chabot said, for example), but David agreed that our suggestion of an incremental approach, starting with schools because they're likely to get the most buy-in, makes sense.
Here's a map I created with the tool, with two neighborhoods highlighted as places to potentially divert the cut-through traffic on 6th Ave: the blocks west of PS 282, and the blocks west of PS 39. The filters I used included:
- Median income <$200K
- % residents who primarily use public transit to get to work >50% (note: these %s are low / don't add to 100 because non-commuters are counted)
- % residents who primarily use car to get to work <20% (note: these %s are low / don't add to 100 because non-commuters are counted)
- Car-free households >40%
- PM2.5 mean pollution concentration level (μg/m³) >6.8
